title: An Introduction to R
text:
Welcome
This is a book about getting an answer out of a dataset, written for people who have never programmed. It began as the week-one worksheet for SPH5421 at the NUS Saw Swee Hock School of Public Health: a few pages of base R with gaps to fill in, no answer key, and, I should own up to this, code that had never been run from top to bottom. Students would hit an error on question four and have no way of knowing whether the error was theirs or mine.
Everything you see here has been run. The outputs on these pages, the plots, the warnings, the place where R prints NaN instead of a number, are all the real thing, produced by the code shown directly above them. If a number in the prose disagrees with the number in the output block, the prose is wrong and I would like to know about it.

title: An Introduction to R
text:
Who this is for
Public health masters students, mostly. If you have used Stata or SPSS through a menu, or done your analysis in Excel and felt the spreadsheet slipping out from under you around row 4,000, you are the reader I had in mind. No programming background is assumed. I do assume you have seen a mean and a median before, and that you know roughly what an epidemic curve is.
By the time you reach the end you should be able to read a CSV into R and form an opinion about whether to trust it; turn cumulative counts into daily ones without silently losing the first day; find missing values, understand why they are missing, and decide what to do rather than letting R decide for you; group a dataset by month and summarise it; build a figure you would be willing to put in front of a supervisor; and write a small function so that the same calculation done six times is written once. The last chapter asks you to produce a monthly situation report from the raw file, with no scaffolding at all.
You will also, and this matters more than the syntax, learn to read an error message.

title: An Introduction to R
text:
The data
One dataset, all the way through. It is Singapore’s 2020 COVID-19 record: 345 daily rows running from 22 January to 31 December 2020, with 13 columns. Cumulative confirmed cases and deaths, the three Oxford government-response indices, and the six Google Community Mobility series. It ends with 58,599 confirmed cases and 29 recorded deaths.
The file was assembled from the COVID-19 Data Hub (Guidotti & Ardia, 2020), which in turn draws on Singapore’s Ministry of Health, the Oxford COVID-19 Government Response Tracker, and Google’s Community Mobility Reports. Appendix B documents every column, including where it is missing and why.
I chose it because it is small enough to look at whole and broken in all the ordinary ways. The death column has 59 leading missing values, and when it finally starts it starts at 2 rather than at 1, so the obvious way of turning it into daily deaths recovers 27 of the 29. Every mobility column is missing its first 24 days, because Google’s baseline period had not finished when the series begins. The case counts are cumulative, so a plot of the raw column is a line that only ever goes up, and it tells you almost nothing about when things were bad. And there is a day in August with 908 cases sitting in a month whose median is 91, which is a reporting artefact rather than a wave. Every one of those turns up later as a lesson.
Here is where the book is going. The code below is the sort of thing you will be writing by the end of Part IV, and none of it needs to make sense yet.

covid <- read_covid()

covid %>%
  arrange(date) %>%
  mutate(daily_cases = confirmed - lag(confirmed, default = 0)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = date, y = daily_cases)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(
    title = "The shape of Singapore's 2020",
    subtitle = "Peak of 1,426 new cases on 20 April, during the circuit breaker",
    x = NULL,
    y = "New cases"
  )



New confirmed cases per day, computed from the cumulative column in the raw file. The single tall bar in August is the 908-case reporting day, not a second wave.



read_covid() is a shortcut defined in the book’s setup file so that every chapter starts from the same place. The import chapter unwraps it and shows you the read_csv() call inside.

title: An Introduction to R
text:
Exercises, hints and solutions
Exercises sit inside the chapters, near the material they exercise. They state a goal in words. They do not give you a code skeleton with holes in it, because filling in holes teaches you to fill in holes.
Under most exercises there is a collapsed hint. Open it when you are stuck in the sense of not knowing which function to reach for. Under that, a link to the worked solution in Appendix A. The solutions are complete and commented, and they are deliberately one click away rather than upside down at the bottom of the page. You are an adult. If you want the answer you can have it. You will learn more if you have made a real attempt first, and you will know perfectly well whether you have.






SPH5421 students: where to stop



For the live session, work Parts I to IV: everything up to and including Showing it to someone. That is the material we will use in the rest of the module, and it is about as much as anyone absorbs in one sitting.
The whole book is roughly five and a half hours if you type the code rather than skim it. Parts V and VI, on writing your own functions and the capstone, are there for the week after, or for when you meet a problem that needs them. Nobody expects you to arrive having finished the book.

title: An Introduction to R
text:
How to use this book
Type the code. Do not paste it. I know that sounds like an instruction from someone who enjoys watching people suffer, so here is the reasoning: pasting moves characters from one window to another and teaches your hands nothing. Typing makes you notice that aes() is inside ggplot() and not next to it, and it makes you produce your own typos in a safe setting where the fix is on the screen above. The error you generate from your own missing bracket in week one is the error you will recognise instantly at 11pm in month six. There is a copy button on every code block on this site. Use it when you are re-running something for the fifth time, not the first.
Read error messages to the end. Beginners tend to see red text, assume it is undifferentiated punishment, and start changing things at random. R’s errors are usually two or three lines and the useful line is rarely the first. The tidyverse ones in particular put the diagnosis under a bullet several lines down, along with a suggestion for what to do about it. When you search for a message, paste it in exactly as R printed it, but delete your own object names first, because nobody else on the internet has a variable called apr_data2.
Run everything as you read. When a chunk produces something, look at it before scrolling on. Then change one thing and run it again. Change the 100 to 50, swap mean for median, remove the na.rm = TRUE and see what breaks. This book is arranged so that breaking it is cheap.
Chapters render in separate R sessions and each one is self-contained, so you can restart R whenever you like and pick up at the top of a chapter. That is a habit worth having anyway, and the good-practice chapter explains why.

title: An Introduction to R
text:
Corrections
Every page has an “Edit this page” link that goes to its source on GitHub, and there is an issue tracker. A wrong number in a teaching resource propagates into other people’s work, so corrections are welcome and I would rather hear about one than not.

title: 1  Getting set up
text:
1.1 R first, then RStudio
R is the language and the engine. It is what actually adds the numbers up. RStudio is a front end: an editor, a console, a plot viewer and a file browser stitched together into one window. RStudio does no statistics of its own. When it starts, it goes looking for an R installation on your machine and talks to it.
Which is why R goes on first. If you launch RStudio with no R installed, it tells you it cannot find one and refuses to start, and you now have two problems to debug instead of none. Install R, confirm it exists, then install RStudio.
R comes from CRAN, at https://cran.r-project.org. Pick your operating system from the links at the top.
On macOS you will be offered two installers and you have to choose. If your Mac has an Apple silicon chip (M1 and later), take the one whose filename contains arm64. If it is an older Intel Mac, take the x86_64 one. Apple menu, then “About This Mac”, tells you which you have. Installing the wrong one is not fatal but it is slow and it will bite you later when a package needs compiling.
On Windows, follow “Download R for Windows”, then “base”, then the big download link. You may see a mention of Rtools on that page. You do not need it for this book. It is for compiling packages from source, which nothing here asks you to do.
On Linux, CRAN has per-distribution instructions and you should follow those rather than whatever your distribution’s default r-base package happens to be, because distribution repositories are often several versions behind.
This book needs R 4.1 or newer. Anything from the last few years is fine.
RStudio comes from Posit, at https://posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop/. You want RStudio Desktop, the free open-source version. There is a paid tier and a server edition. Neither is relevant to you.
Once both are installed, open RStudio and never open R directly again. R does have its own bare window, RGui on Windows and R.app on macOS, and it is austere in a way that helps nobody. Leave it alone.

title: 1  Getting set up
text:
1.2 The four panes
RStudio’s window is divided into four, and the first time you see it there is a lot going on. Here is what each one is for.
The Console, bottom left, is R itself. The > prompt is R waiting for you to say something. Type 1 + 1 there and press Enter and you get an answer. Everything that runs in this book runs through this pane, one way or another.
The Source pane, top left, is where your scripts live. It is empty when you first launch, because you have no scripts. Go to File, New File, R Script and it appears, pushing the console down into the lower half. This is where you will spend most of your time.
The Environment pane, top right, lists the objects R currently holds in memory: your data frames, your variables, anything you have created. It is the answer to “did that actually work?”. If you read a CSV and nothing shows up here, the read did not happen. The History tab next to it keeps a log of everything you have typed.
The bottom right pane is a stack of tabs: Files for browsing your folders, Plots for anything you draw, Packages for what is installed, Help for documentation, and Viewer for things like rendered Quarto pages. You will use Plots and Help constantly and largely ignore the rest.
If the layout does not suit you, Tools, Global Options, Pane Layout will rearrange it.
One thing to recognise now, because it catches almost everybody in the first hour. If your console prompt changes from > to +, R is not broken and it is not thinking. It has decided your command is incomplete and it is waiting for the rest.
> mean(c(1, 2, 3)
+
+
That happens when you leave a bracket or a quote unclosed. Press Esc. The prompt goes back to > and you can start again. Beginners often press Enter harder, which produces more + symbols and more panic.

title: 1  Getting set up
text:
1.3 Three shortcuts, learned today
RStudio has hundreds of keyboard shortcuts and you can see the whole list with Alt+Shift+K on Windows or Option+Shift+K on a Mac. Three of them are worth learning before you write anything.
Run the current line. Ctrl+Enter on Windows and Linux, Cmd+Enter on a Mac. Put your cursor anywhere on a line in your script, press it, and that line is sent to the console and executed. The cursor then drops to the next line, so you can run a script line by line by holding the shortcut down. If you have text selected, it runs the selection instead. This is the one you will use ten thousand times.
Run the current chunk. Ctrl+Shift+Enter, or Cmd+Shift+Enter. In a Quarto or R Markdown document, code lives in fenced chunks, and this runs the whole chunk your cursor is sitting in. Useless in a plain .R script, essential the moment you start writing reports.
Insert the assignment arrow. Alt+-, or Option+-. It types <- with a space either side. R’s assignment operator is two characters, which is a nuisance to type, and the shortcut exists because everybody complained.
You may be wondering why R uses <- at all when = is right there and works. The story usually told is that R inherited the arrow from S, and S was written on terminals whose keyboards, borrowed from APL, had a single ← key, so assignment was one keystroke and nobody minded. The practical answer, which matters more, is that = already has a second job inside function calls, where it names arguments. Compare the two in one line:

x <- mean(c(10, 20, 30), na.rm = TRUE)
x
#> [1] 20

The <- creates an object. The = sets an argument. Keeping them visually distinct means you can read a long function call and see at a glance what is being made and what is being configured. This book uses <- throughout and so should you.

title: 1  Getting set up
section: 1.4 The console is a conversation, the script is the record
text:
1.4 The console is a conversation, the script is the record
Everything you type in the console runs immediately and then, for practical purposes, is gone. Yes, there is a History tab, but the history is an undifferentiated stream of everything you tried, including the five wrong attempts and the typo, in the order you happened to make them. Nobody has ever successfully reconstructed an analysis from RStudio’s history pane.
A script is a file. It runs top to bottom in a fixed order. You can open it in six months, send it to a co-author, put it in a repository, and re-run it to get the same numbers. That is the whole argument.
So: if you are poking at the data to see what is in it, use the console. nrow(covid), names(covid), checking whether a column is a character or a number. Ephemeral questions with ephemeral answers. If you are doing something you would have to redo, or something you would need to defend, it goes in the script. My rule of thumb is that if I had to stop and think about how to write a line, that line belongs in a file.
The unhappy middle ground is the analysis that lives entirely in the console and works beautifully, right up until R restarts. There is no way to recover it. Write the script.

title: 1  Getting set up
text:
1.5 Packages, install.packages() and library()

Base R can do a lot and it is deliberately conservative about what ships in the box. Almost everything you actually want lives in a package, and packages come from CRAN, the Comprehensive R Archive Network. CRAN is a network of mirror servers holding many thousands of packages, each of which has passed an automated check on several operating systems before being accepted. It is not a free-for-all like some language ecosystems. That gatekeeping is why install.packages() from a fresh R install usually works.
There are two verbs and beginners conflate them constantly.
install.packages("tidyverse") downloads the package from CRAN and writes it to your hard disk. You do this once per machine. It takes a while, especially for the tidyverse, because the tidyverse is a meta-package: installing it installs about thirty others.

install.packages("tidyverse")

library(tidyverse) loads an already-installed package into your current R session, so its functions become available by name. You do this every session, at the top of every script. Restart R and it is undone.
The bookshelf analogy is worn out but it is the right one. install.packages() buys the book and puts it on the shelf. library() takes it down and opens it. Buying it again every morning would be strange; opening it every morning is normal.
The quotes are inconsistent and this trips people up. install.packages() needs them, because it takes the package name as a string. library() does not, because of an old piece of R cleverness that lets it accept a bare name. Quotes are accepted by both, so if you would rather not remember which is which, quote both and move on.
When you run library(tidyverse) in a fresh session, this appears:
── Attaching core tidyverse packages ──────────────────────── tidyverse 2.0.0 ──
✔ dplyr     1.2.1     ✔ readr     2.2.0
✔ forcats   1.0.1     ✔ stringr   1.6.0
✔ ggplot2   4.0.3     ✔ tibble    3.3.1
✔ lubridate 1.9.5     ✔ tidyr     1.3.2
✔ purrr     1.2.2
── Conflicts ────────────────────────────────────────── tidyverse_conflicts() ──
✖ dplyr::filter() masks stats::filter()
✖ dplyr::lag()    masks stats::lag()
ℹ Use the conflicted package (<http://conflicted.r-lib.org/>) to force all conflicts to become errors
Your version numbers will differ. The red crosses are not errors. They are telling you that dplyr has a function called filter() and so does base R’s stats package, and since dplyr was loaded second, typing filter() now gets you dplyr’s. That is what you want, and it is a good thing R says so out loud rather than deciding silently. If you ever need the other one, stats::filter() names it explicitly. The :: means “this function, from that package”.
Get used to reading this block rather than scrolling past it. When a function starts behaving strangely, “something else masked it” is a real and common explanation.

title: 1  Getting set up
text:
1.6 Getting the data
The book runs on one file, sg_covid_data.csv. There are two ways to get it.
The thorough way is to take the whole book. Go to https://github.com/CERM-NUS/r-intro, click the green Code button, choose Download ZIP, and unzip it somewhere you will find again. Documents, not Downloads. You now have the data, the source of every chapter, and a .Rproj file. Double-click r-intro.Rproj and RStudio opens with everything pointed at the right place.
The quick way is to take just the CSV. The link in this book’s sidebar, “Download the data”, goes straight to it. Right-click, Save Link As. Then make yourself a folder for this course with a data subfolder inside it, and put the CSV in there:
sph5421/
├── data/
│   └── sg_covid_data.csv
└── analysis.R
Two warnings about that download. Some browsers append .txt to files they think are plain text, so check that what landed on disk is called sg_covid_data.csv and not sg_covid_data.csv.txt. And do not open it in Excel to have a look. Excel will offer to save it back, and when it does it will silently rewrite the date column into whatever your regional settings prefer. If you want to see inside the file, the next chapters show you how to look at it in R, which is non-destructive.

title: 1  Getting set up
text:
1.7 Does it work?
Here is the check. Open a new script, type this in, and run it a line at a time.

library(tidyverse)

covid <- read_csv("data/sg_covid_data.csv")
#> Rows: 345 Columns: 13
#> ── Column specification ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> Delimiter: ","
#> chr   (1): administrative_area_level_1
#> dbl  (11): confirmed, deaths, stringency_index, government_response_index, c...
#> date  (1): date
#> 
#> ℹ Use `spec()` to retrieve the full column specification for this data.
#> ℹ Specify the column types or set `show_col_types = FALSE` to quiet this message.

nrow(covid)
#> [1] 345

You should get 345, and above it a column specification listing 13 columns: one character, eleven numbers and one date. Read that block rather than scrolling past it. It is readr telling you what it decided each column was, and the import chapter comes back to what happens when it guesses wrong.
You will also see the tidyverse startup message from the previous section. It does not appear on this page because the machine that built the book had already loaded the tidyverse before this chapter started, which is a small preview of why sessions matter.
Now check that graphics work:

ggplot(covid, aes(x = date, y = confirmed)) +
  geom_line()



Cumulative confirmed cases, straight from the raw column. It only ever goes up, which is exactly the problem the next few chapters solve.



A line should appear in the Plots pane, climbing from zero in January to just under sixty thousand by December. Yours will have a grey background and mine does not, because this book applies a house theme to every figure. Same data, different paint.
If the plot does not appear and the Plots pane looks squashed, drag the divider between the panes to make it taller. RStudio cannot draw into a pane a few pixels high.

1.7.1 When it does not work
Three failures account for nearly all of them.
Error in library(tidyverse) : there is no package called ‘tidyverse’
The install did not finish, or finished with an error you scrolled past. Run install.packages("tidyverse") again and watch the output this time. On Windows, if it complains that the package is in use, restart R first.
Error:
! 'data/sg_covid_data.csv' does not exist in current working directory:
  '/Users/you/Desktop'.
R is looking in the wrong place. The message tells you exactly where it looked, which is more helpful than most. Either the file is not where you think it is, or R’s working directory is not where you think it is. Type getwd() to see where R currently believes it is standing:

getwd()
#> [1] "/Users/swapnil/Documents/GitHub/r-intro"

Yours will print something else. The whole of the next chapter is about making this stop being a problem, so if you hit this one, keep reading rather than fixing it by hand.
Error: unexpected input in "covid <- read_csv(“"
Something in the line is not valid R. That particular one is a smart quote, the curly “ that Word and Slack substitute for the straight ". R does not recognise it as a quote character at all. If instead you left out a comma you get its sibling:
Error: unexpected symbol in "covid <- read_csv("data/sg_covid_data.csv" nrow"
Both messages quote your line back at you and stop at the point where R gave up parsing. That stopping point is the clue. Look just before it.
If none of those match what you are seeing, copy the error text exactly, without your own file paths and object names, and search for it. Someone has had it before.

title: 2  Good practice in a nutshell
text:
2.1 1. Work in a project
Make a folder for each piece of work, put a .Rproj file in it, and open your work by double-clicking that file.
A .Rproj is a small plain-text file. Here is the whole of the one at the root of this book, r-intro.Rproj, with nothing removed:
That is all it is. What it does is more than it looks. Opening it starts a fresh R session whose working directory is the folder containing the file, on every machine, every time, without you typing a path. It gives the project its own environment and its own command history, so two projects open at once cannot contaminate each other. It carries the settings above with the folder, so a collaborator who opens it gets your tab width and your encoding rather than their own. And it makes the folder findable: a lot of tooling, including here and renv and usethis, works out where “here” is by looking for a .Rproj.
Make one with File, New Project, Existing Directory. It takes about eight seconds and it is the single highest-return habit in this chapter.

title: 2  Good practice in a nutshell
section: 2.2 2. setwd() is the one line that guarantees your code runs on exactly one computer
text:
2.2 2. setwd() is the one line that guarantees your code runs on exactly one computer
You will see this at the top of scripts, in textbooks, and in code your supervisor sends you:

setwd("/Users/swapnil/Documents/GitHub/r-intro")

covid <- read_csv("data/sg_covid_data.csv")

It works. It works on my laptop, and only on my laptop, and only until I reorganise my Documents folder. Send that script to a classmate and the first line fails:
Error in setwd("/Users/swapnil/Documents/GitHub/r-intro") :
  cannot change working directory
There is no version of that path that is correct on two machines. Windows users get a second problem on top, because Windows paths use backslashes and a backslash starts an escape sequence in an R string:
Error: '\U' used without hex digits in character string
That is R reading C:\Users\... and seeing \U, which it expects to be followed by a Unicode code point. You can escape the backslashes, or use forward slashes, which work fine on Windows. Better, do not type absolute paths at all.
The fix is here::here(). It looks for a project marker, a .Rproj file, a .git directory, or a file called .here, walking up from wherever R happens to be standing, and then builds a path down from that root:

here::here("data", "sg_covid_data.csv")
#> [1] "/Users/swapnil/Documents/GitHub/r-intro/data/sg_covid_data.csv"

On my machine that is what it prints. On yours it prints something else, and that is the entire point. The same line of code resolves to the right file on both. It works from a script in the project root, from a Quarto document two folders down, and from the console, because it never depends on where you currently are.
You give here() the path pieces as separate arguments and it joins them with whatever separator the operating system uses. So here("data", "raw", "file.csv") is correct on macOS, Linux and Windows, and you never type a slash of either kind.

title: 2  Good practice in a nutshell
section: 2.3 3. Restart R often, and start every session empty
text:
2.3 3. Restart R often, and start every session empty
Two settings, once, and then a keyboard shortcut for the rest of your life.
Go to Tools, Global Options, General. Untick “Restore .RData into workspace at startup”. Set “Save workspace to .RData on exit” to Never. Out of the box, restore is ticked and save is set to “Ask”, which means that sooner or later, at eleven at night, you will click Yes without reading the dialog. Setting it to Never removes the question. Both defaults date from an era when reloading a workspace was cheaper than recomputing it, and RStudio keeps them for compatibility rather than because anyone thinks they are a good idea.
The .Rproj file overrides the global setting for its own project, which is why the one shown above carries RestoreWorkspace: No and SaveWorkspace: No. Change both in Global Options as well, so that projects you have not configured behave the same way.
Then learn Ctrl+Shift+F10, or Cmd+Shift+F10 on a Mac, which restarts R. Use it several times an hour. It takes under a second.
Here is the failure this prevents. When R saves your workspace on exit and reloads it on startup, your environment accumulates. Objects created weeks ago sit there, invisible unless you go looking. Your script runs beautifully. You send it to someone and it fails on line 12 because line 12 uses an object your script never creates, and you never noticed because it has been sitting in your workspace since March. The script was never complete. Your environment was propping it up.
The subtler version is worse, and it comes from a real bug in the worksheet this book replaces. The worksheet had a loop that built a monthly subset in order to print a count for each month. Something close to this:

covid <- read_covid() %>%
  arrange(date) %>%
  mutate(daily_cases = confirmed - lag(confirmed, default = 0))

for (m in 1:12) {
  month_data <- covid %>% filter(month(date) == m)
  # the original printed a count for month m here
}

The loop does its job and finishes. But m and month_data were created at top level, so they are still in the global environment afterwards, holding whatever the last iteration put there:

m
#> [1] 12
range(month_data$date)
#> [1] "2020-12-01" "2020-12-31"

December. Now forty lines further down the worksheet, after several other exercises, there was a plot of month_data that was supposed to be showing April, because the reader had been asked to build an April subset in the meantime. If they had skipped that exercise, or run it and then restarted, or run the chunks out of order, month_data was still December, and the plot came out looking perfectly reasonable.

# What the reader thought was April's mean daily cases
mean(month_data$daily_cases)
#> [1] 12.29032


# What April actually was
covid %>%
  filter(month(date) == 4) %>%
  summarise(april_mean = mean(daily_cases))
#> # A tibble: 1 × 1
#>   april_mean
#>        <dbl>
#> 1       508.

Twelve, against five hundred and eight. Both are numbers, both print without complaint, and nothing anywhere errors. A stale global is the hardest kind of wrong answer to catch, because the only symptom is that the answer is wrong, and you have no reason to suspect it.
Restarting R and running the script from the top is what catches this. If it runs clean from an empty session, the script is the analysis. If it does not, you have found a dependency you did not know you had, which is worth finding.

title: 2  Good practice in a nutshell
section: 2.4 4. Every library() at the top, and rm(list = ls()) is not a restart
text:
2.4 4. Every library() at the top, and rm(list = ls()) is not a restart
Put every package your script needs in one block at the top of the file. A reader can then see the dependencies in five seconds instead of scrolling. More practically, a script that loads a package halfway down fails differently depending on how far execution got, which makes the failure harder to reproduce than it needs to be.
The thing people reach for instead of restarting is this:

rm(list = ls())

It feels like a fresh start. It is not one. ls() lists the objects in the global environment and rm() removes them, and that is the whole of what happens. Consider what is untouched.
Attached packages stay attached. search() shows R’s chain of environments, and rm(list = ls()) empties exactly one entry in it, the first:

search()
#>  [1] ".GlobalEnv"        "package:scales"    "package:patchwork"
#>  [4] "package:here"      "package:lubridate" "package:forcats"  
#>  [7] "package:stringr"   "package:dplyr"     "package:purrr"    
#> [10] "package:readr"     "package:tidyr"     "package:tibble"   
#> [13] "package:ggplot2"   "package:tidyverse" "package:stats"    
#> [16] "package:graphics"  "package:grDevices" "package:datasets" 
#> [19] "renv:shims"        "package:utils"     "package:methods"  
#> [22] "Autoloads"         "package:base"

Everything from package:scales down is still attached and still masking whatever it was masking. Session-wide settings survive too: an options(digits = 3) you typed an hour ago is still quietly rounding everything you print. Open file connections stay open. And ls() hides names that begin with a dot, so anything dot-named is never passed to rm() in the first place:

set.seed(42)
x <- runif(1)
rm(list = ls())

ls()
#> character(0)
ls(all.names = TRUE)
#> [1] ".main"               ".QuartoInlineRender" ".Random.seed"

.Random.seed is still there after the supposed clean-out, which means your “fresh” session is not even at a fresh random state. Restarting R clears all of it, and takes less time than typing the rm() call.
crumbs: 2  Good practice in a nutshell

title: 2  Good practice in a nutshell
section: 2.5 5. The raw data file is read-only
text:
2.5 5. The raw data file is read-only
Whatever arrives from the source goes in data/ and is never edited again. Not to fix a date format, not to fill in a blank, not to delete the header row someone put in twice.
The dataset in this book is a good argument for the rule. It has 59 missing values at the start of the deaths column, 24 missing days in every one of the six mobility columns, and case counts that are cumulative rather than daily. All three are repaired in this book, and all three are repaired in code, in front of you, in a way you can read and disagree with. If instead I had opened the CSV in Excel and typed zeros over the missing deaths, the file would look tidier and the analysis would be worse, because a zero and a not-yet-reported are different things and nobody downstream would ever know which they were holding.
Every repair belongs in the script. That way the repair has a reason next to it, it survives the arrival of an updated file, and a reviewer can see what you changed. A file edited by hand has none of those properties.
crumbs: 2  Good practice in a nutshell

title: 2  Good practice in a nutshell
section: 2.6 6. Name things so that tomorrow’s you can read them
text:
2.6 6. Name things so that tomorrow’s you can read them
Use snake_case: lowercase words joined by underscores. daily_cases, monthly_summary, covid_april. R is a language where four naming conventions coexist in the base install alone, and you cannot fix that, but you can be internally consistent.
Name data after what it is, using nouns. Name functions after what they do, using verbs. severity is a column; classify_severity() is a function. When you read monthly_report <- summarise_by_month(covid) you know which is which without looking anything up.
Do not call things df, df2, data, temp, or df_final_v2. Two reasons. The first is that six weeks later df2 tells you nothing and you will have to run the code to find out what is in it. The second is that some of those names are already taken. df is a real function in base R, the density of the F distribution:

df(1, 2, 3)
#> [1] 0.2788548

Assign your data frame to df and you have masked it. That particular collision is unlikely to hurt you, but data, c, mean, sum, t and T are all things people name variables, and some of those do hurt.
Long names cost nothing, because Tab completes them. monthly_case_summary is three keystrokes and a Tab.
crumbs: 2  Good practice in a nutshell

title: 2  Good practice in a nutshell
text:
2.7 7. Pin your packages with renv

renv gives a project its own package library and a lockfile recording the exact version of every package in it. Three commands cover ordinary use:

renv::init()      # once, when you start the project
renv::snapshot()  # after you add or update a package
renv::restore()   # on a new machine, or when you come back to it

The claim is narrow and it is this: this repository, plus renv.lock, equals the same numbers in 2029. Without a lockfile, “install the tidyverse and run my script” means whatever the tidyverse happens to be on the day someone tries, and dplyr’s behaviour in 2029 is not something either of us can promise.
This book uses renv, and renv.lock is committed alongside the chapters. If you clone the repository, renv::restore() builds the exact library the book was written against.
Be honest about the limits. renv pins R packages. It does not pin R itself, or your operating system, or the system libraries a package compiles against. For that you need containers, and that is a different course. Pinning packages is the step that removes most of the risk for most of the work.
crumbs: 2  Good practice in a nutshell

title: 2  Good practice in a nutshell
section: 2.8 8. Git, in three commands and one idea
text:
2.8 8. Git, in three commands and one idea
git add -A
git commit -m "Compute daily cases from the cumulative column"
git push
add chooses what goes into the next snapshot, commit takes the snapshot with a message attached, push sends it somewhere that is not your laptop. That is enough to be useful from day one. Everything else in Git is for when you need it.
The idea underneath is that your repository becomes a lab notebook you cannot rewrite by accident. Every commit is a complete state of the project with a timestamp, an author and a message, and once pushed it exists on a machine you do not control. You can rewrite Git history if you set out to, but you cannot do it by mistake, and you cannot do it to a commit somebody else has already pulled without it being obvious. That is a much stronger claim than a folder full of analysis_v3_FINAL_revised.R.
The everyday benefit is smaller and you will feel it sooner. With commits behind you, you can delete code without hesitating. The half-finished approach and the two hundred lines you replaced can both go, the file stays clean, and if you ever need any of it back it is one command away. Untracked code makes people hoard, and hoarded code makes scripts unreadable.
Commit code, small data files, and your lockfile. Do not commit two gigabytes of intermediate output. That is what .gitignore is for.
crumbs: 2  Good practice in a nutshell

title: 2  Good practice in a nutshell
section: 2.9 9. Ask for help with a reprex
text:
2.9 9. Ask for help with a reprex
A reprex is a reproducible example: the smallest piece of code that still shows your problem, together with everything someone needs to run it. The reprex package will build one for you. Copy your code, run reprex::reprex(), and it executes that code in a clean R session and puts the code plus its real output on your clipboard, formatted for GitHub or Slack.
The clean session is the point. A surprising share of the time, the act of writing the reprex fixes the bug, because the bug was an object left over in your environment and the clean session does not have it. That is rule 3 collecting its debt.
What makes a question answerable, in order of how often it is missing:

Code the reader can actually run. Not a screenshot. Not a fragment referring to my_data that nobody else has. Either use a dataset that ships with R, or reduce yours to ten rows and paste the output of dput(head(your_data, 10)).
The error message, copied exactly. Not “it says there’s an error”. Not retyped from memory. The whole thing, including the lines after the first.
What you expected instead. Half of all R questions turn out to be a disagreement about what the function was supposed to do, and stating your expectation surfaces that immediately.
Your versions. sessionInfo() prints your R version and every attached package. Paste it at the bottom.

Cut everything that is not needed to reproduce the problem. If your example is forty lines and the error happens on line 4, the other thirty-six lines are asking your reader to do work you could have done yourself.
crumbs: 2  Good practice in a nutshell

title: 2  Good practice in a nutshell
section: 2.10 10. Write the report and the analysis in the same file
text:
2.10 10. Write the report and the analysis in the same file
The classic workflow is: run the script, copy the numbers into Word, write around them. The moment you do that, the document and the analysis are two separate objects that agree by coincidence. Change a filter, re-run, and the number in the document is now wrong and nothing in the world will tell you.
Quarto removes the copy. A .qmd file holds your prose and your code together, and rendering it runs the code and drops the real output into the finished document. Change the filter, render again, every number updates. Tables, figures, and numbers written inline in a sentence, all of them.
This book is a Quarto book. Every chapter is a .qmd file, every output on every page was produced by the code shown above it, and the whole thing is rebuilt from scratch before it is published. I would not be willing to put numbers under my own name in something a hundred students rely on any other way.
crumbs: 2  Good practice in a nutshell

title: 2  Good practice in a nutshell
text:
2.11 The checklist
One screen. Print it, or keep it open for a week until it stops being something you have to remember.

Habits worth having before you write anything that matters.






Project
One folder per piece of work, with a .Rproj in it. Open by double-clicking that file.


Paths
No setwd(). No absolute paths. here::here("data", "file.csv").


Session
Save workspace: Never. Restore .RData: never. Restart R (Ctrl/Cmd+Shift+F10) several times an hour.


Test
Before you send it: restart R, run the whole script from the top. If it does not run clean, it is not finished.


Packages
All library() calls in one block at the top. rm(list = ls()) is not a restart.


Data

data/ is read-only. Every repair happens in code.


Names

snake_case. Nouns for data, verbs for functions. Never df2.


Versions

renv::init() at the start, renv::snapshot() when you add a package, commit renv.lock.


History

git add -A, git commit -m "...", git push. Commit early, delete freely.


Help

reprex::reprex(). Runnable code, the exact error, your expectation, sessionInfo().


Output
Report and analysis in one .qmd. Never paste a number into Word.

title: 3  Objects, vectors and functions
text:
3.1 Making R keep something
Assignment gives a value a name. R’s assignment operator is a left-pointing arrow, made of a < and a -:
first_case <- as.Date("2020-01-23")
first_case
#> [1] "2020-01-23"
Two things happened. R evaluated the right-hand side, and it bound the result to the name first_case. Assignment produces no output, which surprises people; if you want to see the value, type the name on its own line, as above.
That date is the first day this file records a confirmed case. Day one of the file, 22 January, has confirmed equal to zero.
In RStudio, Alt and minus (Option and minus on a Mac) types <- for you. Learn it early; you will type this operator thousands of times.

title: 3  Objects, vectors and functions
text:
3.1.1 Why an arrow and not an equals sign
R inherited <- from S, and S inherited it from APL, whose keyboards had a single key that produced a real ← character. When S moved to keyboards without that key, the arrow was spelled out as two characters and stuck.
= also works for assignment at the top level. This book does not use it, for one reason: inside a function call, = already means something else. In round(x, digits = 2) the digits = 2 is not creating an object called digits. It is telling round() which argument you are filling. Keeping <- for “make an object” and = for “fill an argument” means you can read a line of code and know which is happening without thinking about it.

3.1.2 Naming things
Names may contain letters, numbers, dots and underscores. They cannot start with a number, and they cannot contain spaces or hyphens. daily_cases is fine, daily cases is a syntax error, and daily-cases is read as daily minus cases.
R is case sensitive. Confirmed and confirmed are different objects, and mixing them up produces the single most common error message in R:

covd
#> Error:
#> ! object 'covd' not found

When you see object 'x' not found, R is telling you it looked everywhere it knows about and there is no such name. Nine times out of ten it is a typo or a chunk you never ran.
This book uses snake_case: lower case, words joined by underscores. The tidyverse does the same, so your code will look like the code around it.
Two names to avoid. TRUE and FALSE are reserved and cannot be reassigned, but their abbreviations T and F are ordinary variables. Someone who writes T <- 0 early in a long script has quietly redefined truth for everything that follows. Write TRUE and FALSE in full. Similarly, avoid naming your own objects c, data, mean or df; R will usually cope, but you will confuse yourself.

title: 3  Objects, vectors and functions
text:
3.2 R has no scalars
Here is the fact that makes the rest of R make sense. There is no such thing in R as a single number. What looks like one is a vector of length one.

total_deaths <- 29
length(total_deaths)
#> [1] 1
length("Singapore")
#> [1] 1

The vector is the atom. c() (for combine) glues values into a longer one:

week_one <- c(0, 1, 3, 3, 4, 5, 7)
week_one
#> [1] 0 1 3 3 4 5 7
length(week_one)
#> [1] 7

Every column of the Singapore file is a vector of length 345. Pull one out with $:

confirmed <- covid$confirmed
length(confirmed)
#> [1] 345
head(confirmed, 10)
#>  [1]  0  1  3  3  4  5  7  7 10 13

Because vectors are the atom, arithmetic works on whole vectors at once. R does not need you to write a loop over 345 days.

head(confirmed * 2, 10)
#>  [1]  0  2  6  6  8 10 14 14 20 26

This is called vectorisation, and it is the reason R code for data analysis is short. Later, when mutate() computes a new column for every row of a data frame in one line, it will feel unremarkable, because you already know that arithmetic on a vector means arithmetic on all of it.
Here is the same idea doing something useful. The confirmed column is cumulative, a running total. The number of new cases on a given day is that day’s total minus the previous day’s. Shift the vector along by one, stick a zero on the front so the lengths still match, and subtract:

previous_day <- c(0, confirmed[-length(confirmed)])
new_cases    <- confirmed - previous_day
head(new_cases, 10)
#>  [1] 0 1 2 0 1 1 2 0 3 3
max(new_cases)
#> [1] 1426
covid$date[which.max(new_cases)]
#> [1] "2020-04-20"

1,426 new cases on 20 April 2020, the peak of the dormitory outbreak. Three lines, no loop, and the answer is right: the new cases add back up to the final total.

sum(new_cases) == max(confirmed)
#> [1] TRUE

The zero on the front is doing real work there, and it is not a fudge. The file starts on 22 January with confirmed equal to zero, so 22 January really did have zero new cases. Writing that day as missing instead would drop a genuine day from every count you make afterwards. dplyr::lag() does this shifting properly and you will meet it soon; the version above is the same idea with the machinery visible.

3.2.1 Subsetting
Square brackets pick elements out by position, counting from 1 rather than 0.

confirmed[1]
#> [1] 0
confirmed[1:5]
#> [1] 0 1 3 3 4
confirmed[length(confirmed)]
#> [1] 58599

A negative index means everything except, which is what confirmed[-length(confirmed)] did above: all of it bar the last day.
You can also subset with a logical vector, which is where this starts to pay off:

covid$date[new_cases > 1000]
#> [1] "2020-04-20" "2020-04-21" "2020-04-22" "2020-04-23"

Four days in 2020 with more than a thousand new cases, and they run consecutively from 20 April. filter() will do this more readably later, but underneath it is this.

title: 3  Objects, vectors and functions
text:
3.3 Four types, and one absence
Every vector has a type, and every element of a vector has the same type. Four types matter for data work:

typeof(TRUE)
#> [1] "logical"
typeof(2L)
#> [1] "integer"
typeof(29)
#> [1] "double"
typeof("Singapore")
#> [1] "character"

Logical, integer, double, character. (There are two more, complex and raw. You can ignore them for the whole of your career unless you go looking.)
Integer and double are both numbers, and R makes the distinction awkwardly. A number you type is a double unless you stick an L on the end. A colon range is an integer.

typeof(1:5)
#> [1] "integer"
typeof(5 / 2)
#> [1] "double"
identical(1, 1L)
#> [1] FALSE
1 == 1L
#> [1] TRUE

identical() says they are different objects; == says they are the same value. Both are correct, and in practice you almost never need to care. Where it bites is that doubles are stored in binary floating point, which cannot represent most decimal fractions exactly:

0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3
#> [1] FALSE
0.1 + 0.2 - 0.3
#> [1] 5.551115e-17

That is not R being broken. Every language using IEEE 754 doubles does this, including the spreadsheet on your other screen. Never test two calculated numbers with ==. Use near(), which allows a tiny tolerance:

near(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3)
#> [1] TRUE

Logical values are TRUE and FALSE, and R treats them as 1 and 0 when you do arithmetic on them. That small fact turns “how many” and “what proportion” into sum() and mean():

sum(covid$confirmed > 10000)
#> [1] 254
mean(covid$stringency_index > 50)
#> [1] 0.5681159

254 days of 2020 with more than ten thousand cumulative cases, and the stringency index was above 50 on 57% of days.

3.3.1 NA
NA is R’s marker for a value that should exist but is not recorded. It is not zero, not an empty string, and not “the data is fine”. It is an admission of ignorance, and R takes it seriously: almost anything you do with an NA gives you NA back, because R refuses to guess.

NA + 1
#> [1] NA
mean(c(1, 2, NA))
#> [1] NA

That propagation is the point. If you do not know one of three numbers, you do not know their mean, and R would rather tell you so than quietly average the two it has.
The deaths column in this file makes it concrete. Singapore recorded no COVID-19 deaths for the first two months of the epidemic, and this file records those days as missing rather than as zero.

head(covid$deaths, 12)
#>  [1] NA NA NA NA NA NA NA NA NA NA NA NA
sum(is.na(covid$deaths))
#> [1] 59
mean(covid$deaths)
#> [1] NA

59 missing days, and so the mean of the column is NA. To get an answer you have to say explicitly that you are willing to ignore the gaps:

mean(covid$deaths, na.rm = TRUE)
#> [1] 23.75874

Whether that is the right thing to do is a question about deaths, not about R. The chapter on missing data returns to it at length. What matters here is that R made you ask.
Two more things about NA. Testing it with == does not work, because “an unknown value” is not equal to anything, including another unknown value:

NA == NA
#> [1] NA

Use is.na() instead:

is.na(c(1, NA, 3))
#> [1] FALSE  TRUE FALSE

And NA has flavours. Bare NA is logical; there are also NA_integer_, NA_real_ and NA_character_, so that a missing value can sit inside a vector without changing its type. You rarely type these yourself, but you will see them in error messages.

typeof(NA)
#> [1] "logical"
typeof(NA_character_)
#> [1] "character"
typeof(c(NA, 1))
#> [1] "double"

title: 3  Objects, vectors and functions
section: 3.4 Coercion, or how a column of numbers becomes text
text:
3.4 Coercion, or how a column of numbers becomes text
A vector holds one type. So what happens when you combine two types?

c(1, "a")
#> [1] "1" "a"

R did not complain. It quietly converted the number 1 into the string "1", because that is the only way to keep everything in one vector. The rule runs one way only, from least to most flexible: logical becomes integer becomes double becomes character.

typeof(c(TRUE, 1L))
#> [1] "integer"
typeof(c(1L, 2.5))
#> [1] "double"
typeof(c(2.5, "Singapore"))
#> [1] "character"

Nothing here is a bug, and no warning is issued at any step. That is exactly why it costs people an evening. Picture a spreadsheet of daily deaths where one cell says "not reported" instead of being left blank. That single cell turns the entire column to character on import, and then:

mean(c("1", "a"))
#> Warning in mean.default(c("1", "a")): argument is not numeric or logical:
#> returning NA
#> [1] NA

The warning is the useful part: argument is not numeric or logical: returning NA. When you see it, you have a character column that you thought was numeric. typeof() on the column confirms it in one line.
Going the other way is explicit, and R does warn:

as.numeric(c("1", "a"))
#> Warning: NAs introduced by coercion
#> [1]  1 NA

NAs introduced by coercion means R turned something into NA because it could not parse it. Sometimes that is what you wanted. Sometimes it has just deleted a fifth of your data. Always check how many NAs appeared.

title: 3  Objects, vectors and functions
text:
3.5 Recycling
When two vectors in an arithmetic expression have different lengths, R repeats the shorter one until it is long enough. You have already relied on this: in confirmed * 2, the 2 is a vector of length one and it got recycled 345 times.
That is the useful case. Here is the other one.






Predict before you run



c(1, 2, 3, 4) + c(10, 20) produces a vector of length four. Write down the four numbers you expect, and whether you expect a warning. Then run it.



c(1, 2, 3, 4) + c(10, 20)
#> [1] 11 22 13 24

No warning at all. Four divides by two, so R considered the recycling clean and said nothing. Change the length to three and it does speak up:

c(1, 2, 3) + c(10, 20)
#> Warning in c(1, 2, 3) + c(10, 20): longer object length is not a multiple of
#> shorter object length
#> [1] 11 22 13

longer object length is not a multiple of shorter object length is R telling you your two vectors do not line up. It is the same silent mechanism either way, and the warning only appears when the arithmetic is untidy, not when it is wrong. This is why length() is worth running on anything you are about to combine.

title: 3  Objects, vectors and functions
text:
3.6 Calling functions
A function has a name, takes arguments in brackets, and gives back a value. mean(new_cases) takes one argument and returns one number. Functions nest, and R works from the inside out:

round(mean(new_cases), 2)
#> [1] 169.85
median(new_cases)
#> [1] 40

A mean of 169.85 new cases a day against a median of 40 tells you the distribution is badly skewed, which for this epidemic it is: most of 2020 was quiet, and a few weeks in April and May were not.
Arguments can be given by position or by name. These three calls are identical:

seq(1, 10, 3)
#> [1]  1  4  7 10
seq(from = 1, to = 10, by = 3)
#> [1]  1  4  7 10
seq(by = 3, to = 10, from = 1)
#> [1]  1  4  7 10

Position only works if you remember the order. Names work regardless, and they document the call for whoever reads it next, including you in three weeks. The convention most people settle on is to pass the first argument or two positionally, because mean(new_cases) is perfectly clear, and to name everything after that.
Most arguments have defaults, so you only supply the ones you want to change. args() shows you what they are:

args(round)
#> function (x, digits = 0, ...) 
#> NULL
args(mean)
#> function (x, ...) 
#> NULL

round(x, digits = 0) means that if you do not say otherwise, you get whole numbers. mean(x, ...) is less helpful, because mean is generic and the real arguments live in the method; this is one of the places where R’s help page tells you more than the code does.
While we are here, round() has an oddity that catches people out:

round(0.5)
#> [1] 0
round(1.5)
#> [1] 2
round(2.5)
#> [1] 2

round(0.5) is 0 and round(1.5) is 2. R rounds halves to the nearest even number rather than always upward, following the IEC 60559 standard, so that rounding a long column of values does not drift upward. ?round says so explicitly. It is documented behaviour, not a bug, and it will still confuse a colleague checking your totals by hand.

3.6.1 Reading a help page
Every function in R ships with documentation. A question mark opens it:

?mean
help("mean")

If you do not know the name, two question marks searches the text of every installed help page:

??"standard deviation"

Help pages have a fixed shape, and reading them in order is a waste of time. Read them in this order instead.
Usage first. It shows the function signature with every default filled in, so you can see at a glance what you are allowed to pass. Arguments second, but only the two or three you care about. Examples, at the very bottom, third and often most useful; they are runnable, and example(mean) runs them for you. Details only when something has already gone wrong, because that is where the awkward truths live, including the rounding rule above. Value when you are unsure what type comes back, which matters more than beginners expect.
Tidyverse functions carry the same documentation, typeset more kindly at https://tidyverse.org. If a help page is impenetrable, that is normal rather than a sign you are slow. Much of base R’s documentation was written for statisticians in the 1990s and reads that way. Search for the function name plus “r” and you will find people explaining it to each other in ordinary language.

title: 3  Objects, vectors and functions
text:
3.7 Packages and where functions live
R ships with a few thousand functions. Everything else lives in packages: bundles of functions, documentation and sometimes data, written by other people and published on CRAN.
Installing is a one-off, per machine. It downloads and compiles code onto your hard disk.

install.packages("tidyverse")

Loading is per session. It takes an installed package and makes its functions available by name.

library(tidyverse)

The distinction trips up everyone once. install.packages() belongs at the console, typed by hand, and should never sit in a script; running it on every render wastes minutes and needs the internet. library() belongs at the top of every script, because a script that does not load what it uses will not run on anyone else’s machine, including yours next month. The quotation marks go on one and not the other, which is an inconsistency in R and not something you did wrong.

3.7.1 The masking message
The first time you ran library(tidyverse) you got a wall of text. Read it rather than scrolling past it.
── Attaching core tidyverse packages ──────────────────────── tidyverse 2.0.0 ──
✔ dplyr     1.2.1     ✔ readr     2.2.0
✔ forcats   1.0.1     ✔ stringr   1.6.0
✔ ggplot2   4.0.3     ✔ tibble    3.3.1
✔ lubridate 1.9.5     ✔ tidyr     1.3.2
✔ purrr     1.2.2
── Conflicts ────────────────────────────────────────── tidyverse_conflicts() ──
✖ dplyr::filter() masks stats::filter()
✖ dplyr::lag()    masks stats::lag()
ℹ Use the conflicted package (<http://conflicted.r-lib.org/>) to force all conflicts to become errors
Load dplyr on its own and it says the same thing more bluntly:
Attaching package: ‘dplyr’

The following objects are masked from ‘package:stats’:

    filter, lag

The following objects are masked from ‘package:base’:

    intersect, setdiff, setequal, union
Nothing has broken. Here is the mechanism. R keeps an ordered list of places to look for a name, called the search path:

head(search(), 15)
#>  [1] ".GlobalEnv"        "package:scales"    "package:patchwork"
#>  [4] "package:here"      "package:lubridate" "package:forcats"  
#>  [7] "package:stringr"   "package:dplyr"     "package:purrr"    
#> [10] "package:readr"     "package:tidyr"     "package:tibble"   
#> [13] "package:ggplot2"   "package:tidyverse" "package:stats"

When you type filter(...), R walks that list from left to right and uses the first filter it finds. Every package you attach is inserted near the front, so a newly loaded package wins against anything loaded before it. package:dplyr sits ahead of package:stats, so filter means dplyr’s.
stats::filter has not been deleted, and you can still reach it by giving its full address. The double colon means “the function called filter from the package called stats, regardless of the search path”:

head(round(stats::filter(covid$confirmed, rep(1/7, 7)), 1), 10)
#> Time Series:
#> Start = 1 
#> End = 10 
#> Frequency = 1 
#>  [1]   NA   NA   NA  3.3  4.3  5.6  7.0  8.9 10.9 12.7

That is a seven-day moving average of the cumulative curve, which is what stats::filter() is for. It returns a time series object, hence the header lines about start, end and frequency, and the first three values are NA because a seven-day window cannot be centred on day one. None of it has anything to do with picking rows out of a table:

dplyr::filter(covid, stringency_index > 80)$date
#> [1] "2020-04-10" "2020-04-25" "2020-05-01"

Two functions, one name, completely different jobs. The message exists so that you find out about the collision when you load the package rather than three hours later when a result looks wrong.
The same applies to lag(). dplyr::lag() shifts a vector along by one position, which is exactly what you did by hand earlier. stats::lag() shifts a time series’ index and leaves the values alone. If you ever compute daily cases and get a column of zeroes, this is why.
The practical consequence, and the reason library() goes at the top of a script: if you forget to load dplyr and call filter() on a data frame, you get stats::filter, and the error tells you nothing about the real problem.
Error: object 'confirmed' not found
stats::filter() has no idea that confirmed is a column of the thing you handed it, so it tries to find an object by that name and fails. The fix is a library(dplyr) or library(tidyverse) line you left out, and the error message does not say so.
You can sidestep the whole business by writing dplyr::filter() in full. That is worth doing in a function you are shipping to other people, and it is too noisy for everyday analysis. Load the package, read the conflicts message, and if you want the collisions to become hard errors instead of quiet precedence, the conflicted package does that.

title: 3  Objects, vectors and functions
text:
3.8 Exercise

Exercise 3.1 (Build a week by hand) The first seven cumulative confirmed counts in the file are 0, 1, 3, 3, 4, 5 and 7.

Store them in a vector called week_one and confirm that R agrees it has seven elements and holds doubles.
Work out how many new cases were recorded on each of days two to seven, using only subsetting and subtraction.
Add the label "week one" to the front of week_one, look at the type again, and then try to multiply the result by two. Explain in one sentence what R did to your numbers and why the arithmetic now fails.
Make a copy of week_one with the fourth element replaced by NA, then find its mean twice, once as R gives it to you and once telling mean() to drop the missing value.








Stuck? Open for a hint (not the answer)





For part 2, two vectors of the same length subtract element by element, so you need one vector holding days two to seven and another holding days one to six. For part 3, look at typeof() before and after.



Worked solution

title: 4  Rectangles: data frames and tibbles
text:
4.1 Three vectors and a problem
Take three days of the Singapore record, in the week the circuit breaker began, and store each variable in its own vector.
day        <- as.Date(c("2020-04-06", "2020-04-07", "2020-04-08"))
confirmed  <- c(1375, 1481, 1623)
stringency <- c(45.37, 62.04, 76.85)
Everything you need is there. The correspondence between them is not written down anywhere; it lives entirely in your head, as a promise that the second element of each vector refers to the same day. R has made no such promise, and will not enforce one.
Watch it break. Sort the stringency values from highest to lowest, which is a reasonable thing to want:
sort(stringency, decreasing = TRUE)
#> [1] 76.85 62.04 45.37
day
#> [1] "2020-04-06" "2020-04-07" "2020-04-08"
stringency has been reordered. day has not. If you assign that sorted vector back over the old one, the 7 April lockdown score is now sitting next to 6 April, and nothing in your session knows. No error, no warning, and a plot that looks entirely plausible. This is the kind of mistake that survives peer review.
Multiply the problem by 345 rows and 13 variables and you have the reason data frames exist.
crumbs: 4  Rectangles: data frames and tibbles

title: 4  Rectangles: data frames and tibbles
section: 4.2 A data frame is a list of columns
text:
4.2 A data frame is a list of columns
data.frame() binds vectors together so that they can only be manipulated as a unit.

three_days <- data.frame(day, confirmed, stringency)
three_days
#>          day confirmed stringency
#> 1 2020-04-06      1375      45.37
#> 2 2020-04-07      1481      62.04
#> 3 2020-04-08      1623      76.85

Now sorting means sorting rows, and the rows carry their contents with them:

three_days[order(three_days$stringency, decreasing = TRUE), ]
#>          day confirmed stringency
#> 3 2020-04-08      1623      76.85
#> 2 2020-04-07      1481      62.04
#> 1 2020-04-06      1375      45.37

The row numbers on the left have gone 3, 2, 1. Each row moved as a piece.
Underneath, a data frame really is a list of vectors, and you can see that by stripping the class off it:

unclass(three_days)
#> $day
#> [1] "2020-04-06" "2020-04-07" "2020-04-08"
#> 
#> $confirmed
#> [1] 1375 1481 1623
#> 
#> $stringency
#> [1] 45.37 62.04 76.85
#> 
#> attr(,"row.names")
#> [1] 1 2 3

A named list of three vectors, plus an attribute recording the row names. That is the whole implementation. Everything else, the printing, the nrow(), the two-dimensional subsetting, is behaviour attached to that list by its class. R will confirm it if you ask directly:

is.list(three_days)
#> [1] TRUE
length(three_days)
#> [1] 3
lengths(three_days)
#>        day  confirmed stringency 
#>          3          3          3

length() on a data frame counts the elements of the underlying list, which is the number of columns. lengths(), with the s, gives the length of each element, which is the number of rows repeated once per column. nrow() and ncol() are friendlier names for the same two facts.
Two properties follow directly from “list of vectors”, and they are the properties that matter.
Columns may be of different types. A list can hold anything, so one element can be a Date vector, the next a double vector, the next a character vector. Each column is internally uniform, which is the vector rule from Section 3.3, but columns need not agree with each other. That is what makes a data frame the right shape for a dataset, where dates, counts and labels sit side by side. A matrix cannot do this; every cell of a matrix has one type.

sapply(three_days, class)
#>        day  confirmed stringency 
#>     "Date"  "numeric"  "numeric"

Rows must line up. The list is not free to hold vectors of any length, because the rectangle would stop being a rectangle. Give data.frame() mismatched lengths and it refuses:

data.frame(day = 1:3, phase = c("pre", "circuit breaker"))
#> Error in `data.frame()`:
#> ! arguments imply differing number of rows: 3, 2

arguments imply differing number of rows: 3, 2 is a good error. It arrives at the moment the mistake is made, not three steps later.
That constraint is the entire point. Every operation you will learn in the next few chapters, filtering rows, creating columns, grouping and summarising, is built on the guarantee that row i of every column refers to the same observation. filter() can drop 200 rows without you checking that anything stayed aligned, because misalignment is not representable.

4.2.1 Where data.frame() lets you down
The constraint has one hole in it, and it is old and unfortunate. If the short vector’s length divides the long one exactly, data.frame() recycles instead of complaining:

data.frame(day = 1:6, phase = c("pre", "circuit breaker"))
#>   day           phase
#> 1   1             pre
#> 2   2 circuit breaker
#> 3   3             pre
#> 4   4 circuit breaker
#> 5   5             pre
#> 6   6 circuit breaker

Six rows, alternating labels, no warning. That is the recycling rule from Section 3.5 applied where it does real damage. It is convenient when you intend it, and silent when you do not, which is a poor trade for data work.
crumbs: 4  Rectangles: data frames and tibbles

title: 4  Rectangles: data frames and tibbles
text:
4.3 Tibbles
A tibble is a data frame with the historical annoyances removed. read_csv() returns one, so this is what you have been holding all along:

class(covid)
#> [1] "spec_tbl_df" "tbl_df"      "tbl"         "data.frame"

Read that from the right. It is a data.frame, so anything that accepts a data frame accepts it. tbl and tbl_df are the tibble classes, which change how it prints and how it is subsetted. spec_tbl_df is readr’s marker, recording the column specification it worked out while reading the file, which Chapter 5 comes back to.
Three things changed, and each of them fixes something that used to cost people time.

4.3.1 Printing tells you what you have

covid
#> # A tibble: 345 × 13
#>    administrative_area_level_1 confirmed deaths date       stringency_index
#>    <chr>                           <dbl>  <dbl> <date>                <dbl>
#>  1 Singapore                           0     NA 2020-01-22             19.4
#>  2 Singapore                           1     NA 2020-01-23             25  
#>  3 Singapore                           3     NA 2020-01-24             25  
#>  4 Singapore                           3     NA 2020-01-25             25  
#>  5 Singapore                           4     NA 2020-01-26             25  
#>  6 Singapore                           5     NA 2020-01-27             25  
#>  7 Singapore                           7     NA 2020-01-28             25  
#>  8 Singapore                           7     NA 2020-01-29             25  
#>  9 Singapore                          10     NA 2020-01-30             25  
#> 10 Singapore                          13     NA 2020-01-31             25  
#> # ℹ 335 more rows
#> # ℹ 8 more variables: government_response_index <dbl>,
#> #   containment_health_index <dbl>,
#> #   retail_and_recreation_percent_change_from_baseline <dbl>,
#> #   grocery_and_pharmacy_percent_change_from_baseline <dbl>,
#> #   parks_percent_change_from_baseline <dbl>,
#> #   transit_stations_percent_change_from_baseline <dbl>, …

Ten rows, then a count of what was left out, then the names and types of the columns too wide to show. The <chr>, <dbl> and <date> labels under the column names are the part to pay attention to. Half the confusion in early R comes from a column being character when you assumed it was numeric, and a tibble tells you before you have written a line of analysis.
An old-style data frame does not do this. Print the same 345 rows as a data.frame and R sends all of them to the console, unlabelled, and you scroll for a while looking for the top. Try it once so you know what it looks like, then use head():

head(as.data.frame(covid)[, 1:5])
#>   administrative_area_level_1 confirmed deaths       date stringency_index
#> 1                   Singapore         0     NA 2020-01-22            19.44
#> 2                   Singapore         1     NA 2020-01-23            25.00
#> 3                   Singapore         3     NA 2020-01-24            25.00
#> 4                   Singapore         3     NA 2020-01-25            25.00
#> 5                   Singapore         4     NA 2020-01-26            25.00
#> 6                   Singapore         5     NA 2020-01-27            25.00


4.3.2 No accidental factors
Before R 4.0.0, released in April 2020, data.frame() and read.csv() converted every character column into a factor by default, because the stringsAsFactors argument defaulted to TRUE. A factor stores its values as integer codes against a table of levels, which is what you want for a categorical variable in a model and emphatically not what you want for a column of free text or identifiers.
The behaviour is still available, and it still surprises people who ask for it:

phase <- data.frame(label = c("pre", "circuit breaker"), stringsAsFactors = TRUE)
phase$label
#> [1] pre             circuit breaker
#> Levels: circuit breaker pre

Levels: circuit breaker pre is alphabetical, so “circuit breaker” now sorts before “pre” and any plot you make will show them in that order. R 4.0.0 changed the default to FALSE, which is one of the few backwards-incompatible changes the language has ever made, and it was made because this had wasted enough people’s time. Tibbles never did the conversion in the first place.
Factors are useful, and this book uses one deliberately when it builds a severity variable later. The difference is that it will be your decision.

4.3.3 Subsetting stays a data frame
Here is the change that saves the most debugging.






Predict before you run



old below is the same data as covid, converted to an old-style data frame. Both of the next two expressions ask for one column with a single pair of square brackets. Decide, before running them, whether each returns a rectangle of 345 rows and 1 column, or a bare vector of 345 numbers.



old <- as.data.frame(covid)
class(old[, "confirmed"])
#> [1] "numeric"
class(covid[, "confirmed"])
#> [1] "tbl_df"     "tbl"        "data.frame"

The data frame silently threw away a dimension and handed back a vector. The tibble kept the rectangle.

covid[, "confirmed"]
#> # A tibble: 345 × 1
#>    confirmed
#>        <dbl>
#>  1         0
#>  2         1
#>  3         3
#>  4         3
#>  5         4
#>  6         5
#>  7         7
#>  8         7
#>  9        10
#> 10        13
#> # ℹ 335 more rows

The old behaviour comes from [.data.frame having a drop argument that defaults to TRUE: ask for a single column and R assumes you wanted the contents rather than a one-column table. It is defensible in an interactive session and awful inside a pipeline, because a function two steps downstream that expected a data frame receives a numeric vector and fails with a message about the wrong thing entirely. Tibbles set drop = FALSE and never guess.
When you do want the bare vector, say so with $ or double brackets, both of which mean “give me the contents of this element” and work identically on both kinds of rectangle:

class(covid$confirmed)
#> [1] "numeric"
class(covid[["confirmed"]])
#> [1] "numeric"


4.3.4 No silent partial matching
$ on an old-style data frame will complete a partial column name for you:

head(old$conf, 5)
#> [1] 0 1 3 3 4

You asked for conf. There is no column called conf. R found confirmed, decided that was probably what you meant, and returned it without comment. Now imagine a file that also has a confirmed_cases_dormitory column: the match becomes ambiguous and you get NULL, on a day when your code worked yesterday.
Tibbles warn:

head(covid$conf, 5)
#> Warning: Unknown or uninitialised column: `conf`.
#> NULL

A warning saying the column is unknown or uninitialised, then NULL. The same warning appears for a straightforward typo, which is how you find out that covid$confrimed is not a thing before it quietly poisons a calculation.

4.3.5 The rule
Use tibbles for anything you write. When an older package rejects one, and a few statistical packages still do, convert at the point of the call:

class(as.data.frame(covid))
#> [1] "data.frame"

as_tibble() converts back. The two are compatible in both directions, so this is a small cost paid at one line, not a decision about your whole project.
crumbs: 4  Rectangles: data frames and tibbles

title: 4  Rectangles: data frames and tibbles
text:
4.4 Tidy data
Rectangles are the container. Tidy data is a rule about what goes in which part of it, and it has three clauses:

Each variable is a column.
Each observation is a row.
Each value is a cell.

The rule sounds obvious until you look at real spreadsheets, where it is broken constantly: twelve columns named January to December, a column holding both a measurement and its unit, two rows per patient because someone recorded before and after side by side.
Every tool in the tidyverse assumes tidy input. That is the whole bargain. Get the shape right once and filter(), mutate(), group_by() and ggplot() all work without argument.
So look at this file through that lens. What is one observation?

nrow(covid)
#> [1] 345
length(unique(covid$date))
#> [1] 345
length(unique(covid$administrative_area_level_1))
#> [1] 1

345 rows, 345 distinct dates, one country. The unit of observation is a country-day, and since the country never varies, in practice it is a day. Each column is a variable measured on that day: a cumulative case count, a cumulative death count, a policy index, six mobility series. One row per observation, one column per variable, one value per cell. The file arrives tidy, which is a piece of luck this book takes advantage of and your own data will not always grant you.

4.4.1 A column that says nothing
administrative_area_level_1 deserves a second look:

table(covid$administrative_area_level_1)
#> 
#> Singapore 
#>       345

One distinct value across all 345 rows. As a variable it is dead: a column that never varies cannot explain, predict, group or distinguish anything. It is here because this extract was cut out of a multi-country archive where that column did vary, and slicing one country out left the label behind.
Counting distinct values in every column is a habit worth forming on any new dataset, because both ends of the result tell you something. A column with one distinct value carries no information. A column with as many distinct values as there are rows is an identifier rather than a measurement, which is what date is here. Anything in between is a variable you can actually work with.

sapply(covid, function(column) length(unique(column)))
#>                        administrative_area_level_1 
#>                                                  1 
#>                                          confirmed 
#>                                                333 
#>                                             deaths 
#>                                                 27 
#>                                               date 
#>                                                345 
#>                                   stringency_index 
#>                                                 13 
#>                          government_response_index 
#>                                                 23 
#>                           containment_health_index 
#>                                                 21 
#> retail_and_recreation_percent_change_from_baseline 
#>                                                 50 
#>  grocery_and_pharmacy_percent_change_from_baseline 
#>                                                 53 
#>                 parks_percent_change_from_baseline 
#>                                                 76 
#>      transit_stations_percent_change_from_baseline 
#>                                                 61 
#>            workplaces_percent_change_from_baseline 
#>                                                 74 
#>           residential_percent_change_from_baseline 
#>                                                 47

stringency_index takes 13 distinct values over the year, which is a hint about how it is constructed: it is a score assembled from a handful of policy indicators, so it moves in steps when a policy changes rather than drifting continuously. Keep that in mind before you read meaning into every wobble in it.

4.4.2 When the file is not tidy
You will be handed untidy files. The common shapes are a header row of dates or months, one column containing two variables mashed together, and observations split across several rows. tidyr has pivot_longer() and pivot_wider() for reshaping between them, and they are worth looking up on the day you need them. This book does not spend a chapter on reshaping, because the Singapore file does not need it, and learning to reshape data is much easier once the rest of this is second nature.
crumbs: 4  Rectangles: data frames and tibbles

title: 4  Rectangles: data frames and tibbles
text:
4.5 Exercise

Exercise 4.1 (Take a tibble apart) Using covid as loaded at the top of this chapter:

Show, with code rather than assertion, that covid is a list, how many elements that list has, and that every element has the same length. Say in one sentence which of those two numbers is the number of rows and which is the number of columns.
Find out the type of every column without printing the whole tibble.
Build a small tibble by hand recording three dates in Singapore’s 2020 policy timeline, 7 April, 2 June and 19 June, alongside a short label for each. Then explain in two sentences why holding those as a tibble is safer than holding the dates and the labels as two separate vectors.
Convert covid to an old-style data frame and find one behaviour, other than printing, that differs from the tibble. Show it.








Stuck? Open for a hint (not the answer)





For part 1, three functions from this chapter do the whole job: one asks whether it is a list, one counts the elements, one measures each element. For part 2, sapply() applies a function to every column and collects the answers into one named vector.



Worked solution

title: 5  Reading the epidemic in
text:
5.1 Where the file is
R has a working directory: the folder it treats as “here” when you hand it a relative path. The chapter on good practice told you never to write setwd() in a script, and this is the payoff for obeying that. A script containing setwd("/Users/swapnil/Documents/GitHub/r-intro") runs on exactly one computer.
