Give it to a colleague, or move the folder, or open it on the machine in the teaching lab, and it fails on line one.
here::here() solves it. The here package looks upward from wherever R happens to be until it finds the top of your project, identified by an .Rproj file, a .git directory or a _quarto.yml, and builds paths from there.
here()
#> [1] "/Users/swapnil/Documents/GitHub/r-intro"
That is this project’s root on the machine that rendered this page; on yours it will be a different string, which is the entire point. Ask it for a file by naming the folders as separate arguments and it assembles a path that works on Windows, macOS and Linux without you thinking about which way the slashes lean.
here("data", "sg_covid_data.csv")
#> [1] "/Users/swapnil/Documents/GitHub/r-intro/data/sg_covid_data.csv"
Write here("data", "sg_covid_data.csv") in every script from now on. It costs a handful of extra characters and removes a whole category of Monday-morning email.

title: 5  Reading the epidemic in
text:
5.2 read_csv()

readr’s read_csv() takes a path and returns a tibble.

covid <- read_csv(here("data", "sg_covid_data.csv"))
#> Rows: 345 Columns: 13
#> ── Column specification ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> Delimiter: ","
#> chr   (1): administrative_area_level_1
#> dbl  (11): confirmed, deaths, stringency_index, government_response_index, c...
#> date  (1): date
#> 
#> ℹ Use `spec()` to retrieve the full column specification for this data.
#> ℹ Specify the column types or set `show_col_types = FALSE` to quiet this message.

That block of text is a message rather than an error, and it repays reading line by line.
Rows: 345 Columns: 13. Check this against what you expect before you do anything else. If you were told the file covers a year of daily data and R reports 345 rows, that is 2020 from 22 January onward, and it adds up. If R had said 344, you would want to know which day went missing and why.
Delimiter: ",". readr worked out the separator by looking at the first few lines. Files exported from European locales often use a semicolon, because the comma is doing duty as a decimal point; read_csv2() handles those.
chr (1), dbl (11), date (1). These are the guessed column types, and this is the part people skip. Three of them matter here.
date came in as a real Date, not as text. readr recognises the ISO 8601 form YYYY-MM-DD and parses it. That single fact is why the rest of this book can subtract one date from another, sort chronologically, and hand dates straight to ggplot() without ceremony.
Every count is dbl, not integer. readr’s guesser does not distinguish whole numbers from decimals; anything numeric arrives as a double. Nothing goes wrong as a result, and it is worth knowing when you wonder why confirmed is <dbl> when it obviously counts people.
One column is chr. That is administrative_area_level_1, the constant “Singapore” you met in Section 4.4.
The two lines at the bottom are hints rather than complaints. spec() prints the full specification, one line per column, and it is the thing to look at when the summary is truncated with a ...:

spec(covid)
#> cols(
#>   administrative_area_level_1 = col_character(),
#>   confirmed = col_double(),
#>   deaths = col_double(),
#>   date = col_date(format = ""),
#>   stringency_index = col_double(),
#>   government_response_index = col_double(),
#>   containment_health_index = col_double(),
#>   retail_and_recreation_percent_change_from_baseline = col_double(),
#>   grocery_and_pharmacy_percent_change_from_baseline = col_double(),
#>   parks_percent_change_from_baseline = col_double(),
#>   transit_stations_percent_change_from_baseline = col_double(),
#>   workplaces_percent_change_from_baseline = col_double(),
#>   residential_percent_change_from_baseline = col_double()
#> )

The empty format = "" on date means readr used its own ISO guesser rather than a format you supplied. The other hint offers you show_col_types = FALSE to silence the message. Take that offer only once you have read the message and pinned the types yourself. Silencing a check you have not performed is not the same as performing it.

5.2.1 The dates readr cannot guess
readr guesses dates only for the ISO form. Hand it anything else and you get character, without a warning, because a column of text is a perfectly valid column of text.

read_csv(I("date,cases\n07/04/2020,106\n08/04/2020,142\n"))
#> Rows: 2 Columns: 2
#> ── Column specification ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> Delimiter: ","
#> chr (1): date
#> dbl (1): cases
#> 
#> ℹ Use `spec()` to retrieve the full column specification for this data.
#> ℹ Specify the column types or set `show_col_types = FALSE` to quiet this message.
#> # A tibble: 2 × 2
#>   date       cases
#>   <chr>      <dbl>
#> 1 07/04/2020   106
#> 2 08/04/2020   142

<chr>. And the trap is that 07/04/2020 is 7 April in Singapore and 4 July in Chicago, so nothing but your knowledge of the source can settle it. Tell readr the format explicitly with the same %d, %m, %Y codes that strptime() uses:

read_csv(
  I("date,cases\n07/04/2020,106\n08/04/2020,142\n"),
  col_types = cols(
    date  = col_date(format = "%d/%m/%Y"),
    cases = col_double()
  )
)
#> # A tibble: 2 × 2
#>   date       cases
#>   <date>     <dbl>
#> 1 2020-04-07   106
#> 2 2020-04-08   142


5.2.2 Missing values that are not blank
read_csv() treats an empty cell and the literal string NA as missing. Health data rarely obliges. If your file codes missing as -99, ., N/A or Not reported, say so, or those values will be read as data:

read_csv(
  here("data", "some_other_file.csv"),
  na = c("", "NA", "N/A", "Not reported")
)

Get this wrong with a numeric sentinel such as -99 and nothing will look broken. Your minimum will be -99, your mean will be dragged down, and every graph will still render. Check the minimum and maximum of every numeric column after import, every time.

title: 5  Reading the epidemic in
section: 5.3 What read.csv() would have given you
text:
5.3 What read.csv() would have given you
Base R has its own reader, spelled with a dot instead of an underscore. Most older course notes use it, so you need to recognise it. The two names are close enough that you will type the wrong one at some point.

old <- read.csv(here("data", "sg_covid_data.csv"))
class(old)
#> [1] "data.frame"
class(old$date)
#> [1] "character"
head(old$date, 3)
#> [1] "2020-01-22" "2020-01-23" "2020-01-24"

No message at all, a plain data.frame rather than a tibble, and date is a character vector of strings that happen to look like dates. R will not stop you doing something silly with them:

old$date - old$date[1]
#> Error in `old$date - old$date[1]`:
#> ! non-numeric argument to binary operator

non-numeric argument to binary operator is R saying you asked it to subtract text from text. This is why every base-R set of instructions you will ever read has a line like df$date <- as.Date(df$date) near the top, and why you do not need one. read_csv() already did it.
There are two smaller differences. read.csv() returns int for whole-number columns where read_csv() returns dbl, and before R 4.0.0 it turned character columns into factors, which is the historical accident described in Section 4.3. It is also slower on large files, though at 345 rows you will never notice.
read.csv() is not broken and you may use it. The reason this book does not is that it tells you nothing on the way in.

title: 5  Reading the epidemic in
text:
5.4 Pinning the types
Guessing is right for exploring a new file and wrong for a script that runs every month. readr guesses from the first 1,000 rows by default, so a column that is numeric for a thousand rows and contains the word pending on row 1,500 will be guessed wrong. The following month’s file changes, the guess changes with it, and your code produces different numbers without saying anything.
The fix is to state the types. cols() lets you name the ones you care about and set a fallback for the rest:

covid_pinned <- read_csv(
  here("data", "sg_covid_data.csv"),
  col_types = cols(
    administrative_area_level_1 = col_character(),
    date                        = col_date(format = "%Y-%m-%d"),
    .default                    = col_double()
  )
)
dim(covid_pinned)
#> [1] 345  13

No specification message this time, because there was nothing to guess. The quickest way to write one of these is to read the file once, run spec(), and paste the output into your script as the col_types argument. From then on, the file has to match your expectations or you hear about it.
Hearing about it looks like this. Insist that every column is numeric, including the two that are not:

bad <- read_csv(
  here("data", "sg_covid_data.csv"),
  col_types = cols(.default = col_double())
)
#> Warning: One or more parsing issues, call `problems()` on your data frame for details,
#> e.g.:
#>   dat <- vroom(...)
#>   problems(dat)

A warning rather than an error, and the data still loads, with NA wherever a value could not be parsed. problems() tells you exactly which cells failed:

head(problems(bad))
#> # A tibble: 6 × 5
#>     row   col expected actual     file 
#>   <int> <int> <chr>    <chr>      <chr>
#> 1     2     1 a double Singapore  ""   
#> 2     2     4 a double 2020-01-22 ""   
#> 3     3     1 a double Singapore  ""   
#> 4     3     4 a double 2020-01-23 ""   
#> 5     4     1 a double Singapore  ""   
#> 6     4     4 a double 2020-01-24 ""

Row 2, column 1, expected a double, found Singapore. That is a report you can act on. Two columns times 345 rows is 690 failures, and if a real import produces a handful rather than hundreds, those handful are usually the interesting rows: the ones where somebody typed a note into a numeric field.
When you only need part of a wide file, cols_only() reads the named columns and skips the rest, which on a large file saves both time and memory:

read_csv(
  here("data", "sg_covid_data.csv"),
  col_types = cols_only(
    date      = col_date(),
    confirmed = col_double(),
    deaths    = col_double()
  )
)
#> # A tibble: 345 × 3
#>    confirmed deaths date      
#>        <dbl>  <dbl> <date>    
#>  1         0     NA 2020-01-22
#>  2         1     NA 2020-01-23
#>  3         3     NA 2020-01-24
#>  4         3     NA 2020-01-25
#>  5         4     NA 2020-01-26
#>  6         5     NA 2020-01-27
#>  7         7     NA 2020-01-28
#>  8         7     NA 2020-01-29
#>  9        10     NA 2020-01-30
#> 10        13     NA 2020-01-31
#> # ℹ 335 more rows

The columns come back in the order they appear in the file, not the order you listed them, which catches people who then index by position.

5.4.1 Other formats
read_tsv() for tab-separated, read_delim() when you have to name the separator yourself, readxl::read_excel() for .xlsx files including a sheet argument, and the haven package for Stata, SPSS and SAS files, which is the one that matters most in public health. All of them return tibbles, and haven keeps the variable labels that survey datasets carry.

title: 5  Reading the epidemic in
section: 5.5 Always look at what you loaded
text:
5.5 Always look at what you loaded
glimpse() is the first thing to run after any import. It transposes the usual view: one line per column, running across the page, so a 13-column table fits on a screen.

glimpse(covid)
#> Rows: 345
#> Columns: 13
#> $ administrative_area_level_1                        <chr> "Singapore", "Singa…
#> $ confirmed                                          <dbl> 0, 1, 3, 3, 4, 5, 7…
#> $ deaths                                             <dbl> NA, NA, NA, NA, NA,…
#> $ date                                               <date> 2020-01-22, 2020-0…
#> $ stringency_index                                   <dbl> 19.44, 25.00, 25.00…
#> $ government_response_index                          <dbl> 19.27, 24.48, 24.48…
#> $ containment_health_index                           <dbl> 22.02, 27.98, 27.98…
#> $ retail_and_recreation_percent_change_from_baseline <dbl> NA, NA, NA, NA, NA,…
#> $ grocery_and_pharmacy_percent_change_from_baseline  <dbl> NA, NA, NA, NA, NA,…
#> $ parks_percent_change_from_baseline                 <dbl> NA, NA, NA, NA, NA,…
#> $ transit_stations_percent_change_from_baseline      <dbl> NA, NA, NA, NA, NA,…
#> $ workplaces_percent_change_from_baseline            <dbl> NA, NA, NA, NA, NA,…
#> $ residential_percent_change_from_baseline           <dbl> NA, NA, NA, NA, NA,…

Read it as three answers at once. The dimensions confirm the import. The type in angle brackets after each name confirms the parse. And the first handful of values confirms the content, which is where the interesting news usually is.
Look down the first values here and seven of the thirteen columns open with NA. Two different things are going on, and they are missing for different lengths of time.

sum(is.na(covid$deaths))
#> [1] 59
sum(is.na(covid$parks_percent_change_from_baseline))
#> [1] 24

deaths is missing for the first 59 rows. The first value the file carries is 2, on 21 March 2020, and it goes straight to 2 without ever passing through 1. Everything before that is stored as missing rather than as zero. Those are different claims. Zero says nobody died; NA says the source is not telling you. The distinction will cost you two deaths later in the book, when you try to recover daily deaths by differencing the column.
The six mobility columns are missing for the first 24 rows, up to and including 14 February. Google’s Community Mobility Reports express each day as a percentage change from a baseline computed over 3 January to 6 February 2020, so the series cannot start until that baseline period has finished. The chapter on missing data takes both of these apart properly; for now, the point is that glimpse() showed you within seconds of loading the file.
Three more worth having in your fingers. head() and tail() show the first and last rows, and tail() is the one that catches the summary row somebody left at the bottom of a spreadsheet. summary() gives a five-number summary of every numeric column plus a count of NAs. View() opens the spreadsheet viewer in RStudio, which is the fastest way to eyeball a small file and useless on a large one; keep it at the console and never in a script, because it does nothing in a rendered document.

View(covid)

title: 5  Reading the epidemic in
5  Reading the epidemic in
text:
5.7 One plot, as a promise
You have not been taught ggplot() yet. Run this anyway.

covid <- read_covid()

ggplot(covid, aes(x = date, y = confirmed)) +
  annotate(
    "rect",
    xmin = as.Date("2020-04-07"), xmax = as.Date("2020-06-01"),
    ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf,
    fill = nus_colours[["grey"]], alpha = 0.4
  ) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = as.Date("2020-05-04"), y = 50000,
    label = "circuit breaker", size = 3.2, colour = nus_colours[["muted"]]
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_comma()) +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "2 months", date_labels = "%b") +
  labs(
    title = "Singapore's 2020 epidemic, exactly as the file records it",
    subtitle = "Cumulative confirmed cases. Every point is a running total, not a daily count.",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Confirmed cases",
    caption = "Source: sg_covid_data.csv, 22 January to 31 December 2020."
  )







Fifty-eight thousand confirmed cases by the end of December, and a curve that turns sharply upward in April and flattens through the second half of the year. The shaded band is Singapore’s circuit breaker, 7 April to 1 June 2020.
The curve is honest and almost useless for reading an epidemic, because a cumulative total can only go up. You cannot see when transmission accelerated or when it stopped. To see that you need the daily difference, which means creating a column, which is the next chapter.

title: 5  Reading the epidemic in
text:
5.8 Exercise

Exercise 5.1 (Land the file yourself) Start a fresh R session, load the tidyverse and here, and do this without using read_covid().

Read data/sg_covid_data.csv with read_csv() and a path built by here(). Write down, in words, the type readr assigned to date, to confirmed and to administrative_area_level_1, and where in the message you found each one.
Read it a second time with the three types above stated explicitly and everything else left as double, and confirm the specification message no longer appears.
Run glimpse() and count the columns whose first value is NA. Then find the number of missing values in each of those columns, and say whether they all have the same number.
Read the same file with read.csv() instead. Find the one difference in the date column that would have forced you to write extra code, and demonstrate it failing.








Stuck? Open for a hint (not the answer)





For part 2, cols() takes named columns plus a .default for everything you did not name. For part 3, is.na() returns a logical vector and sum() counts the TRUEs. For part 4, class() on the column is the fastest tell, and the failure you want is any arithmetic on a date.



Worked solution

title: 6  Transforming data
text:
6.1 One verb, one job
dplyr is built on a small number of functions with deliberately boring names. Each one takes a data frame as its first argument, does one thing to it, and returns a data frame. They are called verbs because they are things you do to a table.
You need five of them for almost everything.

title: 6  Transforming data
text:
6.1.1 filter() keeps rows
Singapore’s circuit breaker ran from 7 April to 1 June 2020. To look at only those days:

filter(covid, date >= "2020-04-07", date <= "2020-06-01")
#> # A tibble: 56 × 13
#>    administrative_area_level_1 confirmed deaths date       stringency_index
#>    <chr>                           <dbl>  <dbl> <date>                <dbl>
#>  1 Singapore                        1481      6 2020-04-07             62.0
#>  2 Singapore                        1623      6 2020-04-08             76.8
#>  3 Singapore                        1910      6 2020-04-09             76.8
#>  4 Singapore                        2108      7 2020-04-10             82.4
#>  5 Singapore                        2299      8 2020-04-11             76.8
#>  6 Singapore                        2532      8 2020-04-12             76.8
#>  7 Singapore                        2918      9 2020-04-13             76.8
#>  8 Singapore                        3252     10 2020-04-14             76.8
#>  9 Singapore                        3699     10 2020-04-15             76.8
#> 10 Singapore                        4427     10 2020-04-16             76.8
#> # ℹ 46 more rows
#> # ℹ 8 more variables: government_response_index <dbl>,
#> #   containment_health_index <dbl>,
#> #   retail_and_recreation_percent_change_from_baseline <dbl>,
#> #   grocery_and_pharmacy_percent_change_from_baseline <dbl>,
#> #   parks_percent_change_from_baseline <dbl>,
#> #   transit_stations_percent_change_from_baseline <dbl>, …

Fifty-six rows, which is 7 April to 1 June counted inclusively. Two things are happening in that call that deserve a moment.
The first is that several conditions separated by commas are combined with and. Every condition has to hold for a row to survive. If you want or, you have to say so with |, because a comma will never mean that.
The second is that date is a proper Date column and you compared it to a piece of text. R quietly converted the text to a date for you, which works because "2020-04-07" is in ISO order: year, month, day. Write the date the way most of the world writes it and R does not complain, it gets a different answer:

as.Date("07/04/2020")
#> [1] "0007-04-20"

The seventh of April, 2020, has become the twentieth of April in the year 7. R read 07 as the year, 04 as the month and 2020 as the day, then rolled the impossible day number forward. No error, no warning, and a filter() built on that comparison would return all 345 rows while looking entirely reasonable. Use ISO dates. This is the reason the standard exists.
There is one more thing about filter() that catches everyone exactly once:

filter(covid, date = "2020-04-07")
#> Error in `filter()`:
#> ! We detected a named input.
#> ℹ This usually means that you've used `=` instead of `==`.
#> ℹ Did you mean `date == "2020-04-07"`?

One equals sign is assignment, two is comparison. dplyr recognises the mistake and tells you which one you meant, which is kinder than most of R. Base R would have silently treated it as an argument name.

6.1.2 arrange() reorders rows

arrange(covid, desc(stringency_index))
#> # A tibble: 345 × 13
#>    administrative_area_level_1 confirmed deaths date       stringency_index
#>    <chr>                           <dbl>  <dbl> <date>                <dbl>
#>  1 Singapore                        2108      7 2020-04-10             82.4
#>  2 Singapore                       12693     12 2020-04-25             82.4
#>  3 Singapore                       17101     16 2020-05-01             82.4
#>  4 Singapore                        1623      6 2020-04-08             76.8
#>  5 Singapore                        1910      6 2020-04-09             76.8
#>  6 Singapore                        2299      8 2020-04-11             76.8
#>  7 Singapore                        2532      8 2020-04-12             76.8
#>  8 Singapore                        2918      9 2020-04-13             76.8
#>  9 Singapore                        3252     10 2020-04-14             76.8
#> 10 Singapore                        3699     10 2020-04-15             76.8
#> # ℹ 335 more rows
#> # ℹ 8 more variables: government_response_index <dbl>,
#> #   containment_health_index <dbl>,
#> #   retail_and_recreation_percent_change_from_baseline <dbl>,
#> #   grocery_and_pharmacy_percent_change_from_baseline <dbl>,
#> #   parks_percent_change_from_baseline <dbl>,
#> #   transit_stations_percent_change_from_baseline <dbl>, …

The Oxford stringency index peaked at 82.41, and three separate days sit at that peak. Sorting does not deduplicate; it puts equal things next to each other and leaves them in the order it found them.
desc() looks like clutter until you try the obvious alternative:

arrange(covid, -date)
#> Error in `arrange()`:
#> ℹ In argument: `..1 = -date`.
#> Caused by error in `-.Date`:
#> ! unary - is not defined for "Date" objects

unary - is not defined for "Date" objects. Negating a number to reverse the sort works for numbers, and dates are stored as numbers underneath, but R refuses to let you do arithmetic that would produce a nonsense date. desc() works on anything that can be sorted, including text and factors, so use it and stop thinking about it.

6.1.3 select() keeps columns

select(covid, date, confirmed, deaths, stringency_index)
#> # A tibble: 345 × 4
#>    date       confirmed deaths stringency_index
#>    <date>         <dbl>  <dbl>            <dbl>
#>  1 2020-01-22         0     NA             19.4
#>  2 2020-01-23         1     NA             25  
#>  3 2020-01-24         3     NA             25  
#>  4 2020-01-25         3     NA             25  
#>  5 2020-01-26         4     NA             25  
#>  6 2020-01-27         5     NA             25  
#>  7 2020-01-28         7     NA             25  
#>  8 2020-01-29         7     NA             25  
#>  9 2020-01-30        10     NA             25  
#> 10 2020-01-31        13     NA             25  
#> # ℹ 335 more rows

The order you name them is the order you get, so select() doubles as a way to move a column to the front. There are helpers for the cases where naming every column is not sensible:

select(covid, date, ends_with("_percent_change_from_baseline"))
#> # A tibble: 345 × 7
#>    date       retail_and_recreation_percent_change_from…¹ grocery_and_pharmacy…²
#>    <date>                                           <dbl>                  <dbl>
#>  1 2020-01-22                                          NA                     NA
#>  2 2020-01-23                                          NA                     NA
#>  3 2020-01-24                                          NA                     NA
#>  4 2020-01-25                                          NA                     NA
#>  5 2020-01-26                                          NA                     NA
#>  6 2020-01-27                                          NA                     NA
#>  7 2020-01-28                                          NA                     NA
#>  8 2020-01-29                                          NA                     NA
#>  9 2020-01-30                                          NA                     NA
#> 10 2020-01-31                                          NA                     NA
#> # ℹ 335 more rows
#> # ℹ abbreviated names: ¹​retail_and_recreation_percent_change_from_baseline,
#> #   ²​grocery_and_pharmacy_percent_change_from_baseline
#> # ℹ 4 more variables: parks_percent_change_from_baseline <dbl>,
#> #   transit_stations_percent_change_from_baseline <dbl>,
#> #   workplaces_percent_change_from_baseline <dbl>,
#> #   residential_percent_change_from_baseline <dbl>

starts_with(), ends_with() and contains() all work inside select() and nowhere else, which is confusing the first time. They are part of a small language called tidyselect that only makes sense in the context of choosing columns. A leading minus drops instead of keeps:

select(covid, -administrative_area_level_1)
#> # A tibble: 345 × 12
#>    confirmed deaths date       stringency_index government_response_index
#>        <dbl>  <dbl> <date>                <dbl>                     <dbl>
#>  1         0     NA 2020-01-22             19.4                      19.3
#>  2         1     NA 2020-01-23             25                        24.5
#>  3         3     NA 2020-01-24             25                        24.5
#>  4         3     NA 2020-01-25             25                        24.5
#>  5         4     NA 2020-01-26             25                        24.5
#>  6         5     NA 2020-01-27             25                        24.5
#>  7         7     NA 2020-01-28             25                        24.5
#>  8         7     NA 2020-01-29             25                        24.5
#>  9        10     NA 2020-01-30             25                        24.5
#> 10        13     NA 2020-01-31             25                        24.5
#> # ℹ 335 more rows
#> # ℹ 7 more variables: containment_health_index <dbl>,
#> #   retail_and_recreation_percent_change_from_baseline <dbl>,
#> #   grocery_and_pharmacy_percent_change_from_baseline <dbl>,
#> #   parks_percent_change_from_baseline <dbl>,
#> #   transit_stations_percent_change_from_baseline <dbl>,
#> #   workplaces_percent_change_from_baseline <dbl>, …

That column is the string "Singapore" in all 345 rows. It is there because the data hub serves many countries from one schema, and it carries no information at all once you have filtered down to one of them.

6.1.4 rename() changes column names
retail_and_recreation_percent_change_from_baseline is fifty characters long and you will be typing it for the rest of the book. Google named it, not you, and the name is descriptive rather than convenient.

mob <- rename(
  covid,
  retail      = retail_and_recreation_percent_change_from_baseline,
  grocery     = grocery_and_pharmacy_percent_change_from_baseline,
  parks       = parks_percent_change_from_baseline,
  transit     = transit_stations_percent_change_from_baseline,
  workplaces  = workplaces_percent_change_from_baseline,
  residential = residential_percent_change_from_baseline
)

select(mob, date, retail, workplaces, residential)
#> # A tibble: 345 × 4
#>    date       retail workplaces residential
#>    <date>      <dbl>      <dbl>       <dbl>
#>  1 2020-01-22     NA         NA          NA
#>  2 2020-01-23     NA         NA          NA
#>  3 2020-01-24     NA         NA          NA
#>  4 2020-01-25     NA         NA          NA
#>  5 2020-01-26     NA         NA          NA
#>  6 2020-01-27     NA         NA          NA
#>  7 2020-01-28     NA         NA          NA
#>  8 2020-01-29     NA         NA          NA
#>  9 2020-01-30     NA         NA          NA
#> 10 2020-01-31     NA         NA          NA
#> # ℹ 335 more rows

New name on the left, old name on the right, which is the opposite of the order most people guess. The way to remember it is that rename() behaves like mutate() and every other function that makes columns: the thing being created is always on the left of the =.
The rest of this book keeps the long names, because that is what the file ships with and because a chapter that renames things in secret is a chapter you cannot copy code out of. In your own analysis, rename early and rename once.

6.1.5 mutate() makes new columns

select(
  mutate(covid, cfr = deaths / confirmed * 100),
  date, confirmed, deaths, cfr
)
#> # A tibble: 345 × 4
#>    date       confirmed deaths   cfr
#>    <date>         <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl>
#>  1 2020-01-22         0     NA    NA
#>  2 2020-01-23         1     NA    NA
#>  3 2020-01-24         3     NA    NA
#>  4 2020-01-25         3     NA    NA
#>  5 2020-01-26         4     NA    NA
#>  6 2020-01-27         5     NA    NA
#>  7 2020-01-28         7     NA    NA
#>  8 2020-01-29         7     NA    NA
#>  9 2020-01-30        10     NA    NA
#> 10 2020-01-31        13     NA    NA
#> # ℹ 335 more rows

mutate() works on whole columns at a time. There is no loop over rows; deaths / confirmed divides two vectors of 345 numbers element by element and hands back a third. This is the single biggest habit shift coming from a spreadsheet, and once it clicks, most of R gets easier.
The case fatality ratio at the end of 2020 was 29 in 58,599, or about 0.05%. That is a very low number by any international comparison of that year, and the reason is demographic before it is clinical: the great majority of Singapore’s 2020 cases came from the migrant-worker dormitory outbreak that dominated April to August, in a population of working-age adults. The ratio does not mean much until you say that.

title: 6  Transforming data
text:
6.2 Stringing verbs together
Look at what that last call became. To make a column and then choose four columns, the code reads inside out: mutate() is buried in the middle, select() wraps around it, and the data frame you started from is somewhere in the interior. Add a filter() and an arrange() and it becomes unreadable:

head(
  arrange(
    select(
      filter(covid, date >= "2020-04-07", date <= "2020-06-01"),
      date, confirmed, stringency_index
    ),
    desc(stringency_index)
  ),
  4
)
#> # A tibble: 4 × 3
#>   date       confirmed stringency_index
#>   <date>         <dbl>            <dbl>
#> 1 2020-04-10      2108             82.4
#> 2 2020-04-25     12693             82.4
#> 3 2020-05-01     17101             82.4
#> 4 2020-04-08      1623             76.8

You have to read that from the innermost bracket outwards, which is backwards from the order the operations happen and backwards from how you thought about the problem. The pipe fixes it:

covid %>%
  filter(date >= "2020-04-07", date <= "2020-06-01") %>%
  select(date, confirmed, stringency_index) %>%
  arrange(desc(stringency_index)) %>%
  head(4)
#> # A tibble: 4 × 3
#>   date       confirmed stringency_index
#>   <date>         <dbl>            <dbl>
#> 1 2020-04-10      2108             82.4
#> 2 2020-04-25     12693             82.4
#> 3 2020-05-01     17101             82.4
#> 4 2020-04-08      1623             76.8

x %>% f(y) means f(x, y). The thing on the left is passed in as the first argument of the function on the right. Because every dplyr verb takes a data frame first and returns a data frame, they chain without any glue.
Read %>% as “and then”. Take covid, and then keep the circuit-breaker days, and then keep three columns, and then sort by stringency, and then show me four rows. That is the order the sentence happens in and the order the code is written in.
Some habits worth forming now. Put the %>% at the end of the line, never at the start of the next one, because R needs to see that the line is unfinished. Indent the continuation lines. Build the chain one verb at a time, running it after each addition, rather than writing eight lines and then trying to work out which one broke. RStudio has a keyboard shortcut for the pipe: Ctrl+Shift+M on Windows and Linux, Cmd+Shift+M on a Mac.






The other pipe



R gained a pipe of its own in version 4.1, written |>. It does the same basic thing and needs no packages. It differs in the details: %>% lets you write . to put the incoming value somewhere other than the first argument, while |> has a narrower placeholder with different rules, and the two behave differently with anonymous functions. This book uses %>% throughout, so if you see |> in code you find elsewhere, it is the same idea and not a typo.

title: 6  Transforming data
text:
6.3 Cumulative counts are not incidence
Here is the epidemiology that the rest of the chapter exists to support.
confirmed only ever goes up. It went up when Singapore was recording three cases a day in February, it went up when Singapore recorded 1,426 in a single day in April, and it went up in December when the epidemic was essentially over. A cumulative curve cannot fall, so it can never show you a peak or a turn. What it shows is the total damage so far, which is a real quantity and almost never the one you want.
Incidence is the number of new cases per unit time. It is what an epidemic is: a rate, going up and coming down. It is what you fit a model to and what you compute a reproduction number from, and it is the only one of the two that can tell you whether last week was better than the week before.
Both curves below are made from the same 345 numbers.

covid_inc <- covid %>%
  arrange(date) %>%
  mutate(daily_cases = confirmed - lag(confirmed, default = 0))

p_cum <- ggplot(covid_inc, aes(date, confirmed)) +
  geom_line() +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_comma()) +
  labs(title = "Cumulative confirmed cases", x = NULL, y = NULL)

p_inc <- ggplot(covid_inc, aes(date, daily_cases)) +
  geom_col(width = 1) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_comma()) +
  labs(title = "New cases each day", x = NULL, y = NULL)

p_cum / p_inc






Figure 6.1: The same epidemic, twice. Above, the cumulative confirmed count. Below, new cases per day, derived from it.




The top panel is the shape every dashboard showed in 2020, and for judging anything it is close to useless. It rises steeply through the middle of the year and flattens at the right-hand edge, and that is all it can ever do. The peak is invisible in it. So is the fact that half the year’s cases had been confirmed by 20 May.
The bottom panel shows an epidemic. It climbs through April to a single highest day of 1,426 on 20 April, stays high through May, then falls unevenly until the week of 5 July, before a second rise carries it back up through late July into early August and it dies away from mid-August onwards. The tall isolated spike is 5 August, which recorded 908 cases against an August median of 91 and a next-highest August day of 313. Singapore’s Ministry of Health attributed that day to clearance testing in the dormitories detecting past infections. Whatever you make of the explanation, a cumulative curve would never have prompted the question.
There is a rhetorical consequence worth being alert to. A cumulative curve flatters every intervention, because after any intervention it keeps rising and can always be described as “flattening”. An incidence curve makes the claim falsifiable: either the number came down or it did not.

title: 6  Transforming data
section: 6.4 lag(), and the precondition nobody states
text:
6.4 lag(), and the precondition nobody states
The line that did the work was this:

daily_cases = confirmed - lag(confirmed, default = 0)

lag() shifts a vector one position to the right, so that each element lines up with the one before it. On a short example:

x <- c(0, 1, 3, 3, 4)
lag(x)
#> [1] NA  0  1  3  3
x - lag(x)
#> [1] NA  1  2  0  1

Element two of lag(x) is element one of x. Subtracting gives the difference between consecutive elements: the increments. The first element has nothing before it, so lag() puts NA there, and the subtraction propagates it.
Now the part that matters. lag() is positional, not date-aware. It has no idea that your data has a date column. It takes the row physically above, whatever that row happens to be. If your rows are in some other order, lag() will not warn you, will not error, and will happily compute differences between days that are months apart.
Suppose you had sorted by stringency index earlier in your session, for a perfectly good reason, and then computed daily cases without re-sorting.






Predict before you run



Of the 345 daily case counts produced from wrongly ordered rows, how many will come out negative? Commit to a number before you scroll.



scrambled <- covid %>%
  arrange(desc(stringency_index)) %>%
  mutate(daily_cases = confirmed - lag(confirmed, default = 0))

sum(scrambled$daily_cases < 0)
#> [1] 8
median(scrambled$daily_cases)
#> [1] 42

Eight. Eight rows out of 345 are negative, and the median of the wrong answer is 42 against a true value of 40. Sort the table by anything other than date and roughly 97% of the resulting daily counts still look like plausible daily counts. Some of them are even right, by accident, wherever two adjacent rows happened to be adjacent days.
This is what makes the mistake dangerous. A bug that produces obvious garbage gets caught in the first thirty seconds. A bug that produces 337 plausible numbers and 8 impossible ones gets caught when a reviewer asks about a negative value in a figure, three months later.
So: put arrange(date) in the chain, immediately before the mutate(), every time. It costs one line. It does nothing at all when the data was already sorted, which this file is.

covid <- covid %>%
  arrange(date) %>%
  mutate(daily_cases = confirmed - lag(confirmed, default = 0))

covid %>% select(date, confirmed, daily_cases)
#> # A tibble: 345 × 3
#>    date       confirmed daily_cases
#>    <date>         <dbl>       <dbl>
#>  1 2020-01-22         0           0
#>  2 2020-01-23         1           1
#>  3 2020-01-24         3           2
#>  4 2020-01-25         3           0
#>  5 2020-01-26         4           1
#>  6 2020-01-27         5           1
#>  7 2020-01-28         7           2
#>  8 2020-01-29         7           0
#>  9 2020-01-30        10           3
#> 10 2020-01-31        13           3
#> # ℹ 335 more rows

title: 6  Transforming data
section: 6.5 What belongs in the first row
text:
6.5 What belongs in the first row
lag() on its own leaves NA at the top, because there is no previous row to subtract. The default = 0 argument fills that gap with a zero instead. Whether that is right is a question about your data, not a question about R, and it is the kind of decision that gets made by accident far more often than it gets made on purpose.
Here it is right, and you can see why in the first row of the table:

covid %>% select(date, confirmed, daily_cases) %>% head(3)
#> # A tibble: 3 × 3
#>   date       confirmed daily_cases
#>   <date>         <dbl>       <dbl>
#> 1 2020-01-22         0           0
#> 2 2020-01-23         1           1
#> 3 2020-01-24         3           2

confirmed is 0 on 22 January 2020. Zero cases had been confirmed by the end of that day, so zero cases were confirmed during it. That is a real observation, not a gap. Recording it as NA would throw away a genuine zero and quietly shorten the series by one day in every count, sum and plot downstream.
The picture changes completely if the series does not start at zero. Suppose your extract began on 1 March, when the cumulative total was already 106. Then default = 0 would compute 106 new cases on 1 March, which is not what happened; those 106 accumulated over the preceding weeks. On that series the honest answer is NA, because you have no information about how many cases occurred on the first day of a window you did not observe the start of.
Two conventions, two different datasets, and no default to memorise. Look at the first value. If it is zero, default = 0 records a true zero. If it is not, plain lag() and an NA tells the truth about what you do not know. The book uses default = 0 from here on because this file starts at zero, and that is the only reason.

title: 6  Transforming data
section: 6.6 Two checks worth running every time
text:
6.6 Two checks worth running every time
Derived columns are where quiet errors live, because nothing about them looks different from data that came out of a file. Two cheap checks catch most of what can go wrong with a difference of a cumulative series.
The first is that a difference of a non-decreasing count cannot be negative. If a negative appears, either the rows are out of order or the source revised its figures downward.

covid %>% filter(daily_cases < 0)
#> # A tibble: 0 × 14
#> # ℹ 14 variables: administrative_area_level_1 <chr>, confirmed <dbl>,
#> #   deaths <dbl>, date <date>, stringency_index <dbl>,
#> #   government_response_index <dbl>, containment_health_index <dbl>,
#> #   retail_and_recreation_percent_change_from_baseline <dbl>,
#> #   grocery_and_pharmacy_percent_change_from_baseline <dbl>,
#> #   parks_percent_change_from_baseline <dbl>,
#> #   transit_stations_percent_change_from_baseline <dbl>, …

Zero rows. What comes back is an empty tibble rather than nothing at all, and the empty tibble still knows its column names and types, which is how you can tell the check ran instead of failing silently.
The second is that the daily numbers must add back up to the cumulative total. The increments telescope: every intermediate value cancels, leaving the last one.

sum(covid$daily_cases) == max(covid$confirmed)
#> [1] TRUE
sum(covid$daily_cases)
#> [1] 58599

58,599 either way. Run the same check on the scrambled version and it fails, because the “last” row in stringency order is 22 January, where the cumulative total is 0.

sum(scrambled$daily_cases) == max(scrambled$confirmed)
#> [1] FALSE

A test that fails when the code is wrong and passes when it is right is worth the two lines it takes to write. Keep both of these near the top of any script that differences a cumulative series.
One warning about applying the same recipe to deaths. It has 59 missing values at the start, the differencing will not reconcile, and you will recover 27 of the 29 deaths rather than all of them. That is not a mistake you made and it is the subject of Chapter 7.

title: 6  Transforming data
text:
6.7 Exercises

Exercise 6.1 (Build a circuit-breaker table) Using only filter(), select(), rename(), arrange() and the pipe, produce a table covering the circuit breaker (7 April to 1 June 2020 inclusive) that contains the date, the cumulative confirmed count, the stringency index, and the retail and workplace mobility columns under short names of your choosing. Sort it so that the deepest workplace mobility drops appear first.
Then answer two things from the result. How many rows does it have, and does that match the number of calendar days in the period? And what do the top three rows have in common as dates, once you look them up?







Stuck? Open for a hint (not the answer)





rename() and select() can both give a column a new name, so you can do it in one step or two. For the second question, count the days from 7 April to 1 June by hand and remember that both endpoints are included.



Worked solution

Exercise 6.2 (Difference the deaths series) Apply the same pattern you used for cases to the deaths column: sort by date, then make a daily_deaths column by subtracting the lagged cumulative count.
Then run both of the checks from this chapter on it. Are there any negative values? Does the total of the daily numbers equal the final cumulative figure? Report exactly what you get from each check, including anything R does with missing values along the way.
Finally, find the largest single-day increase in deaths and the date it happened. Do not repair the shortfall you find; the next chapter is about where it went.







Stuck? Open for a hint (not the answer)





sum() on a vector containing NA returns NA, so you will need to decide what to tell it to do about that, and the decision is part of the answer. Look at the rows around the first date on which deaths is not missing.



Worked solution

title: 7  Missing values
text:
7.1 Where the gaps are
Counting missing values is sum() over is.na(). is.na() returns TRUE or FALSE for each element, and sum() treats TRUE as 1.
covid %>%
  summarise(
    confirmed   = sum(is.na(confirmed)),
    deaths      = sum(is.na(deaths)),
    stringency  = sum(is.na(stringency_index)),
    retail      = sum(is.na(retail_and_recreation_percent_change_from_baseline)),
    workplaces  = sum(is.na(workplaces_percent_change_from_baseline)),
    residential = sum(is.na(residential_percent_change_from_baseline))
  )
#> # A tibble: 1 × 6
#>   confirmed deaths stringency retail workplaces residential
#>       <int>  <int>      <int>  <int>      <int>       <int>
#> 1         0     59          0     24         24          24
Naming six columns by hand does not scale, and there is a version later in the book that runs the same count across every column at once. For now the answer is stark enough: the case counts and the policy indices are complete for all 345 days, deaths is missing on 59 of them, and every mobility column is missing on exactly 24.
Exactly 24, in all six. That is a strong hint that they went missing together, for one shared reason, and they did.
covid %>%
  filter(is.na(retail_and_recreation_percent_change_from_baseline)) %>%
  summarise(n = n(), first = min(date), last = max(date))
#> # A tibble: 1 × 3
#>       n first      last      
#>   <int> <date>     <date>    
#> 1    24 2020-01-22 2020-02-14

covid %>%
  filter(is.na(deaths)) %>%
  summarise(n = n(), first = min(date), last = max(date))
#> # A tibble: 1 × 3
#>       n first      last      
#>   <int> <date>     <date>    
#> 1    59 2020-01-22 2020-03-20
Two solid blocks at the start of the year, of different lengths, ending on different days. Neither is scattered, and neither is random.

title: 7  Missing values
text:
7.2 Two kinds of missing
The mobility gap runs from 22 January to 14 February. Google’s Community Mobility Reports express each day as a percentage change from a baseline, and that baseline is the median for the corresponding day of the week over the five weeks from 3 January to 6 February 2020. A percentage change from a baseline cannot be computed before the baseline period has closed, and Google’s published series begins on 15 February. The missing days are a property of the instrument. Nothing happened in Singapore on 3 February that made mobility unmeasurable; the yardstick did not exist yet.
The deaths gap runs from 22 January to 20 March, and it ends because Singapore’s first recorded COVID-19 deaths appear in the data on 21 March. Before that there was no death count to report, and the data hub carries nothing rather than a zero. This gap is a property of the epidemic.
That difference decides everything downstream. For deaths, you know what the missing value would have been if someone had written it down: zero. Zero deaths had been recorded, so the cumulative count was zero, and substituting a zero is recovering a fact rather than inventing one. For mobility, you have no idea. Substituting a zero would assert that retail activity in early February sat exactly at its baseline, which is a measurement Google never made and you cannot make on their behalf.
A blank in a spreadsheet looks the same in both cases. Only you know which one you have.
Here is what the mobility gap looks like when you plot straight over it:

ggplot(covid, aes(date, retail_and_recreation_percent_change_from_baseline)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(
    title = "Retail and recreation mobility",
    x = NULL, y = "% change from baseline"
  )
#> Warning: Removed 24 rows containing missing values or values outside the scale range
#> (`geom_line()`).






Figure 7.1: Retail and recreation mobility, plotted without doing anything about the missing days.




The missing days leave no hole. The line starts later, the x-axis quietly begins in February, and unless you already knew the file covered January you would never ask. The warning printed above the figure is the only thing that tells you, which is a reason to leave warnings switched on in your own work rather than tidying them away.

title: 7  Missing values
text:
7.3 What NA does to arithmetic
NA in R means “there is a value here and I do not know it”. Any calculation involving an unknown produces an unknown:

retail_sample <- c(-15, NA, -51, NA, -63)

sum(retail_sample)
#> [1] NA
mean(retail_sample)
#> [1] NA

This is deliberate and it is a feature. R refuses to give you an average that quietly ignores two fifths of your data. If you want it to ignore them, say so:

sum(retail_sample, na.rm = TRUE)
#> [1] -129
mean(retail_sample, na.rm = TRUE)
#> [1] -43

na.rm = TRUE means “remove the missing values before doing the sum”. What comes back is the mean of the three days you have, and calling it “the mean” without saying so is where a lot of quietly wrong analysis starts.
Comparisons behave the same way, and this is the part that bites:

retail_sample < -30
#> [1] FALSE    NA  TRUE    NA  TRUE

NA < -30 is NA, not FALSE. R does not know what the value is, so it cannot know whether it is below −30. Refusing to guess is the right behaviour and it is about to cause a great deal of trouble.
The same logic explains why you cannot test for missingness with ==:

NA == NA
#> [1] NA

Two unknowns are not known to be equal. That is what is.na() is for, and it is the only thing that works.

7.3.1 When na.rm runs out of data
Try to average January’s retail mobility, where every single value is missing:

january <- covid %>% filter(date < "2020-02-01")

nrow(january)
#> [1] 10
sum(is.na(january$retail_and_recreation_percent_change_from_baseline))
#> [1] 10

mean(january$retail_and_recreation_percent_change_from_baseline, na.rm = TRUE)
#> [1] NaN

NaN, not NA and not an error. Ten rows, ten missing values. na.rm = TRUE removed all ten, leaving a vector of length zero. mean() on nothing is the sum of nothing divided by the count of nothing, which is 0 divided by 0, which is NaN: not a number.

sum(numeric(0))
#> [1] 0
0 / 0
#> [1] NaN

NaN stands for a computation that has no meaningful answer, as distinct from NA, which stands for a value you do not have. is.na() returns TRUE for both, so a missing-value check will not distinguish them, and is.nan() will:

is.na(NaN)
#> [1] TRUE
is.nan(NA)
#> [1] FALSE

If a monthly summary comes back with NaN in one row, you have not found a strange bug. You have found a month with no data in it at all, and na.rm = TRUE did exactly what you told it to.

title: 7  Missing values
text:
7.4 Filling in and dropping out
Two more tools, both from the tidyverse, both easy to reach for too quickly.
coalesce() takes the first non-missing value across its arguments, element by element:

coalesce(retail_sample, 0)
#> [1] -15   0 -51   0 -63

This is the right thing to do to deaths and the wrong thing to do to mobility, for the reason set out above. The recipe below is defensible because the claim it encodes is true: before 21 March, Singapore’s cumulative recorded COVID-19 deaths were zero.

covid %>%
  arrange(date) %>%
  mutate(deaths_filled = coalesce(deaths, 0)) %>%
  filter(date >= "2020-03-19", date <= "2020-03-22") %>%
  select(date, deaths, deaths_filled)
#> # A tibble: 4 × 3
#>   date       deaths deaths_filled
#>   <date>      <dbl>         <dbl>
#> 1 2020-03-19     NA             0
#> 2 2020-03-20     NA             0
#> 3 2020-03-21      2             2
#> 4 2020-03-22      2             2

drop_na() removes whole rows. Applied to the entire table it is blunter than people expect:

nrow(covid)
#> [1] 345
nrow(drop_na(covid))
#> [1] 286

Fifty-nine days gone, and not because their mobility or stringency data was bad. They went because deaths was missing, and drop_na() with no arguments drops a row if any column in it is missing. Those 59 days include 35 days of perfectly good mobility readings and 59 days of case counts, all thrown away to fix a problem in a column you might not even have been using.
Name the columns you actually care about and the damage is proportionate:

nrow(drop_na(covid, ends_with("_percent_change_from_baseline")))
#> [1] 321

title: 7  Missing values
section: 7.5 The 112 rows that should have been 88
text:
7.5 The 112 rows that should have been 88
Now the bug.
A reasonable question about the circuit breaker: on how many days did retail and recreation mobility sit more than 30% below baseline? The worksheet asked it in base R, which is how most people were taught to subset a data frame, and how most people still write it when they are in a hurry.






Predict before you run



You are about to ask that question twice, once in base R and once with filter(). Write down whether you expect the two to agree. If you expect them to differ, write down by how much.



low_retail <- covid[covid$retail_and_recreation_percent_change_from_baseline < -30, ]
nrow(low_retail)
#> [1] 112

112 days. Now the dplyr version of the identical question:

low_retail_tidy <- covid %>%
  filter(retail_and_recreation_percent_change_from_baseline < -30)

nrow(low_retail_tidy)
#> [1] 88


The two answers differ by 24, which is a number you have already met on this page.

Look at what came back from the first one:

low_retail %>%
  select(date, confirmed, retail_and_recreation_percent_change_from_baseline)
#> # A tibble: 112 × 3
#>    date   confirmed retail_and_recreation_percent_change_from_baseline
#>    <date>     <dbl>                                              <dbl>
#>  1 NA            NA                                                 NA
#>  2 NA            NA                                                 NA
#>  3 NA            NA                                                 NA
#>  4 NA            NA                                                 NA
#>  5 NA            NA                                                 NA
#>  6 NA            NA                                                 NA
#>  7 NA            NA                                                 NA
#>  8 NA            NA                                                 NA
#>  9 NA            NA                                                 NA
#> 10 NA            NA                                                 NA
#> # ℹ 102 more rows

Twenty-four rows in which every column is missing, including date, including confirmed, sitting at the top of the result. Those days are not in the data twice. They are not in the result at all, in any meaningful sense. They are artefacts of how base R indexes with a logical vector.
The chain runs like this. The comparison is evaluated first, giving one TRUE, FALSE or NA per row:

head(covid$retail_and_recreation_percent_change_from_baseline, 3)
#> [1] NA NA NA
head(covid$retail_and_recreation_percent_change_from_baseline < -30, 3)
#> [1] NA NA NA

Twenty-four of those 345 values are NA, because NA < -30 is NA. Then that vector goes to [, and base R’s rule for logical indexing is that TRUE returns the element, FALSE skips it, and NA returns a missing element. On a plain vector this is visible in one line:

retail_sample
#> [1] -15  NA -51  NA -63
retail_sample[retail_sample < -30]
#> [1]  NA -51  NA -63

Four elements out of five, from a condition that only two of them satisfy. Applied to a data frame, “return a missing element” means “return a row of nothing”, so each of the 24 unknown days becomes a full row of NA. 88 real rows plus 24 phantoms is 112.
The worksheet’s next line asked which days those were. A student who had done everything correctly up to that point got this:

head(low_retail$date, 5)
#> [1] NA NA NA NA NA

Five missing dates, from a variable that has no missing dates anywhere in the file. Nothing about that output tells you what went wrong, and the natural conclusion is that you broke something.
filter() takes the opposite position and documents it in one sentence: it treats NA like FALSE. A row that might qualify is not a row that does qualify, so it does not come back. What you get is the 88 days filter() can vouch for, dates intact:

head(low_retail_tidy$date, 5)
#> [1] "2020-04-07" "2020-04-08" "2020-04-09" "2020-04-10" "2020-04-11"
max(low_retail_tidy$date)
#> [1] "2020-07-13"

7 April, the first day of the circuit breaker, and the last such day is 13 July, a little over three weeks into Phase 2 reopening.
This is not a base-R-versus-tidyverse argument, and base R gives you two ways to get the right answer. subset() drops NA rows for the same reason filter() does, and wrapping the condition in which() converts it from a logical vector into positions, which discards the NAs on the way:

nrow(subset(covid, retail_and_recreation_percent_change_from_baseline < -30))
#> [1] 88
nrow(covid[which(covid$retail_and_recreation_percent_change_from_baseline < -30), ])
#> [1] 88

Three functions agree on 88. The single-bracket subscript is the odd one out, and it is the one that beginners are taught first.

quiet_days <- covid %>%
  filter(retail_and_recreation_percent_change_from_baseline < -30)

ggplot(covid, aes(date, retail_and_recreation_percent_change_from_baseline)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = -30, colour = nus_colours[["muted"]], linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_line(colour = nus_colours[["grey"]]) +
  geom_point(data = quiet_days, colour = nus_colours[["crimson"]], size = 0.9) +
  labs(
    title = "88 days more than 30% below baseline",
    subtitle = "First 7 April, last 13 July",
    x = NULL, y = "% change from baseline"
  )
#> Warning: Removed 24 rows containing missing values or values outside the scale range
#> (`geom_line()`).






Figure 7.2: The 88 days on which retail and recreation mobility sat more than 30% below Google’s baseline.




Eighty-eight is a defensible answer to the question that was asked. One hundred and twelve is 27% too large, and the 24 days it added are days on which nobody knows what Singapore’s retail mobility was, which is precisely why they should not be counted as days it was low.

title: 7  Missing values
section: 7.6 The two deaths that differencing loses
text:
7.6 The two deaths that differencing loses
Chapter 6 left you with a warning about deaths, and now you have the machinery to see it. Difference the cumulative death count exactly as you differenced cases:

deaths_daily <- covid %>%
  arrange(date) %>%
  mutate(daily_deaths = deaths - lag(deaths, default = 0))

sum(deaths_daily$daily_deaths, na.rm = TRUE)
#> [1] 27
max(deaths_daily$deaths, na.rm = TRUE)
#> [1] 29

Twenty-seven against a true total of 29. The check from the last chapter fails, and the two missing deaths are both on one row:

deaths_daily %>%
  filter(date >= "2020-03-19", date <= "2020-03-23") %>%
  select(date, deaths, daily_deaths)
#> # A tibble: 5 × 3
#>   date       deaths daily_deaths
#>   <date>      <dbl>        <dbl>
#> 1 2020-03-19     NA           NA
#> 2 2020-03-20     NA           NA
#> 3 2020-03-21      2           NA
#> 4 2020-03-22      2            0
#> 5 2020-03-23      2            0

On 21 March the cumulative count goes from missing to 2. Two and not one, because the record shows both of Singapore’s first COVID-19 deaths on the same day. Subtracting the previous row gives 2 - NA, which is NA, and sum(na.rm = TRUE) then quietly drops it. Two deaths, lost to a data-processing convention.
Coalescing first fixes it, and now you can say out loud why that is legitimate rather than convenient:

covid %>%
  arrange(date) %>%
  mutate(
    deaths = coalesce(deaths, 0),
    daily_deaths = deaths - lag(deaths, default = 0)
  ) %>%
  summarise(total = sum(daily_deaths))
#> # A tibble: 1 × 1
#>   total
#>   <dbl>
#> 1    29

The covid_daily() helper that later chapters open with does not do this. It differences deaths as it finds them, so its daily_deaths column carries NA for the first 60 days and sums to 27. That is a choice to stay close to what the file says rather than to what you believe about it, and it is defensible in the other direction. What is not defensible is summing that column with na.rm = TRUE, calling the result the 2020 death toll, and never noticing the two you dropped.

title: 7  Missing values
text:
7.7 Exercise

Exercise 7.1 (Interrogate the mobility gap)  

Establish whether the 24 missing days are the same 24 days in all six mobility columns, or merely the same number of days in each. Counting is not enough here; you need to compare which rows.
Compute the mean parks mobility for February 2020 with na.rm = TRUE. Report the number, then report how many days it is actually the mean of, and write one sentence explaining why “February’s average parks mobility” would be a misleading label for it.
Ask how many days parks mobility fell below −40, twice: once with the single-bracket subscript and once with filter(). Predict the size of the gap between the two answers before you run either, then explain the gap you get in one sentence.








Stuck? Open for a hint (not the answer)





For part 1, which(is.na(x)) gives you the row numbers rather than a count, and two sets of row numbers can be compared directly. For part 3, the difference between the two answers is the same number for every mobility column, and you already know what it is.



Worked solution

title: 8  Making decisions
text:
8.1 Where we are
Everything here starts from the daily counts you built in the previous chapter. The file ships cumulative totals, so a day’s new cases is today’s total minus yesterday’s, and lag(confirmed, default = 0) supplies the “yesterday” for the very first row. That default matters: confirmed is 0 on 22 January, so day one had a real zero of new cases, not a missing one.
covid <- read_covid() %>%
  arrange(date) %>%
  mutate(daily_cases = confirmed - lag(confirmed, default = 0))

covid %>%
  select(date, confirmed, daily_cases) %>%
  slice(85:90)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 3
#>   date       confirmed daily_cases
#>   <date>         <dbl>       <dbl>
#> 1 2020-04-15      3699         447
#> 2 2020-04-16      4427         728
#> 3 2020-04-17      5050         623
#> 4 2020-04-18      5992         942
#> 5 2020-04-19      6588         596
#> 6 2020-04-20      8014        1426

title: 8  Making decisions
text:
8.2 if asks exactly one question
R’s if is a control-flow statement. It looks at a single TRUE or FALSE and picks which block of code to run. It is the right tool when you are deciding something about your analysis as a whole.

worst <- max(covid$daily_cases)
worst
#> [1] 1426

if (worst > 1000) {
  "Singapore recorded a four-figure day."
} else {
  "No day reached a thousand."
}
#> [1] "Singapore recorded a four-figure day."

worst is one number. worst > 1000 is one TRUE. if is happy.
Now the mistake. Suppose you want a label on every row, and you write the thing that reads like English:

if (covid$daily_cases > 300) "High" else "Not high"
#> Error in `if (covid$daily_cases > 300) ...`:
#> ! the condition has length > 1

covid$daily_cases > 300 is not one TRUE. It is 345 of them.

length(covid$daily_cases > 300)
#> [1] 345

if has no way to act on 345 answers at once, so it refuses. The message to search for is the condition has length > 1.
This error is newer than you might expect. Up to R 4.1, that same code ran: R warned you, silently took the first element, and carried on. A script could label the entire dataset “Not high” because 22 January happened to have zero cases, and the only sign of trouble was a warning most people scroll past. R 4.2 promoted it to an error. If you find an old script or a Stack Overflow answer that relies on the old behaviour, that is why it no longer works, and the change was an improvement.
When you do want a whole-dataset question, collapse the vector to one value first. any() and all() are built for this.

if (any(covid$daily_cases > 1000)) {
  "At least one day topped a thousand."
}
#> [1] "At least one day topped a thousand."

title: 8  Making decisions
text:
8.3 if_else() builds a column
For a label on every row you want a vectorised choice: one input vector in, one output vector out, same length. dplyr’s if_else() does that.

covid %>%
  mutate(big_day = if_else(daily_cases > 300, "High", "Not high")) %>%
  count(big_day)
#> # A tibble: 2 × 2
#>   big_day      n
#>   <chr>    <int>
#> 1 High        77
#> 2 Not high   268

Read the arguments as a sentence: for each row, test daily_cases > 300; where it is TRUE use "High", where it is FALSE use "Not high".
if_else() is fussy about types, and the fussiness is deliberate:

covid %>%
  mutate(big_day = if_else(daily_cases > 300, "High", 0))
#> Error in `mutate()` at magrittr/R/pipe.R:136:3:
#> ℹ In argument: `big_day = if_else(daily_cases > 300, "High", 0)`.
#> Caused by error in `if_else()`:
#> ! Can't combine `true` <character> and `false` <double>.

Can’t combine true  and false  means you asked for a column that would be text on some rows and a number on others. R will not guess which one you meant. Base R’s ifelse() will guess, and its guesses are how people lose data. Watch what happens to a date column:

big <- covid %>%
  filter(daily_cases > 300) %>%
  slice(1:3)

ifelse(big$daily_cases > 300, big$date, as.Date(NA))
#> [1] 18365 18366 18367

Those five-digit numbers are days since 1 January 1970, which is how R stores a Date underneath. ifelse() stripped the class and handed back the raw integers. Somebody has spent an evening trying to work out why their outbreak started in 1970.

if_else(big$daily_cases > 300, big$date, as.Date(NA))
#> [1] "2020-04-13" "2020-04-14" "2020-04-15"

Same question, dates intact. Use if_else().

title: 8  Making decisions
section: 8.4 case_when() when there are more than two answers
text:
8.4 case_when() when there are more than two answers
Two labels is one test. Three labels needs two tests, and nesting if_else() inside if_else() inside if_else() produces code nobody can read six months later. case_when() replaces the nesting with a list of conditions, each paired with the value to use when it matches.
The cutoffs the course uses: under 100 new cases is Low, 100 up to and including 300 is Medium, over 300 is High.

covid <- covid %>%
  mutate(
    severity = case_when(
      daily_cases <  100 ~ "Low",
      daily_cases <= 300 ~ "Medium",
      daily_cases >  300 ~ "High"
    )
  )

covid %>% count(severity)
#> # A tibble: 3 × 2
#>   severity     n
#>   <chr>    <int>
#> 1 High        77
#> 2 Low        215
#> 3 Medium      53

The ~ separates the test from the result. You will meet that squiggle again in formulas and in ggplot facets; here it means “gives”.
case_when() works top to bottom and first match wins. Once a row matches a line, later lines never see it. That is what lets the second condition be daily_cases <= 300 and not daily_cases >= 100 & daily_cases <= 300: any row still being tested on line two already failed line one, so it already has at least 100 cases.
Which also means the order is load-bearing. Swap the first two lines and the arithmetic is identical but the answer is not:

covid %>%
  mutate(
    wrong = case_when(
      daily_cases <= 300 ~ "Medium",
      daily_cases <  100 ~ "Low",
      daily_cases >  300 ~ "High"
    )
  ) %>%
  count(wrong)
#> # A tibble: 2 × 2
#>   wrong      n
#>   <chr>  <int>
#> 1 High      77
#> 2 Medium   268

Every Low day matched “Medium” on the way past and never reached its own line. No error, no warning, 215 days mislabelled. When a case_when() gives you a category with a suspiciously round zero or a suspiciously large count, read the order before you read anything else.
The other failure mode is a row that matches nothing at all. Drop the last line and the 77 High days have nowhere to go:

covid %>%
  mutate(
    incomplete = case_when(
      daily_cases <  100 ~ "Low",
      daily_cases <= 300 ~ "Medium"
    )
  ) %>%
  count(incomplete)
#> # A tibble: 3 × 2
#>   incomplete     n
#>   <chr>      <int>
#> 1 Low          215
#> 2 Medium        53
#> 3 <NA>          77

case_when() returns NA for unmatched rows rather than complaining, so this only shows up if you look. .default catches everything that falls through and is worth using whenever your conditions are meant to be exhaustive:

covid %>%
  mutate(
    severity_alt = case_when(
      daily_cases <  100 ~ "Low",
      daily_cases <= 300 ~ "Medium",
      .default = "High"
    )
  ) %>%
  count(severity_alt)
#> # A tibble: 3 × 2
#>   severity_alt     n
#>   <chr>        <int>
#> 1 High            77
#> 2 Low            215
#> 3 Medium          53

title: 8  Making decisions
text:
8.5 The boundaries are real days
“100 to 300” is ambiguous in English and unambiguous in code, which is exactly where specifications go wrong. Is a day with exactly 100 cases Low or Medium? Is 300 Medium or High? Somebody has to decide, and in a real outbreak that somebody is you, at half past five, on the phone.
This dataset contains days sitting on both ends of the rule.






Predict before you run



Two days in August: 18 August had exactly 100 new cases, and 6 August had 301. Under the cutoffs written above, write down the label each of them gets before you look. If you are not sure, that is the point of the exercise.



covid %>%
  filter(date %in% as.Date(c("2020-08-06", "2020-08-18"))) %>%
  select(date, confirmed, daily_cases, severity)
#> # A tibble: 2 × 4
#>   date       confirmed daily_cases severity
#>   <date>         <dbl>       <dbl> <chr>   
#> 1 2020-08-06     54555         301 High    
#> 2 2020-08-18     55938         100 Medium

18 August is Medium because daily_cases < 100 is FALSE at exactly 100, so it fell through to the <= 300 line. 6 August is High because 301 is one case past <= 300. Change < to <= on the first line and 18 August becomes Low. One character, one day, and if that day is the one in the headline you will hear about it.
Write your thresholds down in prose next to the code, with the inequalities spelled out. “Fewer than 100” and “up to 100” are different rules and they will disagree on real days.

title: 8  Making decisions
text:
8.6 Missing values fall straight through
Neither if_else() nor case_when() treats NA as FALSE. NA > 0 is NA, which is neither branch, so the result is NA. Deaths in this file are missing for the first 59 days, so they show it plainly:

covid %>%
  mutate(
    daily_deaths = deaths - lag(deaths, default = 0),
    death_day = if_else(daily_deaths > 0, "yes", "no")
  ) %>%
  count(death_day)
#> # A tibble: 3 × 2
#>   death_day     n
#>   <chr>     <int>
#> 1 no          260
#> 2 yes          25
#> 3 <NA>         60

Sixty rows came back NA: the 59 days before any death total was published, plus the first day that had one, which has no valid predecessor to difference against. if_else() gives you a missing = argument to label them explicitly:

covid %>%
  mutate(
    daily_deaths = deaths - lag(deaths, default = 0),
    death_day = if_else(daily_deaths > 0, "yes", "no", missing = "not reported yet")
  ) %>%
  count(death_day)
#> # A tibble: 3 × 2
#>   death_day            n
#>   <chr>            <int>
#> 1 no                 260
#> 2 not reported yet    60
#> 3 yes                 25

In case_when() you do the same thing with an is.na() line placed first, so that missing rows are claimed before any comparison gets a chance to return NA. “No deaths reported” and “deaths not reported” are different findings and a table that merges them is a table that misleads.

title: 8  Making decisions
section: 8.7 table() sorts alphabetically, and that is wrong here
text:
8.7 table() sorts alphabetically, and that is wrong here
count() is the dplyr way. Base R’s table() is shorter and you will meet it in other people’s code, so look at what it does with the labels:

table(covid$severity)
#> 
#>   High    Low Medium 
#>     77    215     53

High, Low, Medium. Alphabetical order, and alphabetical order for an ordered variable is meaningless. It puts the worst category first and the middle category last, and every bar chart, every legend and every summary table you build from that column will inherit the nonsense.
R sorts alphabetically because severity is currently plain text:

class(covid$severity)
#> [1] "character"

Text has no order except the dictionary’s. Telling R that these three strings are levels of a categorical variable, in a specific order, is what factor() is for.

covid <- covid %>%
  mutate(severity = factor(severity, levels = c("Low", "Medium", "High")))

table(covid$severity)
#> 
#>    Low Medium   High 
#>    215     53     77

215 Low, 53 Medium, 77 High. They sum to 345, which is every day of the dataset, so nothing fell through the conditions.
A factor stores small integers plus a lookup table of labels, which is why the ordering sticks:

levels(covid$severity)
#> [1] "Low"    "Medium" "High"
as.integer(head(covid$severity, 5))
#> [1] 1 1 1 1 1
head(covid$severity, 5)
#> [1] Low Low Low Low Low
#> Levels: Low Medium High

Rows 1 to 5 are stored as 1, displayed as Low, and sorted first because Low is level one. ggplot reads exactly the same information, so the same fix that repairs table() repairs your axes:

p_chr <- ggplot(covid, aes(x = as.character(severity))) +
  geom_bar() +
  labs(title = "Stored as text", x = NULL, y = "Days")

p_fct <- ggplot(covid, aes(x = severity)) +
  geom_bar() +
  labs(title = "Stored as a factor", x = NULL, y = "Days")

p_chr + p_fct






Figure 8.1: The same 345 days, counted twice. Only the ordering differs.




You will be doing this for the rest of your career. Age bands, Likert scales, disease stages, income quintiles, WHO regions ordered by anything other than the alphabet: every one of them arrives as text and every one of them needs factor(levels = ...) before it plots correctly. It is not a beginner’s workaround. It is the fix.
One trap while you are learning it. factor() silently converts any value not listed in levels to NA, including one that differs only in case:

head(factor(as.character(covid$severity), levels = c("low", "Medium", "High")))
#> [1] <NA> <NA> <NA> <NA> <NA> <NA>
#> Levels: low Medium High
table(factor(as.character(covid$severity), levels = c("low", "Medium", "High")), useNA = "ifany")
#> 
#>    low Medium   High   <NA> 
#>      0     53     77    215

A lower-case l sent 215 days to NA without a word of complaint. After you create a factor, run table(..., useNA = "ifany") or count() once and check the total still matches your row count. Two seconds, and it catches this every time.

title: 8  Making decisions
section: 8.8 What the rest of the book starts from
text:
8.8 What the rest of the book starts from
Putting the pieces together, here is the dataset from this point on: the file as it ships, sorted by date, with daily counts differenced out of the cumulative columns, a severity factor in sensible order, and a month column produced by rounding each date down to the first of its month.

covid <- read_covid() %>%
  arrange(date) %>%
  mutate(
    daily_cases  = confirmed - lag(confirmed, default = 0),
    daily_deaths = deaths - lag(deaths, default = 0),
    severity = case_when(
      daily_cases <  100 ~ "Low",
      daily_cases <= 300 ~ "Medium",
      daily_cases >  300 ~ "High"
    ),
    severity = factor(severity, levels = c("Low", "Medium", "High")),
    month = floor_date(date, "month")
  )

covid %>%
  select(date, daily_cases, daily_deaths, severity, month) %>%
  slice(85:88)
#> # A tibble: 4 × 5
#>   date       daily_cases daily_deaths severity month     
#>   <date>           <dbl>        <dbl> <fct>    <date>    
#> 1 2020-04-15         447            0 High     2020-04-01
#> 2 2020-04-16         728            0 High     2020-04-01
#> 3 2020-04-17         623            1 High     2020-04-01
#> 4 2020-04-18         942            0 High     2020-04-01

That block is exactly what covid_daily() runs. Later chapters open with covid <- covid_daily() instead of retyping it, and _common.R in the project root holds the definition if you want to read it. Nothing is hidden in there that you have not now built by hand.

title: 8  Making decisions
text:
8.9 Exercises

Exercise 8.1 (Audit your severity column) Do not trust severity because you wrote it. Check it.

Confirm the three counts add up to 345 and that no day came back NA.
For each label, report the smallest and the largest daily_cases it contains.
Look at the numbers from step 2 either side of each cutoff, and say how far you could move the 100 threshold, in either direction, before a single day changed its label.

Step 3 is the one worth thinking about. Write down what it tells you about how much the labelling really depends on the exact number 100.







Stuck? Open for a hint (not the answer)





group_by(severity) followed by a summarise() containing n(), min() and max() answers steps 1 and 2 in one call, and grouping is the next chapter so treat this as a preview rather than something you should already know. For the NA check, count() shows a missing category if one exists.



Worked solution

Exercise 8.2 (Move the cutoffs and watch the headline move) The 100 and 300 thresholds were chosen by whoever wrote the original worksheet, not by nature. Rebuild severity with cutoffs at 50 and 500 instead, keeping the same boundary conventions (under 50 is Low, 50 up to and including 500 is Medium, over 500 is High).
Report the three counts under the new rule, and compare them with 215 / 53 / 77. Then write two sentences you would be willing to put in a report under each set of cutoffs, describing how severe 2020 was. Both sentences must be true of the same 345 days.







Stuck? Open for a hint (not the answer)





Copy the case_when() block, change the two numbers, and give the new column a different name so you can count() both and put the results side by side. Do not forget the factor() line, or your new column will sort alphabetically again.



Worked solution

title: 9  Grouping and summarising
text:
9.1 count() does the obvious thing
covid %>% count(severity)
#> # A tibble: 3 × 2
#>   severity     n
#>   <fct>    <int>
#> 1 Low        215
#> 2 Medium      53
#> 3 High        77
215 days Low, 53 Medium, 77 High. The column of counts is called n, which is dplyr’s convention everywhere.
sort = TRUE puts the biggest pile first, which is what you want when there are forty categories and you care about the top few:
covid %>% count(severity, sort = TRUE)
#> # A tibble: 3 × 2
#>   severity     n
#>   <fct>    <int>
#> 1 Low        215
#> 2 High        77
#> 3 Medium      53
Give it two columns and it counts every combination that occurs:
covid %>% count(month, severity)
#> # A tibble: 18 × 3
#>    month      severity     n
#>    <date>     <fct>    <int>
#>  1 2020-01-01 Low         10
#>  2 2020-02-01 Low         29
#>  3 2020-03-01 Low         31
#>  4 2020-04-01 Low          5
#>  5 2020-04-01 Medium       7
#>  6 2020-04-01 High        18
#>  7 2020-05-01 High        31
#>  8 2020-06-01 Medium      18
#>  9 2020-06-01 High        12
#> 10 2020-07-01 Medium      19
#> 11 2020-07-01 High        12
#> 12 2020-08-01 Low         18
#> 13 2020-08-01 Medium       9
#> 14 2020-08-01 High         4
#> 15 2020-09-01 Low         30
#> 16 2020-10-01 Low         31
#> 17 2020-11-01 Low         30
#> 18 2020-12-01 Low         31
Combinations that never happened are absent rather than zero. January has one row, not three, because there were no Medium or High days in January.
