If that loop had been accumulating a total instead of printing, you would now have NA where the right answer was “there were no such days”.
seq_len() and seq_along() never count backwards. They return an empty sequence when there is nothing to iterate over, and a loop over an empty sequence does not run:

seq_len(nrow(quiet))
#> integer(0)

for (i in seq_len(nrow(quiet))) {
  cat("Day", format(quiet$date[i]), "had", quiet$daily_cases[i], "new cases\n")
}

cat("finished, and printed nothing\n")
#> finished, and printed nothing

Use seq_along(x) when you are walking a vector or list, and seq_len(nrow(df)) when you are walking the rows of a data frame. It costs three extra characters and removes a whole category of bug.
crumbs: 12  Loops, and when you need them

title: 12  Loops, and when you need them
section: 12.6 while, when you do not know how many steps
text:
12.6 while, when you do not know how many steps
for needs to know the number of iterations before it starts. When the stopping condition depends on what you find, use while.
Half of Singapore’s 2020 cases is 29,300 or thereabouts. Which day did the cumulative count cross that?

target <- max(covid$confirmed) / 2
i <- 1

while (covid$confirmed[i] < target) {
  i <- i + 1
}

covid$date[i]
#> [1] "2020-05-20"
covid$confirmed[i]
#> [1] 29364
i
#> [1] 120
nrow(covid) - i
#> [1] 225

Half the year’s cases had accumulated by 20 May, on day 120 of 345, with 225 days of the year still to run. That asymmetry is the dormitory outbreak, and it is worth sitting with for a moment.
Two things about while. Something inside the body must change the condition, or it runs forever; here it is i <- i + 1, and forgetting that line is the classic way to hang your R session. (Escape, or the stop button in RStudio, gets you out.) And the condition must eventually become false. If no day had crossed the target, i would keep climbing past 345 and covid$confirmed[346] would be NA, at which point R stops with a real error rather than looping forever:
Error in while (covid$confirmed[i] < target) { :
  missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed
That message is worth memorising. It nearly always means a comparison produced NA, and NA is neither true nor false, so while and if refuse to guess.
crumbs: 12  Loops, and when you need them

title: 12  Loops, and when you need them
text:
12.7 map() and friends
Loops that build a result one element at a time are common enough that purrr, part of the tidyverse, gives them a shorter form. map(x, f) calls f on each element of x and returns a list of the results, always the same length as x.
Let me bring month_summary() across from Chapter 11. Chapters render in fresh sessions, so it has to be defined again here:

month_summary <- function(df, which_month) {
  start <- floor_date(as.Date(which_month), "month")

  if (!start %in% df$month) {
    stop("No data for ", format(start, "%B %Y"), ". The data covers ",
         format(min(df$month), "%B %Y"), " to ",
         format(max(df$month), "%B %Y"), ".", call. = FALSE)
  }

  df %>%
    filter(month == start) %>%
    summarise(
      month      = start,
      days       = n(),
      total      = sum(daily_cases),
      mean_daily = round(mean(daily_cases), 1),
      peak       = max(daily_cases),
      peak_date  = date[which.max(daily_cases)],
      high_days  = sum(severity == "High")
    )
}

all_months <- unique(covid$month)
all_months
#>  [1] "2020-01-01" "2020-02-01" "2020-03-01" "2020-04-01" "2020-05-01"
#>  [6] "2020-06-01" "2020-07-01" "2020-08-01" "2020-09-01" "2020-10-01"
#> [11] "2020-11-01" "2020-12-01"

Now the payoff for having made it return a one-row tibble:

monthly <- all_months %>%
  map(function(m) month_summary(covid, m)) %>%
  list_rbind()

monthly
#> # A tibble: 12 × 7
#>    month       days total mean_daily  peak peak_date  high_days
#>    <date>     <int> <dbl>      <dbl> <dbl> <date>         <int>
#>  1 2020-01-01    10    13        1.3     3 2020-01-30         0
#>  2 2020-02-01    29    89        3.1     9 2020-02-14         0
#>  3 2020-03-01    31   824       26.6    73 2020-03-25         0
#>  4 2020-04-01    30 15243      508.   1426 2020-04-20        18
#>  5 2020-05-01    31 18715      604.    932 2020-05-01        31
#>  6 2020-06-01    30  9023      301.    569 2020-06-03        12
#>  7 2020-07-01    31  8298      268.    513 2020-07-25        12
#>  8 2020-08-01    31  4607      149.    908 2020-08-05         4
#>  9 2020-09-01    30   953       31.8    86 2020-09-11         0
#> 10 2020-10-01    31   250        8.1    19 2020-10-01         0
#> 11 2020-11-01    30   203        6.8    18 2020-11-11         0
#> 12 2020-12-01    31   381       12.3    30 2020-12-31         0

Twelve calls, twelve one-row tibbles, stacked into a table, in three lines. map() did the iterating and list_rbind() did the stacking. Had month_summary() returned a list, list_rbind() would have refused, which is the argument made at the end of Chapter 11.
Check the arithmetic against something you already know:

sum(monthly$total) == max(covid$confirmed)
#> [1] TRUE

The monthly totals add back to 58,599. May was the worst month by volume, with 18,715 cases and every single one of its 31 days classed High. April held the single worst day, 1,426 on the 20th.
map() always returns a list. When you know each result is a single number, map_dbl() returns a plain numeric vector instead, which is usually what you want:

map_dbl(all_months, function(m) month_summary(covid, m)$mean_daily)
#>  [1]   1.3   3.1  26.6 508.1 603.7 300.8 267.7 148.6  31.8   8.1   6.8  12.3

There is a whole family: map_chr() for strings, map_int() for integers, map_lgl() for TRUE/FALSE. They are stricter than map() on purpose. If one of your twelve results comes back as text when you asked for map_dbl(), you get an error instead of a silently mixed list.
walk() is for when you want the side effect and not the value: printing, saving files, writing plots to disk.

walk(all_months, function(m) {
  s <- month_summary(covid, m)
  cat(format(s$month, "%B"), "-", s$total, "cases,", s$high_days, "High days\n")
})
#> January - 13 cases, 0 High days
#> February - 89 cases, 0 High days
#> March - 824 cases, 0 High days
#> April - 15243 cases, 18 High days
#> May - 18715 cases, 31 High days
#> June - 9023 cases, 12 High days
#> July - 8298 cases, 12 High days
#> August - 4607 cases, 4 High days
#> September - 953 cases, 0 High days
#> October - 250 cases, 0 High days
#> November - 203 cases, 0 High days
#> December - 381 cases, 0 High days

walk() returns its input invisibly, so nothing clutters the console except what you asked to print. Using map() here would work and would also dump twelve tibbles underneath your report.

title: 12  Loops, and when you need them
text:
12.8 The loop you cannot vectorise
Here is the case that justifies the whole chapter.
A deterministic SIR model splits a closed population into susceptible, infectious and recovered, and steps forward in time. In each step, some susceptibles become infectious at a rate proportional to how many of each there are, and some infectious people recover:
\[
S_{t+1} = S_t - \beta \frac{S_t I_t}{N}, \qquad
I_{t+1} = I_t + \beta \frac{S_t I_t}{N} - \gamma I_t, \qquad
R_{t+1} = R_t + \gamma I_t
\]
Every quantity on the right has a subscript \(t\) and every quantity on the left has \(t+1\). You cannot compute day 40 without day 39, which needs day 38, and so on back to the start. lag() cannot help, because lag() shifts a column that already exists and here the column is what you are creating. This is a loop, and it will always be a loop.
The numbers below are made up. This is not a fit to Singapore and it is not meant to be; it is the smallest thing that shows the mechanism.

N     <- 100000    # a closed hypothetical population
beta  <- 0.3       # transmission rate per day
gamma <- 0.1       # recovery rate per day, so an average 10 infectious days
days  <- 150

# Pre-allocate, as above.
S <- numeric(days)
I <- numeric(days)
R <- numeric(days)

# Seed: ten infectious people on day one.
S[1] <- N - 10
I[1] <- 10
R[1] <- 0

for (t in 2:days) {
  new_infections <- beta * S[t - 1] * I[t - 1] / N
  new_removals   <- gamma * I[t - 1]

  S[t] <- S[t - 1] - new_infections
  I[t] <- I[t - 1] + new_infections - new_removals
  R[t] <- R[t - 1] + new_removals
}

epidemic <- tibble(day = 1:days, S = S, I = I, R = R)

epidemic %>% slice(c(1, 55, 150))
#> # A tibble: 3 × 4
#>     day      S       I      R
#>   <int>  <dbl>   <dbl>  <dbl>
#> 1     1 99990     10       0 
#> 2    55 30338. 31211.  38451.
#> 3   150  5335.    15.6 94649.

The loop starts at t = 2, not t = 1, because day one is the seed and has nothing before it to compute from. That is the same edge case as the if (i == 1) branch in the very first loop of this chapter, handled by starting the counter one step in.

epidemic %>%
  pivot_longer(c(S, I, R), names_to = "compartment", values_to = "people") %>%
  mutate(compartment = factor(compartment, levels = c("S", "I", "R"))) %>%
  ggplot(aes(day, people, colour = compartment)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_comma()) +
  labs(
    x = "Day", y = "People", colour = NULL,
    title = "One epidemic, computed one day at a time",
    caption = "Illustrative parameters. Not a model of Singapore."
  )



A deterministic SIR model with \(\beta = 0.3\), \(\gamma = 0.1\) in a closed population of 100,000. Illustrative parameters, not fitted to any data.



Susceptibles fall, infections peak around day 55 and then collapse, and recoveries flatten out near the top. The peak is not caused by anything you told the model to do on day 55. It happens because susceptibles run low enough that each infectious person stops replacing themselves, and it falls out of the arithmetic.
Change beta to 0.2 and run it again. Then try 0.5. Then push I[1] to 1,000 and watch how little the final size moves. Three minutes of that teaches more about \(R_0\) than three pages about it.
What you have written is Euler’s method with a step of one day, which is the crudest way to integrate a differential equation and is fine at this scale. Later in the course you will hand the same equations to deSolve or odin, which choose their own step sizes and take the error seriously. Underneath, both are running a loop very like this one.
crumbs: 12  Loops, and when you need them

title: 12  Loops, and when you need them
text:
12.9 Exercises

Exercise 12.1 (Cumulative deaths, both ways) Do for deaths what this chapter did for confirmed: compute daily deaths with an explicit for loop, then again with lag(), then check the two against each other with identical().
The deaths column will not behave like the cases column, and finding out how is the exercise. Compare the sum of your daily deaths against the final cumulative figure of 29 and account for any difference before you move on.







Stuck? Open for a hint (not the answer)





deaths starts with a long run of missing values, and the first number that appears is not 1. Look at head(covid$deaths, 65) and ask what differencing can possibly recover from a series that begins part-way up.



Worked solution

Exercise 12.2 (An SIR model with an intervention) Take the SIR loop and add a circuit breaker. From day 40 to day 95, transmission is reduced: use a lower value of beta inside that window and the original value outside it.
Run it, plot the infectious compartment against the unmodified version on the same axes, and answer two questions from your own output. Does the peak get smaller, and does it get later? What happens after day 95, and would you have predicted it?







Stuck? Open for a hint (not the answer)





beta does not have to be a single number. Make it a vector of length days, set the intervention window with something like beta[40:95] <- 0.15, and use beta[t - 1] inside the loop. Keep the two runs in one tibble so you can plot them together.



Worked solution
crumbs: 12  Loops, and when you need them

title: 13  A monthly situation report
text:
13.1 The brief
One month. One page. On that page:
a table that gives the reader the month in numbers, two figures that show something the table can’t, and three sentences of interpretation. Three sentences, not three paragraphs. The sentence limit is the hard part and it’s deliberate. Anyone can produce eight paragraphs of hedged description. Deciding which three things matter is the work.
Assume the reader is a public health officer who knows Singapore and does not know R. They will not read your code. They will look at the figures first, the table second, and your sentences only if the figures made them curious.

title: 13  A monthly situation report
text:
13.2 What a good report contains
There are six things I look for, and they are all things you already know how to do.


The month is stated, and so is the denominator. How many days does the month have, and how many of them carry data? Every month in this file is complete, but saying so is what separates a report from an assumption.

A count and a shape. A total tells you the size of the month. A median, a maximum and the date of the maximum tell you whether that total came from a steady grind or one bad day. Report both.

A table with a unit the reader can hold. Days are too fine for a monthly table and the month itself is too coarse. Weeks work.

Two figures that answer different questions. Two views of the case curve is one figure drawn twice. Pair the epidemic curve with something else in the file: mobility, the stringency index, the severity mix.

Every figure has a title that states a finding. “Daily cases, April 2020” is a label. “Cases rose for 13 days after the circuit breaker began” is a finding. Titles that make a claim force you to check the claim.

At least one caveat that comes from looking at the data, not from a template. “Data may be incomplete” is a template. “The 5 August count is four times the next highest August day and needs an explanation before it goes in a mean” is analysis.

title: 13  A monthly situation report
text:
13.3 April 2020, worked

13.3.1 A script that stands on its own
Your report script must be readable from the top without any hidden state. That means it reads the file and builds its own columns, in view, before it uses them. This is exactly the pipeline from the conditionals chapter, written out once so nothing in the report depends on something you can’t see.

covid <- read_covid() %>%
  arrange(date) %>%
  mutate(
    daily_cases  = confirmed - lag(confirmed, default = 0),
    daily_deaths = deaths - lag(deaths, default = 0),
    severity = case_when(
      daily_cases <  100 ~ "Low",
      daily_cases <= 300 ~ "Medium",
      daily_cases >  300 ~ "High"
    ),
    severity = factor(severity, levels = c("Low", "Medium", "High")),
    month = floor_date(date, "month")
  )

If you’re writing this in a script of your own rather than inside the book’s project, swap read_covid() for read_csv(here("data", "sg_covid_data.csv")). That helper exists so the chapters don’t repeat a file path forty times, and nothing else in the pipeline depends on it.
Then pick the month once, at the top, in a named object. When August comes round you change one line rather than hunting for "2020-04" scattered through twenty chunks.

report_month <- as.Date("2020-04-01")

april <- covid %>%
  filter(month == report_month)

nrow(april)
#> [1] 30

Thirty rows for a thirty-day month. That check takes two seconds and it is the cheapest error you will ever catch.

13.3.2 How heavy was the month






Predict before you run this



April 2020 has one day that dwarfs the rest. Write down the date you think it fell on before you read the next output. Most people put it in the first week, on the theory that the circuit breaker started on 7 April and things improved from there.



april %>%
  summarise(
    days         = n(),
    cases        = sum(daily_cases),
    mean_daily   = mean(daily_cases),
    median_daily = median(daily_cases),
    peak         = max(daily_cases),
    peak_date    = date[which.max(daily_cases)],
    deaths       = sum(daily_deaths)
  )
#> # A tibble: 1 × 7
#>    days cases mean_daily median_daily  peak peak_date  deaths
#>   <int> <dbl>      <dbl>        <dbl> <dbl> <date>      <dbl>
#> 1    30 15243       508.         488.  1426 2020-04-20     12

The peak is 20 April, thirteen days after the circuit breaker began. Cases went up, and kept going up, for two weeks after Singapore closed workplaces and told everyone to stay home.
That is not a paradox and it is worth being precise about why. Reported cases are the output of a testing programme, not a direct measurement of infection. Through April, testing in the migrant-worker dormitories was expanding fast, and the dormitory outbreak dominated the national count from April to August. A rising reported curve during that period is partly transmission and partly the swab rate catching up with infections that had already happened. You cannot separate the two from this file, which is a thing to say in your report rather than a thing to hide.
Two small notes on that output. median_daily prints as 488. with a trailing full stop, which is the tibble telling you the value isn’t a whole number. It’s 487.5, the average of the two middle days. And deaths is 12 here, which is trustworthy for April because the deaths column has no missing values from 21 March onwards. Earlier in the year it does, 59 leading NAs, and lag-differencing across them recovers only 27 of the year’s 29 deaths. If your chosen month is January, February or March, say that out loud.

april %>%
  count(severity)
#> # A tibble: 3 × 2
#>   severity     n
#>   <fct>    <int>
#> 1 Low          5
#> 2 Medium       7
#> 3 High        18

Eighteen of April’s thirty days were over 300 cases. Across the whole year only 77 days were, so April holds nearly a quarter of the year’s worst days in a single month.

13.3.3 The table
Weeks are the right grain for a monthly table. floor_date(date, "week", week_start = 1) puts each date on its Monday. I set week_start explicitly because lubridate’s default is Sunday and half the people reading this expect Monday. Making the assumption visible costs one argument.

april_weeks <- april %>%
  mutate(week = floor_date(date, "week", week_start = 1)) %>%
  group_by(week) %>%
  summarise(
    days       = n(),
    cases      = sum(daily_cases),
    mean_daily = round(mean(daily_cases)),
    peak       = max(daily_cases),
    retail     = round(mean(retail_and_recreation_percent_change_from_baseline)),
    stringency = round(mean(stringency_index), 1)
  )

april_weeks
#> # A tibble: 5 × 7
#>   week        days cases mean_daily  peak retail stringency
#>   <date>     <int> <dbl>      <dbl> <dbl>  <dbl>      <dbl>
#> 1 2020-03-30     5   383         77   120    -23       41.7
#> 2 2020-04-06     7  1223        175   287    -53       71  
#> 3 2020-04-13     7  4056        579   942    -61       76.8
#> 4 2020-04-20     7  7036       1005  1426    -67       77.6
#> 5 2020-04-27     4  2545        636   799    -67       76.8

Look at the days column before you look at anything else. The first row covers five days, not seven, because April 2020 started on a Wednesday and the week beginning 30 March mostly belongs to March. The last row covers four. Any comparison of cases across those rows is comparing different amounts of time, which is why mean_daily is in the table and why days is in it too. Leave days out and a reader will read 383 against 1,223 as a threefold rise when part of it is nothing more than two extra days.
The rest of the table tells a fairly clean story. Weekly totals climb from 383 to 7,036 and then fall back. Mean retail mobility drops from 23% below baseline in the first partial week to 67% below in each of the last two. Mean stringency goes from 41.7 to 71 in one step and sits in the seventies for the rest of the month.

13.3.4 The first figure: the epidemic curve

cb_start <- as.Date("2020-04-07")

ggplot(april, aes(date, daily_cases)) +
  geom_col(fill = nus_colours[["blue"]]) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = cb_start, colour = nus_colours[["crimson"]],
             linetype = "dashed") +
  annotate("text", x = cb_start + 1, y = 1350, hjust = 0, size = 3.2,
           colour = nus_colours[["crimson"]], label = "Circuit breaker begins") +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "1 week", date_labels = "%d %b") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_comma()) +
  labs(
    title = "Cases rose for 13 days after the circuit breaker began",
    subtitle = "Singapore, new COVID-19 cases reported each day, April 2020",
    x = NULL, y = "New cases reported",
    caption = "Source: COVID-19 Data Hub. Reported cases, not infections."
  )






Figure 13.1: Daily reported cases in Singapore, April 2020, with the start of the circuit breaker marked.




Columns rather than a line, because these are counts of things that happened on discrete days and a line implies you could read a value off it halfway between two dates. The dashed rule and the label do the work that a paragraph of text would otherwise have to do. The caption carries the source and the one warning the reader most needs.
The date breaks are weekly and the labels are "%d %b", so the axis reads 06 Apr, 13 Apr, 20 Apr. Left to itself ggplot2 would have chosen something reasonable but not necessarily aligned with the weeks in your table, and a reader who is trying to match figure to table will notice.

13.3.5 The second figure: what people actually did
The case curve says what was reported. The mobility columns say what people did, which is a different question and the reason this file is more interesting than a case line on its own.
Two series on one set of axes means one row per series per date, so the two columns have to become one column of values plus one column of labels. pivot_longer() does that. It’s from tidyr, which came in with the tidyverse, and it’s the only function in this chapter you haven’t already met.

april_mobility <- april %>%
  select(
    date,
    `Retail and recreation` = retail_and_recreation_percent_change_from_baseline,
    Workplaces              = workplaces_percent_change_from_baseline
  ) %>%
  pivot_longer(-date, names_to = "series", values_to = "change")

april_mobility
#> # A tibble: 60 × 3
#>    date       series                change
#>    <date>     <chr>                  <dbl>
#>  1 2020-04-01 Retail and recreation    -23
#>  2 2020-04-01 Workplaces               -22
#>  3 2020-04-02 Retail and recreation    -25
#>  4 2020-04-02 Workplaces               -27
#>  5 2020-04-03 Retail and recreation    -21
#>  6 2020-04-03 Workplaces               -20
#>  7 2020-04-04 Retail and recreation    -24
#>  8 2020-04-04 Workplaces                -7
#>  9 2020-04-05 Retail and recreation    -23
#> 10 2020-04-05 Workplaces               -10
#> # ℹ 50 more rows

Renaming inside select() is what gets you a readable legend without a second call. Backticks around Retail and recreation because it has spaces in it; R will accept a name like that as long as you quote it that way, and here it’s worth it because that string goes straight onto the plot.

ggplot(april_mobility, aes(date, change, colour = series)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = nus_colours[["muted"]], linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = cb_start, colour = nus_colours[["crimson"]],
             linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "1 week", date_labels = "%d %b") +
  labs(
    title = "Movement fell the day the rules changed, and stayed down",
    subtitle = "Percent change from Google's 3 January to 6 February 2020 baseline",
    x = NULL, y = "Change from baseline (%)", colour = NULL,
    caption = "Weekends are not comparable with weekdays: the baseline is a median by day of week."
  )






Figure 13.2: Retail and workplace mobility in April 2020, as percent change from Google’s pre-pandemic baseline.




The step at 7 April is the whole point of the figure. Retail goes from 15% below baseline on 6 April to 51% below on 7 April; workplaces go from 24% below to 52% below on the same day. Behaviour changed overnight. The case curve took a fortnight to turn.
Now the two things in that figure that are not what they look like. The deep spike down to 83% below baseline is 10 April, which was Good Friday, a public holiday. The eight deepest workplace-mobility days in the entire year are all public holidays, so any dip you see in this series should be checked against a calendar before it’s called a policy effect.
The regular bumps upwards are weekends, and they run the opposite way to intuition. Google’s baseline is a median computed separately for each day of the week, so a Sunday is compared with pre-pandemic Sundays. Workplace activity on a normal Sunday was already low, which leaves less room to fall.

april %>%
  filter(date >= cb_start) %>%
  mutate(weekday = wday(date, label = TRUE)) %>%
  group_by(weekday) %>%
  summarise(
    days       = n(),
    workplaces = mean(workplaces_percent_change_from_baseline)
  )
#> # A tibble: 7 × 3
#>   weekday  days workplaces
#>   <ord>   <int>      <dbl>
#> 1 Sun         3      -50  
#> 2 Mon         3      -66  
#> 3 Tue         4      -63  
#> 4 Wed         4      -66.5
#> 5 Thu         4      -67  
#> 6 Fri         3      -71.7
#> 7 Sat         3      -52.3

Weekdays sit between 63 and 72 points below baseline. Saturday and Sunday sit around 50. Nobody went back to the office at the weekend. The denominator changed.
If you want the two figures stacked as a single image for a one-page PDF, patchwork will do it with p_cases / p_mobility once you’ve assigned each plot to a name. I’ve kept them separate here so each keeps its full height on screen.

13.3.6 The three sentences

April carried 15,243 reported cases, 26% of Singapore’s 2020 total, with 18 of its 30 days above 300 cases and 12 deaths; only May, at 18,715, was heavier.
Reported cases kept climbing for 13 days after the circuit breaker took effect on 7 April, peaking at 1,426 on 20 April, a pattern that reflects the pace of testing in the migrant-worker dormitories as much as the timing of infection.
Movement changed the day the rules did, with retail activity falling from 15% below baseline on 6 April to 51% below on 7 April and staying within a few points of its floor for the rest of the month, so the behavioural response was immediate even though the case curve was not.

Three sentences, three different jobs. The first sizes the month against the year. The second addresses the thing a reader will get wrong if you don’t. The third brings in the second data source and draws the contrast that makes the report worth reading.
Notice what isn’t in there. No recommendation, because nothing in this file supports one. No claim that the circuit breaker worked or didn’t, because a single month of a single country with no counterfactual cannot tell you. A situation report describes the situation. Resist the pull to conclude.

title: 13  A monthly situation report
section: 13.4 What this analysis does not tell you
text:
13.4 What this analysis does not tell you
This section is not decoration. Write a version of it for your own month, and make it specific.
Raw counts ignore population. Fifteen thousand cases is a number of people, not a rate. To turn it into a rate you need a denominator, and the honest denominator here is not obvious. Roughly 323,000 work-permit holders lived in dormitories of all types in 2020, of whom about 200,000 were in the 43 purpose-built dormitories. A case rate computed over the national population and a case rate computed over the dormitory-resident population are different quantities, and in April 2020 they were not remotely close. This file gives you neither denominator.
Raw counts ignore testing volume. A reported case requires a test, a positive result and a report. Change the number of tests and the case count changes without a single extra infection. There’s no test-count column in this file, so you cannot compute test positivity, which is the standard way of asking whether a rise in cases is a rise in transmission or a rise in looking. When your curve rises, you are entitled to say that reported cases rose. You are not entitled to say that infections rose.
One national count is averaging two epidemics. From April to August 2020 the dormitory outbreak dominated Singapore’s case counts, and it had different dynamics from transmission in the wider community: different living density, different age structure, different testing regime, different intervention. MOH’s own daily updates reported those streams separately at the time. This file carries a single national total, so every mean you compute over those months is a weighted average of two processes, with weights you can’t see and that change from week to week. That is a limitation of the file, not of the epidemiology, and you should say which one you’re reporting.
5 August 2020 is the sharpest example. That day records 908 cases, against an August median of 91 and a next-highest August day of 313. Nine hundred and three of those 908 were dormitory residents, and 581 were linked to a single cluster at Acacia Lodge. MOH attributed the day’s numbers to clearance testing in dormitories picking up past infections. Put that day in a mean without comment and you have published a wave that did not happen on that day.
One more, and I’m flagging it as my own reading rather than something you can verify from the data. Google’s mobility series are built from location history on the phones of users who have that setting switched on, and Google does not publish these series broken down by nationality or work-permit status. Whether the movement of people confined to dormitories under quarantine appears in these curves at all is not a question this file can answer. I would not lean on mobility to describe what happened inside the dormitories in April. That is the difference between running the code and doing the epidemiology: the code will compute a mean of anything you hand it.

title: 13  A monthly situation report
text:
13.5 Your turn

Exercise 13.1 (Write the August 2020 situation report) Produce the one-page report for August 2020: a table, two figures, three sentences of interpretation, and a short note on what your analysis does not tell you.
August is a harder month than April, and not because the code is harder. The code is the same code. August is harder because the month contains a decision that April doesn’t, and how you handle it is most of what separates a good report from a competent one.
You are done when someone who has never seen the data could read your page and come away with a correct impression of what August 2020 was like.







Stuck? Open for a hint (not the answer)





Compute the maximum, the median and the date of the maximum before you compute anything else, and put those three numbers next to each other. If a single day is several times the next highest day, the mean is describing that day rather than the month, and your report has to decide out loud what to do about it.



Worked solution
If you want a second month after that, September 2020 is the quiet counterpart: 30 days, every one of them under 100 cases, a mean of 31.8. Writing an interesting report about a month where nothing happens is its own skill, and you will be asked for one eventually.

title: 14  Where to go next
text:
14.1 What the rest of the course does with all this
The modelling weeks turn the direction of travel around. Everything so far started with data and went looking for a description. A compartmental model starts with a description, some assumptions about how people move between states, and produces data you can compare with the real thing.
The mechanics are less exotic than they sound. You divide a population into compartments, susceptible, infectious, recovered in the simplest case. You write down the rate at which people leave each compartment and enter the next. Then you hand those rates to a solver, which steps them forward in small increments and hands back a trajectory.
In R the solver is usually deSolve, and its main function is ode(). The shape of the code is this.
sir <- function(t, state, parameters) {
  with(as.list(c(state, parameters)), {
    dS <- -beta * S * I / N
    dI <-  beta * S * I / N - gamma * I
    dR <-  gamma * I
    list(c(dS, dI, dR))
  })
}

state      <- c(S = 99999, I = 1, R = 0)
parameters <- c(beta = 0.4, gamma = 0.2, N = 1e5)
times      <- seq(0, 180, by = 1)

out <- ode(y = state, times = times, func = sir, parms = parameters)
Read that against what you already know and almost all of it is familiar. sir is a function with three arguments whose value is whatever the last expression evaluates to, which is the functions chapter. state and parameters are named numeric vectors, and as.list() and with() are there so you can write beta instead of parameters[["beta"]], which is the foundations chapter. The return value is a list containing one vector, because ode() insists on a list, and knowing the difference between c(dS, dI, dR) and list(c(dS, dI, dR)) is why that chapter spent time on lists.
What ode() gives back is a matrix, not a tibble. Your first move will be as_tibble(), then pivot_longer() so you can draw three lines on one plot, then the ggplot2 grammar from the visualising chapter. Two evenings of this course will be spent on models and about ten minutes of each of them on plotting, because you already did the plotting.
Two things will catch you, so they’re worth naming now.
The time column that comes out of ode() counts steps from zero. It is not a date. If you want to line a trajectory up against the daily_cases column you built, you have to decide what day zero means and add it: start_date + out$time. Model time and calendar time are different quantities and mixing them silently is a classic way to get a plot that looks fine and is wrong by a fortnight.
The second is that you will want to run the model more than once. Sweeping over ten values of beta, or a hundred, is the iteration chapter’s problem exactly: write the model run as a function of the parameter you’re varying, then map over the values and bind the results, rather than copying the call ten times with a number changed.
Once your models get big enough that speed matters, or you’re running thousands of stochastic replicates, R’s own loop overhead starts to hurt. odin is the usual answer: you write the equations in a small R-like language and it generates and compiles C for you. The equations look much like the ones above. The habits of writing them carefully, naming parameters properly and checking a trajectory before believing it are the same habits.
Fitting a model to Singapore’s 2020 curve is where the two halves of the course meet, and it’s also where the caveats from the capstone come back. You’d be fitting to reported cases, which are a function of testing as well as transmission, over a period when the national count was dominated by the dormitory outbreak. A model fitted to that series without a term for either is answering a question you didn’t ask.

title: 14  Where to go next
text:
14.2 Five things worth reading
Short list, because a long one gets ignored.
R for Data Science, 2nd edition, by Wickham, Çetinkaya-Rundel and Grolemund. Free online. This is the book this course is a week-long trailer for. The chapters on data transformation and visualisation cover the same ground with more room, and the chapters on joins, factors, strings and dates cover the things I had to leave out. If you read one thing from this list, read this one, and read it with your hands on the keyboard.
The Epidemiologist R Handbook, by Neale Batra and a large group of contributors. Free online. This is a recipe book rather than a textbook, written by field epidemiologists for field epidemiologists, and it is the fastest route from “I need an epi curve with a moving average and a case fatality ratio by age group” to working code. Its examples are outbreak data. Use it when you know what you want and not how to spell it.
Happy Git and GitHub for the useR, by Jenny Bryan. Free online. Version control is the single habit with the best ratio of effort to regret avoided, and this is the book that gets R users over the initial hostility of git. Read the first eight or so chapters, get one project under version control, stop there. You do not need to understand rebasing.
The tidyverse style guide, by Hadley Wickham. An afternoon’s read, mostly skimmable. It’s where the conventions this book uses come from: spaces around <-, lowercase names with underscores, one dplyr verb per line. Consistency matters less for its own sake than because it lets you read your own code from three months ago without decoding it first.
Advanced R, 2nd edition, by Hadley Wickham. Free online. Not for now. Bookmark it and come back when you find yourself asking why something behaves the way it does rather than how to make it work. The chapters on environments and on functionals are the ones that explain the odd corners of R that this book has been telling you to accept.
Notice what is not on that list. There’s no reference manual, because R’s own help pages are the reference manual and ?filter is faster than any book. There’s no book on statistics in R, because the statistics course is a statistics course and the R is the easy part of it.

title: 14  Where to go next
text:
14.3 When it breaks
Something will break tonight. Here is the order to do things in.

14.3.1 Read the message, all of it
R’s error messages have improved enormously and most people still read the first line and panic. The tidyverse ones in particular are built to be read from top to bottom. Here’s one you can produce on purpose.

month_summary <- function(data, month_start) {
  data %>%
    filter(month == month_start) %>%
    summarise(cases = sum(daily_cases), peak = max(daily_cases))
}

month_summary(covid, "2020-08")
#> Error in `filter()` at dplyr/R/summarise.R:113:3:
#> ℹ In argument: `month == month_start`.
#> Caused by error in `charToDate()`:
#> ! character string is not in a standard unambiguous format

Four lines, four separate pieces of information. The first says which verb failed: filter(), not summarise(), so the pipeline died before it got to the summary. The reference to dplyr/R/summarise.R is dplyr telling you where in its own source the call was recorded, and it is not about your file. The second line names the argument that blew up, month == month_start. The third says the actual failure happened inside charToDate(), which is a base R function for turning text into dates and not a function you called. The fourth is the complaint itself.
Put those together and the story is complete. Comparing a Date column with a character string makes R try to convert the string to a date, and "2020-08" isn’t a date because R has no idea whether you meant the first of the month or the whole of it. It refuses to guess.

month_summary(covid, as.Date("2020-08-01"))
#> # A tibble: 1 × 2
#>   cases  peak
#>   <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1  4607   908

The habit worth building: when you read an error, work out which line names your code and which lines name the machinery underneath it. The fix is almost always at the boundary between them.
If you’re working in RStudio you’ll also see Run rlang::last_trace() to see where the error occurred. Do that. It prints the full chain of calls with your own function at the top and the failing one at the bottom, and for a pipeline buried inside a function it’s often the quickest way to find which of your six lines actually broke.

14.3.2 traceback(), for the errors that don’t tell you where they came from
Base R errors are terser. This is one from a function calling another function.
> daily_mean <- function(x, i, k) mean(x[(i - k):(i + k)])
> smooth_at <- function(data, i) daily_mean(data$daily_cases, i, 3)
> smooth_at(covid, "100")
Error in i - k : non-numeric argument to binary operator
That tells you what went wrong and says nothing about where. traceback(), run immediately afterwards, does.
> traceback()
3: mean(x[(i - k):(i + k)]) at #1
2: daily_mean(data$daily_cases, i, 3) at #1
1: smooth_at(covid, "100")
Read it from the bottom. Line 1 is the call you typed. Line 2 is what it called. Line 3 is where it died. So smooth_at() passed the string "100" straight through to daily_mean(), which tried to subtract 3 from it. The at #1 is the line number in the source; when your functions live in a file rather than being typed at the console, you get something like at report.R#12, which is the number you want.
RStudio puts a “Show Traceback” button next to errors in the console. Same thing, one click.

14.3.3 browser(), for when you need to be inside it
When the traceback tells you which function died but not why, put browser() on the line before the trouble and run the call again. R stops there and hands you a prompt with the function’s own variables in scope.

month_summary <- function(data, month_start) {
  browser()
  data %>%
    filter(month == month_start) %>%
    summarise(cases = sum(daily_cases))
}

month_summary(covid, "2020-08")

Called from: month_summary(covid, "2020-08")
Browse[1]> month_start
[1] "2020-08"
Browse[1]> class(month_start)
[1] "character"
Browse[1]> class(data$month)
[1] "Date"
Browse[1]> Q
Three questions and the bug is obvious: you’re comparing a character against a Date. Type Q to quit the browser, n to run the next line, c to let it finish. Then take the browser() back out, which everyone forgets to do at least once and then wonders why their script keeps stopping.
debugonce(month_summary) does the same thing without editing the function, which is the better move when the function belongs to a package.

14.3.4 The failures that don’t announce themselves
Errors are the good case. R stops and tells you. The dangerous failures are the ones that return a number.

covid$date[which.max(covid$daily_case)]
#> Warning: Unknown or uninitialised column: `daily_case`.
#> Date of length 0

One missing letter in the column name. R gives you a warning and a zero-length date rather than an error, because $ on a tibble returns NULL for a column that isn’t there and which.max() of nothing is nothing. Inside a longer pipeline that warning scrolls past and you publish a report with a blank where the peak date should be.
Here’s a worse one, and it’s from this dataset.

max(covid$deaths, na.rm = TRUE)
#> [1] 29
sum(covid$daily_deaths, na.rm = TRUE)
#> [1] 27

Singapore recorded 29 COVID-19 deaths in 2020. Differencing the cumulative column recovers 27 of them, because deaths has 59 leading missing values and the first number that appears is already 2, on 21 March. The two missing deaths are hidden inside that first observation. Neither line above errors. Neither warns. One of them is wrong for the question “how many people died”, and which one depends entirely on what you meant.
The defence isn’t cleverness, it’s arithmetic you can check. Does the total match a number you know from somewhere else? Does the number of rows match the number of days? Does the maximum land on the date you expected? Every one of those takes a line of code and catches the kind of mistake that no amount of careful reading will.

title: 14  Where to go next
section: 14.4 How to ask a question that gets answered
text:
14.4 How to ask a question that gets answered
You will get stuck in a way that fifteen minutes of your own effort won’t fix. When that happens, how you ask determines whether you wait five minutes or five days.
A question that gets answered has four parts. What you were trying to do, stated in terms of the result you wanted. The code you ran, as text. What actually happened, with the error message copied exactly. And what you already tried, so nobody wastes their time suggesting it.
The exact error text matters more than anything else in that list. Paste it, don’t describe it. “It says something about a non-numeric argument” is unsearchable. non-numeric argument to binary operator is one search away from a thousand people who’ve had the same problem. Before you ask anyone, put the message in a search engine with the word r and the name of the package. That solves a good half of everything.
Make it small. If your pipeline is forty lines, cut it in half and see if the error survives. Keep cutting. Most bugs collapse to three or four lines, and the act of cutting finds the answer often enough that it’s worth doing even when you’re planning to ask anyway. If the problem needs data, don’t attach a 30 MB CSV. dput(head(covid, 5)) prints a few rows as code that anyone can paste into their own session.
The reprex package automates the tidy version of this. You copy your minimal example to the clipboard, run reprex::reprex(), and it runs the code in a clean session and puts a formatted block on your clipboard with the code and its real output interleaved, ready to paste.

reprex::reprex({
  library(dplyr)
  x <- c(1, 2, NA)
  mean(x)
})

The clean session is the point. It catches the case where your code only works because of something you loaded an hour ago and forgot about, which is a surprisingly large fraction of problems that feel like package bugs.
Include your R version and package versions when the problem smells like a version difference. sessionInfo() prints them.
Ask your classmates first. They’re on the same data, the same versions and the same week, and somebody hit your problem yesterday. After that, the Posit Community forum is patient with beginners, and Stack Overflow is faster but less forgiving, so read a few answered R questions there before posting your first one. Report an issue on a package’s GitHub only once you can show the maintainer a reproducible example and you’re fairly sure the package is at fault rather than you.
One thing not to do: don’t post a photograph of your screen. Nobody can copy code out of a photograph, and the people most able to help you are the ones least willing to retype it.
And when you work something out that took you two hours, write down what the fix was, in a comment in the script, in the words you’d have needed at the start. You’ll meet it again in March. So will whoever asks the question after you.

title: Appendix A — Worked solutions
text:
A.1 Build a week by hand
week_one <- c(0, 1, 3, 3, 4, 5, 7)

length(week_one)
#> [1] 7
typeof(week_one)
#> [1] "double"
Seven elements, and the type is double rather than integer even though every value is a whole number. c(0, 1, 3) writes doubles unless you ask for integers with 0L, 1L, 3L. This catches people out when they compare typeof() output against what they expected, and it almost never matters in practice.
Part two. Two vectors of the same length subtract element by element, so you need days two to seven in one and days one to six in the other:
week_one[2:7] - week_one[1:6]
#> [1] 1 2 0 1 1 2
One, two, zero, one, one, two. Day four had no new cases at all. This is the same arithmetic that lag() does across all 345 rows in Chapter 6, written out small enough to see.
What this does not give you is a number for day one. There is no day zero to subtract, so six differences come out of seven values. In the full dataset the book handles that with lag(confirmed, default = 0), which is defensible here because confirmed[1] really is 0.
Part three. Add a label to the front:
labelled <- c("week one", week_one)

typeof(labelled)
#> [1] "character"
labelled
#> [1] "week one" "0"        "1"        "3"        "3"        "4"        "5"       
#> [8] "7"
Every number became text. A vector holds one type, and when c() is handed a mixture it picks the type that can represent all of it. Character wins over double because any number can be written as a string, whereas "week one" cannot be written as a number. That is coercion, and it is silent by design.
The arithmetic now fails:
labelled * 2
#> Error in `labelled * 2`:
#> ! non-numeric argument to binary operator
non-numeric argument to binary operator is the error you will meet most often in your first month of R, and nine times out of ten the cause is exactly this: a stray label, a footnote marker, or a "N/A" typed by hand into a spreadsheet column, coercing an entire column of numbers to text on import.
Part four:
week_na <- week_one
week_na[4] <- NA

mean(week_na)
#> [1] NA
mean(week_na, na.rm = TRUE)
#> [1] 3.333333
NA in, NA out. R will not guess what the missing value was, so any arithmetic that touches it is undefined and R says so. na.rm = TRUE drops it and averages the remaining six, giving 3.33.
What people get wrong. They reach for na.rm = TRUE as a reflex, because it makes the NA go away and the code stops complaining. It also silently changes the denominator: the second mean is over six days, not seven, and nothing in the output says so. Chapter 7 is about the cases where that matters, and Singapore’s mobility columns are one of them.

title: Appendix A — Worked solutions
text: From the chapter on objects, vectors and functions: store the first seven cumulative counts, difference them, break the vector with a string, and see what one NA does to a mean.

title: Appendix A — Worked solutions
text:
A.2 Take a tibble apart

From the chapter on rectangles: show with code that a tibble is a list, get the type of every column, build a small tibble of policy dates, and find a behaviour that a plain data frame does differently.

Part one. Three functions do the whole job:

is.list(covid_raw)
#> [1] TRUE
length(covid_raw)
#> [1] 13
unique(lengths(covid_raw))
#> [1] 345

length() counts the elements of the underlying list, which is 13 columns. lengths(), with the s, measures each element, and unique() collapsing to a single value of 345 is the proof that every column has the same length. 345 is the number of rows, 13 the number of columns. Row i of every column refers to the same day, and that guarantee is what makes filter() safe.
Part two:

sapply(covid_raw, class)
#>                        administrative_area_level_1 
#>                                        "character" 
#>                                          confirmed 
#>                                          "numeric" 
#>                                             deaths 
#>                                          "numeric" 
#>                                               date 
#>                                             "Date" 
#>                                   stringency_index 
#>                                          "numeric" 
#>                          government_response_index 
#>                                          "numeric" 
#>                           containment_health_index 
#>                                          "numeric" 
#> retail_and_recreation_percent_change_from_baseline 
#>                                          "numeric" 
#>  grocery_and_pharmacy_percent_change_from_baseline 
#>                                          "numeric" 
#>                 parks_percent_change_from_baseline 
#>                                          "numeric" 
#>      transit_stations_percent_change_from_baseline 
#>                                          "numeric" 
#>            workplaces_percent_change_from_baseline 
#>                                          "numeric" 
#>           residential_percent_change_from_baseline 
#>                                          "numeric"

sapply() applies class() to each column and collects the answers into a named character vector. If you want the storage type rather than the class, sapply(covid_raw, typeof) gives double where this gives numeric, and double where this gives Date, because a Date is a double with an attribute attached.
Part three:

policy <- tibble(
  date  = as.Date(c("2020-04-07", "2020-06-02", "2020-06-19")),
  phase = c("Circuit breaker begins", "Phase 1 reopening", "Phase 2 reopening")
)

policy
#> # A tibble: 3 × 2
#>   date       phase                 
#>   <date>     <chr>                 
#> 1 2020-04-07 Circuit breaker begins
#> 2 2020-06-02 Phase 1 reopening     
#> 3 2020-06-19 Phase 2 reopening

Why a tibble rather than two vectors: sorting or filtering a tibble moves whole rows, so a date can never lose its label. With two loose vectors, sort(phase) reorders one and leaves the other alone, and nothing errors. The second reason is that the correspondence is now written down. Anyone reading policy can see that 2 June is Phase 1; with two vectors that fact lives only in the head of whoever typed them.
Part four. Convert to an old-style data frame and the difference shows up straight away:

covid_df <- as.data.frame(covid_raw)

head(covid_df$conf, 5)
#> [1] 0 1 3 3 4

Partial matching. covid_df$conf is not a column, and the data frame helpfully decided you meant confirmed. The tibble refuses:

head(covid_raw$conf, 5)
#> Warning: Unknown or uninitialised column: `conf`.
#> NULL

NULL, plus a warning naming the column you asked for. That is the behaviour you want, because partial matching turns a typo into a plausible answer. If a data frame has both confirmed and confirmed_smoothed, $conf is ambiguous and returns NULL anyway, so the convenience is unreliable as well as dangerous.
The other classic difference is single-bracket subsetting:

class(covid_df[, "confirmed"])
#> [1] "numeric"
class(covid_raw[, "confirmed"])
#> [1] "tbl_df"     "tbl"        "data.frame"

The data frame drops to a bare vector when you ask for one column. The tibble stays a tibble. Code written as df[, cols] and then piped into something expecting a rectangle works or breaks depending on how many columns cols happened to contain that day, which is the kind of bug that only shows up on the run where a filter left you with one column.

title: Appendix A — Worked solutions
text:
A.3 Land the file yourself

From the chapter on reading the epidemic in: read the CSV yourself with read_csv(), state the types explicitly, count the missing values, then read it with read.csv() and find what breaks.

Part one. In a fresh session you would need library(tidyverse) and library(here) first; this page already has them.

raw <- read_csv(here("data", "sg_covid_data.csv"))
#> Rows: 345 Columns: 13
#> ── Column specification ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> Delimiter: ","
#> chr   (1): administrative_area_level_1
#> dbl  (11): confirmed, deaths, stringency_index, government_response_index, c...
#> date  (1): date
#> 
#> ℹ Use `spec()` to retrieve the full column specification for this data.
#> ℹ Specify the column types or set `show_col_types = FALSE` to quiet this message.

The specification message is the answer. date (1): date means readr recognised the ISO-8601 strings and parsed the column to Date. dbl (11) covers confirmed, deaths, the three policy indices and the six mobility columns. chr (1): administrative_area_level_1 is the country name, which is "Singapore" on all 345 rows and would have been the first thing to check if it were not.
Reading that message is a habit worth forming now. It is the only moment R tells you what it decided about your file, and by the time a column of counts has silently become character, you are three chunks downstream wondering why mean() failed.
Part two. cols() names the columns you care about and .default mops up:

typed <- read_csv(
  here("data", "sg_covid_data.csv"),
  col_types = cols(
    date                        = col_date(),
    confirmed                   = col_double(),
    administrative_area_level_1 = col_character(),
    .default                    = col_double()
  )
)

dim(typed)
#> [1] 345  13

No message this time. readr only reports a specification it guessed, and you did not ask it to guess. Writing the spec out is what you do when a file is going into a pipeline that runs weekly, because it turns “the column changed type when they added a row” from a silent surprise into a loud parsing failure.
Part three:

glimpse(raw)
#> Rows: 345
#> Columns: 13
#> $ administrative_area_level_1                        <chr> "Singapore", "Singa…
#> $ confirmed                                          <dbl> 0, 1, 3, 3, 4, 5, 7…
#> $ deaths                                             <dbl> NA, NA, NA, NA, NA,…
#> $ date                                               <date> 2020-01-22, 2020-0…
#> $ stringency_index                                   <dbl> 19.44, 25.00, 25.00…
#> $ government_response_index                          <dbl> 19.27, 24.48, 24.48…
#> $ containment_health_index                           <dbl> 22.02, 27.98, 27.98…
#> $ retail_and_recreation_percent_change_from_baseline <dbl> NA, NA, NA, NA, NA,…
#> $ grocery_and_pharmacy_percent_change_from_baseline  <dbl> NA, NA, NA, NA, NA,…
#> $ parks_percent_change_from_baseline                 <dbl> NA, NA, NA, NA, NA,…
#> $ transit_stations_percent_change_from_baseline      <dbl> NA, NA, NA, NA, NA,…
#> $ workplaces_percent_change_from_baseline            <dbl> NA, NA, NA, NA, NA,…
#> $ residential_percent_change_from_baseline           <dbl> NA, NA, NA, NA, NA,…

Seven columns start with NA: deaths and the six mobility columns. Count them properly:

raw %>%
  summarise(across(everything(), ~ sum(is.na(.x)))) %>%
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "column", values_to = "n_missing") %>%
  filter(n_missing > 0)
#> # A tibble: 7 × 2
#>   column                                             n_missing
#>   <chr>                                                  <int>
#> 1 deaths                                                    59
#> 2 retail_and_recreation_percent_change_from_baseline        24
#> 3 grocery_and_pharmacy_percent_change_from_baseline         24
#> 4 parks_percent_change_from_baseline                        24
#> 5 transit_stations_percent_change_from_baseline             24
#> 6 workplaces_percent_change_from_baseline                   24
#> 7 residential_percent_change_from_baseline                  24

They do not all have the same number. The six mobility columns have 24 apiece and deaths has 59, and the two gaps have nothing to do with each other. The mobility gap runs from 22 January to 14 February because Google’s baseline period, the median by weekday over 3 January to 6 February 2020, had not finished. The deaths gap runs to 20 March because Singapore had not recorded a COVID-19 death yet, and the source file encodes “none yet” as missing rather than as zero. Two different reasons, two different repairs, and Chapter 7 takes them apart.
If across() and pivot_longer() are new, colSums(is.na(raw)) gets you the same numbers in one line of base R.
Part four:

base_df <- read.csv(here("data", "sg_covid_data.csv"))

class(base_df$date)
#> [1] "character"
head(base_df$date, 3)
#> [1] "2020-01-22" "2020-01-23" "2020-01-24"

Character. read.csv() has no date parser, so the dates arrive as strings that look right and behave like text. Anything date-shaped then fails:

base_df$date[2] - base_df$date[1]
#> Error in `base_df$date[2] - base_df$date[1]`:
#> ! non-numeric argument to binary operator

Whereas the readr version answers:

raw$date[2] - raw$date[1]
#> Time difference of 1 days

What people get wrong. Sorting. sort() on character dates in ISO-8601 format gives the right answer by accident, because "2020-04-07" sorts after "2020-04-06" alphabetically as well as chronologically. Hand it dates written 07/04/2020 and the sort is silently wrong. If your dates are text, arrange(date) will look like it worked.

title: Appendix A — Worked solutions
text:
A.4 Build a circuit-breaker table

From the chapter on transforming data: use filter(), select(), rename() and arrange() to pull the circuit-breaker period into a small table sorted by the deepest workplace mobility drops.

select() renames as it selects, so this is one call rather than two:

cb <- covid %>%
  filter(date >= as.Date("2020-04-07"), date <= as.Date("2020-06-01")) %>%
  select(
    date,
    confirmed,
    stringency = stringency_index,
    retail     = retail_and_recreation_percent_change_from_baseline,
    workplaces = workplaces_percent_change_from_baseline
  ) %>%
  arrange(workplaces)

cb
#> # A tibble: 56 × 5
#>    date       confirmed stringency retail workplaces
#>    <date>         <dbl>      <dbl>  <dbl>      <dbl>
#>  1 2020-04-10      2108       82.4    -63        -83
#>  2 2020-05-01     17101       82.4    -68        -83
#>  3 2020-05-07     20939       76.8    -66        -83
#>  4 2020-05-25     31960       73.2    -62        -82
#>  5 2020-04-23     11178       76.8    -68        -69
#>  6 2020-04-29     15641       76.8    -67        -69
#>  7 2020-04-30     16169       76.8    -67        -69
#>  8 2020-04-22     10141       76.8    -66        -68
#>  9 2020-04-27     14423       76.8    -67        -68
#> 10 2020-04-28     14951       76.8    -66        -68
#> # ℹ 46 more rows

Two filter() conditions separated by a comma are combined with AND, which is what you want for a date range. Writing filter(date >= start & date <= end) is identical; the comma is the house style because it reads as a list of requirements.
arrange(workplaces) sorts ascending, and mobility drops are negative, so ascending puts the deepest drops first. If you wanted the same thing for a series where bigger means worse, you would need arrange(desc(...)). Getting this backwards is worth checking every time, because a sorted table always looks convincing.
How many rows:

nrow(cb)
#> [1] 56

as.integer(as.Date("2020-06-01") - as.Date("2020-04-07")) + 1
#> [1] 56

Fifty-six both ways. Twenty-four days of April, thirty-one of May, and the first of June. The + 1 is there because subtracting two dates counts the gaps between them, not the days, and forgetting it is how a period ends up one day short in a report. The agreement between the two numbers is the check: if nrow() had come back 55, you would have a missing day in the file rather than an off-by-one in your head.
The top three rows are 10 April, 1 May and 7 May, all at 83% below baseline. They are Good Friday, Labour Day and Vesak Day. The three deepest workplace-mobility days inside Singapore’s strictest eight weeks of 2020 are public holidays, and the same holds across the whole year: the eight deepest workplace days in 2020 are all public holidays.
What people get wrong. Reading a mobility trough as a policy effect. Before you write a sentence about any dip in these series, check the date against a calendar. Chapter 11 comes back to this with the full list of eight.

title: Appendix A — Worked solutions
text:
A.5 Difference the deaths series

Also from the chapter on transforming data: apply the cases recipe to deaths, run both checks on the result, and find the largest single-day rise.


deaths_daily <- covid_raw %>%
  arrange(date) %>%
  mutate(daily_deaths = deaths - lag(deaths, default = 0))

deaths_daily %>%
  select(date, deaths, daily_deaths) %>%
  slice(58:63)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 3
#>   date       deaths daily_deaths
#>   <date>      <dbl>        <dbl>
#> 1 2020-03-19     NA           NA
#> 2 2020-03-20     NA           NA
#> 3 2020-03-21      2           NA
#> 4 2020-03-22      2            0
#> 5 2020-03-23      2            0
#> 6 2020-03-24      2            0

The first check, for negative values:

any(deaths_daily$daily_deaths < 0)
#> [1] NA

NA, not FALSE. This is the part of the exercise worth slowing down for. NA < 0 is NA, because R has no idea whether the missing value was negative. any() then has a vector containing NAs and FALSEs and no TRUE at all, and the honest answer to “is at least one of these true?” when some of them are unknown is “I cannot tell”. So it returns NA.
Tell it to ignore the unknowns and you get the answer you wanted:

any(deaths_daily$daily_deaths < 0, na.rm = TRUE)
#> [1] FALSE

No negative daily deaths. The cumulative series never goes backwards.
The second check, that the daily figures add back to the cumulative total:

sum(deaths_daily$daily_deaths)
#> [1] NA

sum(deaths_daily$daily_deaths, na.rm = TRUE)
#> [1] 27

max(deaths_daily$deaths, na.rm = TRUE)
#> [1] 29

The plain sum() is NA for the same reason. With na.rm = TRUE you get 27, and the cumulative column ends at 29. The check fails, and it is supposed to.
Here is where the two went. deaths is missing for the first 59 rows and the first recorded value, on 21 March 2020, is already 2. So the difference on 21 March is 2 - NA, which is NA, and those two deaths never enter the sum:

deaths_daily %>%
  filter(!is.na(deaths)) %>%
  slice_head(n = 3) %>%
  select(date, deaths, daily_deaths)
#> # A tibble: 3 × 3
#>   date       deaths daily_deaths
#>   <date>      <dbl>        <dbl>
#> 1 2020-03-21      2           NA
#> 2 2020-03-22      2            0
#> 3 2020-03-23      2            0

Differencing recovers changes. It cannot recover a level. A series that starts part-way up loses everything below the step, and no amount of na.rm = TRUE puts it back. Chapter 7 shows the repair, which is a decision about what the leading NAs mean rather than a piece of code.
The largest single-day rise:

deaths_daily %>%
  slice_max(daily_deaths, n = 1) %>%
  select(date, deaths, daily_deaths)
#> # A tibble: 2 × 3
#>   date       deaths daily_deaths
#>   <date>      <dbl>        <dbl>
#> 1 2020-04-27     14            2
#> 2 2020-05-06     20            2

Two days tie at two deaths, so slice_max(n = 1) returns both. with_ties = FALSE would give you one arbitrarily, which is fine when you want a single row and wrong when the tie is the finding. In a year with 29 deaths, the fact that no day recorded more than two is worth a sentence on its own.

title: Appendix A — Worked solutions
text:
A.6 Interrogate the mobility gap

From the chapter on missing values: check whether the six mobility columns are missing on the same days, take a monthly mean that has almost no data behind it, and count days two ways.

Part one. which(is.na(x)) gives row numbers rather than a count, and row numbers can be compared:

mobility <- covid %>% select(ends_with("percent_change_from_baseline"))

na_rows <- lapply(mobility, function(x) which(is.na(x)))

lengths(na_rows)
#> retail_and_recreation_percent_change_from_baseline 
#>                                                 24 
#>  grocery_and_pharmacy_percent_change_from_baseline 
#>                                                 24 
#>                 parks_percent_change_from_baseline 
#>                                                 24 
#>      transit_stations_percent_change_from_baseline 
#>                                                 24 
#>            workplaces_percent_change_from_baseline 
#>                                                 24 
#>           residential_percent_change_from_baseline 
#>                                                 24

all(sapply(na_rows, identical, na_rows[[1]]))
#> [1] TRUE

The same 24 rows in all six columns, not merely 24 in each. identical() is doing real work there: it compares length, type and every element, so two different sets of 24 rows would come back FALSE.
Which days:

range(covid$date[na_rows[[1]]])
#> [1] "2020-01-22" "2020-02-14"

22 January to 14 February 2020, one unbroken block at the start of the file. All six series are absent for the same reason: Google’s baseline is the median for each day of the week over 3 January to 6 February 2020, and until that window closed there was nothing to compute a percentage change against. One cause, one shape of gap, which is why the six columns move together.
Part two:

feb <- covid %>% filter(month == as.Date("2020-02-01"))

nrow(feb)
#> [1] 29

mean(feb$parks_percent_change_from_baseline, na.rm = TRUE)
#> [1] -7.533333

sum(!is.na(feb$parks_percent_change_from_baseline))
#> [1] 15

The number is −7.53. It is the mean of 15 days out of 29, and all 15 fall in the second half of the month:

range(feb$date[!is.na(feb$parks_percent_change_from_baseline)])
#> [1] "2020-02-15" "2020-02-29"

Calling that “February’s average parks mobility” would tell a reader that Singaporeans spent 7.5% less time in parks across February 2020, when what the number describes is 15 February to 29 February. The first half of the month is not averaged low. It is not averaged at all, and half of February is missing from a number labelled February.
January is the harsher version. Retail mobility is 100% missing that month, and mean() with na.rm = TRUE returns NaN rather than a number, because you have asked it to average nothing. NaN at least stops you. A mean over 15 of 29 days does not.
Part three. The prediction: the gap should be 24, because the missing rows are the same 24 rows for every mobility column, and the two tools treat them differently.

nrow(covid[covid$parks_percent_change_from_baseline < -40, ])
#> [1] 101

covid %>%
  filter(parks_percent_change_from_baseline < -40) %>%
  nrow()
#> [1] 77

101 against 77, a gap of exactly 24. covid$parks... < -40 is a logical vector containing TRUE, FALSE and 24 NAs. The single-bracket subscript keeps every row that is not FALSE, so each NA becomes a row of nothing:

bracket <- covid[covid$parks_percent_change_from_baseline < -40, ]

sum(is.na(bracket$date))
#> [1] 24

Twenty-four rows in that result have no date and no case count. filter() drops NA rows because a row that might match is not a row that does, and for the question “on how many days did parks mobility fall below −40” the honest answer is 77, with a footnote saying 24 days cannot be assessed.
What people get wrong. Reporting the 101. It is a bigger number, it comes out of code that ran without complaint, and nothing on screen says a quarter of those rows are phantoms. The same arithmetic applies to every mobility column in this file, and the gap is always 24.

title: Appendix A — Worked solutions
text:
A.7 Audit your severity column

From the chapter on making decisions: check the three severity counts, find the range of daily_cases inside each label, and work out how far the 100 cutoff could move before anything changed.

Steps one and two in one call. group_by() and summarise() are the subject of Chapter 9, so treat this as a preview:

covid %>%
  group_by(severity) %>%
  summarise(
    days    = n(),
    lowest  = min(daily_cases),
    highest = max(daily_cases)
  )
#> # A tibble: 3 × 4
#>   severity  days lowest highest
#>   <fct>    <int>  <dbl>   <dbl>
#> 1 Low        215      0      94
#> 2 Medium      53    100     295
#> 3 High        77    301    1426

215, 53 and 77 add to 345, which is every row in the file. count() is the other route and it has one advantage here: it shows an NA category if one exists.

covid %>% count(severity)
#> # A tibble: 3 × 2
#>   severity     n
#>   <fct>    <int>
#> 1 Low        215
#> 2 Medium      53
#> 3 High        77

Three rows, no fourth row labelled NA. If a day had come back missing, this is where it would show, and the cause would be a gap in case_when()’s conditions rather than a gap in the data. case_when() returns NA when nothing matches, silently, so this check is the one that catches a cutoff you forgot to cover.
Step three is the one worth thinking about. The largest Low day is 94 and the smallest Medium day is 100. Nothing in 2020 landed in between:

covid %>%
  filter(daily_cases >= 90, daily_cases <= 110) %>%
  count(daily_cases, severity)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 3
#>   daily_cases severity     n
#>         <dbl> <fct>    <int>
#> 1          91 Low          1
#> 2          93 Low          1
#> 3          94 Low          1
#> 4         100 Medium       1
#> 5         102 Medium       1
#> 6         106 Medium       1

So the cutoff could sit anywhere from 95 to 100 and every one of the 345 days would keep the label it has. Move it to 101 and 18 August, which recorded exactly 100 cases, becomes Low. Move it to 94 and the same day is unaffected but the 94-case day changes. Prove it rather than trusting the argument:

relabel <- function(lower) {
  s <- case_when(
    covid$daily_cases <  lower ~ "Low",
    covid$daily_cases <= 300   ~ "Medium",
    covid$daily_cases >  300   ~ "High"
  )
  factor(s, levels = c("Low", "Medium", "High"))
}

as_written <- relabel(100)

sapply(90:105, function(t) identical(relabel(t), as_written))
#>  [1] FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE  TRUE  TRUE  TRUE  TRUE  TRUE  TRUE FALSE
#> [13] FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE

TRUE from 95 through 100 and FALSE either side. The upper cutoff behaves the same way: the largest Medium day is 295 and the smallest High day is 301, so 295 through 300 are interchangeable.
What that tells you is that the exact number 100 is not carrying the classification. Any cutoff from 95 to 100 produces the identical table, and the same is true of 295 to 300 at the top, so nobody can argue that your headline depends on a round number picked by a worksheet author. What they can argue is what happens at 50, or at 500, and that is the next exercise.

title: Appendix A — Worked solutions
section: A.8 Move the cutoffs and watch the headline move
text:
A.8 Move the cutoffs and watch the headline move

Also from the chapter on making decisions: rebuild severity with cutoffs at 50 and 500, compare the counts with 215 / 53 / 77, and write a defensible sentence under each rule.


recut <- covid %>%
  mutate(
    severity_wide = case_when(
      daily_cases <  50  ~ "Low",
      daily_cases <= 500 ~ "Medium",
      daily_cases >  500 ~ "High"
    ),
    severity_wide = factor(severity_wide, levels = c("Low", "Medium", "High"))
  )

recut %>% count(severity_wide)
#> # A tibble: 3 × 2
#>   severity_wide     n
#>   <fct>         <int>
#> 1 Low             189
#> 2 Medium          114
#> 3 High             42

189 Low, 114 Medium, 42 High, against 215 / 53 / 77 under the original rule. Put them side by side to see where the days went:

recut %>% count(severity, severity_wide)
#> # A tibble: 5 × 3
#>   severity severity_wide     n
#>   <fct>    <fct>         <int>
#> 1 Low      Low             189
#> 2 Low      Medium           26
#> 3 Medium   Medium           53
#> 4 High     Medium           35
#> 5 High     High             42

Twenty-six days that were Low are now Medium, and 35 days that were High are now Medium. Nothing crossed two boundaries. The wider Medium band swallowed the edges of both neighbours, and the count of High days fell by nearly half.
The factor() line matters. Leave it out and count() sorts High, Low, Medium alphabetically, which looks like a bug in your analysis and is not.
Two sentences, both true of the same 345 days:

Under the original thresholds, 77 of Singapore’s 345 reported days in 2020, 22%, exceeded 300 new cases, and 62% stayed below 100.


Under thresholds of 50 and 500, only 42 days in 2020, 12%, exceeded 500 new cases, and a further 114 sat in a broad middle band.

Neither is false. The first invites the reader to conclude that a fifth of Singapore’s 2020 was a bad day. The second invites them to conclude that high-burden days were rare. A reader who sees only one of the two takes away a different impression of the same year.
A threshold is an argument, and the place for an argument is your methods section, next to a reason. “300 was chosen because it is roughly the daily capacity of the contact-tracing system” is a cutoff you can defend. “300 was on the worksheet” is not, and until somebody asks you, nobody will know which one you had.

title: Appendix A — Worked solutions
text:
A.9 High-severity days by month

From the chapter on grouping and summarising: one row per month, counting High, Medium and Low days plus the days of data in the month.

Three sum() calls inside one summarise() put the columns in the order you choose, which count() plus pivot_wider() does not:

monthly_severity <- covid %>%
  group_by(month) %>%
  summarise(
    days   = n(),
    low    = sum(severity == "Low"),
    medium = sum(severity == "Medium"),
    high   = sum(severity == "High"),
    cases  = sum(daily_cases)
  )

monthly_severity
#> # A tibble: 12 × 6
#>    month       days   low medium  high cases
#>    <date>     <int> <int>  <int> <int> <dbl>
#>  1 2020-01-01    10    10      0     0    13
#>  2 2020-02-01    29    29      0     0    89
#>  3 2020-03-01    31    31      0     0   824
#>  4 2020-04-01    30     5      7    18 15243
#>  5 2020-05-01    31     0      0    31 18715
#>  6 2020-06-01    30     0     18    12  9023
#>  7 2020-07-01    31     0     19    12  8298
#>  8 2020-08-01    31    18      9     4  4607
#>  9 2020-09-01    30    30      0     0   953
#> 10 2020-10-01    31    31      0     0   250
#> 11 2020-11-01    30    30      0     0   203
#> 12 2020-12-01    31    31      0     0   381

sum(severity == "High") works because == gives a logical vector and sum() treats TRUE as 1. It is the standard idiom for “count the rows where this holds” and it composes inside summarise() in a way that nrow(filter(...)) does not.
Check the row that will trip you up before anything else. January has 10 days, not 31, because the file starts on 22 January. Every other month is complete. That is why days is in the table: without it, January’s 13 cases read as a whole quiet month rather than as the last ten days of one.
The two questions:

monthly_severity %>% slice_max(high, n = 2)
#> # A tibble: 2 × 6
#>   month       days   low medium  high cases
#>   <date>     <int> <int>  <int> <int> <dbl>
#> 1 2020-05-01    31     0      0    31 18715
#> 2 2020-04-01    30     5      7    18 15243

monthly_severity %>% slice_max(cases, n = 2)
#> # A tibble: 2 × 6
#>   month       days   low medium  high cases
#>   <date>     <int> <int>  <int> <int> <dbl>
#> 1 2020-05-01    31     0      0    31 18715
#> 2 2020-04-01    30     5      7    18 15243

May wins both. Every one of its 31 days was above 300 cases, and it carried 18,715 of the year’s 58,599.
They can come apart, and August is the near-miss that shows how. August has 4 High days and 4,607 cases, more than September through December combined, while March has 0 High days and 824. A count of days above a threshold is insensitive to how far above the threshold those days sat, so a month of steady 320s and a month carrying one 908 can produce very different High counts for similar totals. Report both, or report the one whose question you are answering.

title: Appendix A — Worked solutions
section: A.10 A monthly alert table you can defend
text:
A.10 A monthly alert table you can defend

Also from the chapter on grouping and summarising: three statuses instead of two, then the same table under a rate-based rule, and which of the two you would defend.


alerts <- covid %>%
  group_by(month) %>%
  summarise(
    days       = n(),
    high_days  = sum(severity == "High"),
    mean_daily = round(mean(daily_cases), 1)
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    status_days = case_when(
      high_days >  5 ~ "Alert",
      high_days >= 1 ~ "Watch",
      TRUE           ~ "All clear"
    )
  )

alerts
#> # A tibble: 12 × 5
#>    month       days high_days mean_daily status_days
#>    <date>     <int>     <int>      <dbl> <chr>      
#>  1 2020-01-01    10         0        1.3 All clear  
#>  2 2020-02-01    29         0        3.1 All clear  
#>  3 2020-03-01    31         0       26.6 All clear  
#>  4 2020-04-01    30        18      508.  Alert      
#>  5 2020-05-01    31        31      604.  Alert      
#>  6 2020-06-01    30        12      301.  Alert      
#>  7 2020-07-01    31        12      268.  Alert      
#>  8 2020-08-01    31         4      149.  Watch      
#>  9 2020-09-01    30         0       31.8 All clear  
#> 10 2020-10-01    31         0        8.1 All clear  
#> 11 2020-11-01    30         0        6.8 All clear  
#> 12 2020-12-01    31         0       12.3 All clear
