The ordering carries the logic. case_when() takes the first condition that matches, so high_days > 5 has to come before high_days >= 1; a month with 18 High days satisfies both, and if the >= 1 line came first, April would be labelled “Watch”. The final TRUE ~ "All clear" is the catch-all, and without it the months with zero High days would come back NA rather than falling through to a sensible default.
Now the rate-based rule. I have picked 100 mean daily cases, and stating the number out loud is half the exercise:

alerts <- alerts %>%
  mutate(status_rate = if_else(mean_daily > 100, "Alert", "All clear"))

alerts %>%
  filter(status_days != status_rate) %>%
  select(month, days, high_days, mean_daily, status_days, status_rate)
#> # A tibble: 1 × 6
#>   month       days high_days mean_daily status_days status_rate
#>   <date>     <int>     <int>      <dbl> <chr>       <chr>      
#> 1 2020-08-01    31         4       149. Watch       Alert

One month changes: August, “Watch” under the day-count rule and “Alert” under the rate rule. August had 4 High days and a mean of 148.6, and the mean is being pulled up by 5 August, which recorded 908 cases against a monthly median of 91. Recompute August’s mean without that single day and it falls to 123.3, still above 100 but by much less.
Which rule I would rather defend: the day-count rule, and not because it is kinder to August. A count of days above a threshold cannot be moved by one extreme value, and 5 August is an extreme value with a known cause. MOH attributed the day’s numbers to clearance testing in the dormitories picking up past infections, 903 of the 908 were dormitory residents, and 581 were linked to a single cluster at Acacia Lodge. A rule that escalates a whole month on the strength of one day of retrospective testing is a rule that will escalate again the next time a backlog clears.
The honest version of the answer is that I would report both columns and let the meeting see the disagreement, because the disagreement is the finding. A single status column hides the fact that August was one thing by one measure and another thing by another.

title: Appendix A — Worked solutions
section: A.11 Cross-check a month that is not September
text:
A.11 Cross-check a month that is not September

Also from the chapter on grouping and summarising: compute a month’s mean daily cases two ways, then try the same trick on January and fix what breaks.

October, the differenced way:

october <- covid %>% filter(month == as.Date("2020-10-01"))

nrow(october)
#> [1] 31
mean(october$daily_cases)
#> [1] 8.064516

Now the telescoping route, which never touches daily_cases at all. Every day’s increment cancels against the next one, so the total for October is the cumulative count on 31 October minus the cumulative count on 30 September:

end_october   <- covid %>% filter(date == as.Date("2020-10-31")) %>% pull(confirmed)
end_september <- covid %>% filter(date == as.Date("2020-09-30")) %>% pull(confirmed)

(end_october - end_september) / nrow(october)
#> [1] 8.064516

8.06 both ways. Two routes that share no intermediate column, which is what makes the agreement evidence rather than a tautology. Comparing mean() against a loop that performs the same division proves only that R can divide.
Wrap it up so January can break it:

month_mean_telescoped <- function(df, which_month) {
  m    <- as.Date(which_month)
  this <- df %>% filter(month == m)
  prev <- df %>% filter(month == m - months(1))

  end_this <- this %>% slice_max(date, n = 1) %>% pull(confirmed)
  end_prev <- prev %>% slice_max(date, n = 1) %>% pull(confirmed)

  (end_this - end_prev) / nrow(this)
}

month_mean_telescoped(covid, "2020-10-01")
#> [1] 8.064516

January:

month_mean_telescoped(covid, "2020-01-01")
#> numeric(0)

numeric(0). Not an error, not NA, an empty vector. There is no December 2019 in this file, so prev has zero rows, pull(confirmed) returns a length-zero vector, and arithmetic between a length-1 vector and a length-0 vector gives length 0. R does exactly what it was asked and the answer has nothing in it.
That is worse than an error, because numeric(0) will travel. Put it in a mutate() and you get a length mismatch three steps later. Print it in a report and you get a blank cell nobody notices.
The fix uses a fact about this specific file:

covid$confirmed[1]
#> [1] 0
covid$date[1]
#> [1] "2020-01-22"

confirmed is 0 on the first day of the record. There is nothing before the file to subtract, because the cumulative count starts at zero:

month_mean_telescoped <- function(df, which_month) {
  m    <- as.Date(which_month)
  this <- df %>% filter(month == m)
  prev <- df %>% filter(month == m - months(1))

  end_this <- this %>% slice_max(date, n = 1) %>% pull(confirmed)
  end_prev <- prev %>% slice_max(date, n = 1) %>% pull(confirmed)

  if (length(end_prev) == 0) end_prev <- 0

  (end_this - end_prev) / nrow(this)
}

month_mean_telescoped(covid, "2020-01-01")
#> [1] 1.3

january <- covid %>% filter(month == as.Date("2020-01-01"))
mean(january$daily_cases)
#> [1] 1.3

1.3 both ways.
Two assumptions are buried in that if. The first is that a cumulative series starting at 0 means no cases occurred before the record begins, which happens to be true here and is false for any dataset that starts mid-epidemic. The second is that January’s denominator is 10, the days present in the file, not 31, the days in the month. Both are defensible for this file and both are things you must write down, because the function will happily return a number for a file where neither holds.

title: Appendix A — Worked solutions
section: A.12 Draw a publication-ready epidemic curve
text:
A.12 Draw a publication-ready epidemic curve

From the chapter on plots: a single figure of daily cases across 2020 that stands on its own, with the circuit breaker marked, saved as a 300 dpi PNG about 3.5 inches wide.

Build it as an object so it can be printed and saved without being drawn twice:

cb_start <- as.Date("2020-04-07")
cb_end   <- as.Date("2020-06-01")

p_epi <- ggplot(covid, aes(x = date, y = daily_cases)) +
  annotate(
    "rect",
    xmin = cb_start, xmax = cb_end, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf,
    fill = nus_colours[["muted"]], alpha = 0.25
  ) +
  geom_col(fill = nus_colours[["blue"]], width = 1) +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "2 months", date_labels = "%b") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_comma()) +
  labs(
    title    = "Singapore's reported cases peaked on 20 April 2020",
    subtitle = "Shaded band: circuit breaker, 7 April to 1 June",
    x = NULL,
    y = "New cases per day",
    caption  = "Counts differenced from the cumulative confirmed series.\nSource: COVID-19 Data Hub."
  )

p_epi



The figure as drawn at the book’s default width of 7 inches.



Three decisions in there are worth naming. annotate("rect", ...) with ymin = -Inf and ymax = Inf shades the full height of the panel whatever the y range turns out to be, so the band does not need adjusting when the data changes. It comes before geom_col() so the bars sit on top of it rather than under it; layers are drawn in the order you add them. And date_breaks = "2 months" is a deliberate choice about collision: monthly ticks fit at 7 inches and do not fit at 3.5.
Now save it at the size it will actually be printed:

out <- tempfile(fileext = ".png")

ggsave(out, plot = p_epi, width = 3.5, height = 2.6, dpi = 300)

file.exists(out)
#> [1] TRUE

In your own script that path would be "figures/epi-curve-2020.png" rather than a temporary file, and the directory has to exist first; ggsave() will not create it for you.
Then the part the exercise actually asks about. Open that PNG. ggplot2 measures text in points rather than as a fraction of the canvas, so halving the width does not halve the type. theme_nus() has a base size of 12 and puts the title at 1.15 times that, which is a bold 13.8-point line that fits comfortably across 7 inches and runs off the edge of 3.5. The six month labels collide for the same reason. The fix is to give the small version its own text and its own axis, rather than drawing the big one and shrinking it:

p_small <- p_epi +
  labs(
    title    = "Cases peaked on 20 April 2020",
    subtitle = "Shaded: circuit breaker",
    caption  = "Differenced from cumulative counts."
  ) +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "3 months", date_labels = "%b") +
  theme(
    plot.title    = element_text(size = 10),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 8),
    plot.caption  = element_text(size = 6.5),
    axis.title    = element_text(size = 8),
    axis.text     = element_text(size = 7)
  )
#> Scale for x is already present.
#> Adding another scale for x, which will replace the existing scale.

p_small



The same figure with type sized for a single journal column.



ggsave(tempfile(fileext = ".png"), plot = p_small,
       width = 3.5, height = 2.6, dpi = 300)

Shorter title, shorter caption, and four month ticks instead of six. The message about a scale being replaced is ggplot2 telling you that the second scale_x_date() overwrote the first, which is what was intended here and is something to look at hard when it is not.
What people get wrong. Drawing the figure at 7 inches, saving it at 7 inches, and letting the journal or the slide deck shrink it afterwards. That shrink does scale the type, because it is scaling the finished image, and 13.8-point text at half size is 7-point text nobody can read. Size the figure for its final home.

title: Appendix A — Worked solutions
section: A.13 Make the distribution legible, and say what it cost
text:
A.13 Make the distribution legible, and say what it cost

Also from the chapter on plots: fix the histogram of daily_cases, state exactly which days your fix removed, then facet it by month in calendar order.

The raw version first, so there is something to compare against:

ggplot(covid, aes(x = daily_cases)) +
  geom_histogram()
#> `stat_bin()` using `bins = 30`. Pick better value `binwidth`.



The default. Over half the year lands in the leftmost bar.



The message about bins = 30 is ggplot2 telling you it guessed, and the guess is the wrong tool for a distribution this skewed. Thirty bins across a range of 0 to 1,426 is a bin width of 47.5, and 183 of the 345 days fall in the first one. The leftmost bar swallows the year and the rest of the panel is white space.
Here is a version with a bin width you chose and a restricted view:

ggplot(covid, aes(x = daily_cases)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 20) +
  xlim(0, 400) +
  labs(
    x = "New cases per day",
    y = "Days",
    title = "Most of 2020 was quiet, and the tail is long",
    caption = "55 days above 400 cases are not shown."
  )
#> Warning: Removed 55 rows containing non-finite outside the scale range
#> (`stat_bin()`).
#> Warning: Removed 2 rows containing missing values or values outside the scale range
#> (`geom_bar()`).



Twenty-case bins, x axis cut at 400.



Read the warning, because it writes your caption for you. Removed 55 rows containing non-finite outside the scale range is the exact count: xlim() does not crop the picture, it drops the rows before the bins are computed, so those 55 days are not in this figure at all. They are the 55 days above 400 cases, which between them carry 36,379 of the year’s 58,599 cases. A figure that omits 62% of the epidemic needs to say so, and the caption above does. The second warning, about 2 rows removed by geom_bar(), is the two bins that straddle the edge of the new limits.
coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 400)) is the alternative and behaves differently: it zooms the finished plot instead of filtering the data, so the bins are computed over all 345 days, nothing is removed, and you cannot see past 400. No warning appears, which is convenient and is also why I prefer xlim() here. The warning is a receipt.
Now the faceted version. The factor is what puts the panels in calendar order:

covid %>%
  mutate(month_name = factor(format(date, "%B"), levels = month.name)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = daily_cases)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 50) +
  facet_wrap(~ month_name) +
  labs(
    x = "New cases per day",
    y = "Days",
    title = "Twelve distributions, not one"
  )



The same distribution, cut by month, panels in calendar order.



month.name is a base R constant holding the twelve month names in order. Without the factor() call the panels come out April, August, December, February, and the plot looks broken for a reason that has nothing to do with plotting.
Which one goes in the report: the faceted one, if the question is about how the year changed. The single histogram answers “what did a typical day in 2020 look like”, and the answer, that most days were under 100 cases, is true and close to useless, because 2020 in Singapore was not one epidemic curve at one intensity. The facets show January to March sitting flat against the axis, April to July spread right across it, August straddling both with its one 908-case day out on its own, and September to December back where the year started. That contrast is the finding, and a single histogram flattens it into a shape that describes no month in particular.

title: Appendix A — Worked solutions
section: A.14 Put policy next to cases
text:
A.14 Put policy next to cases

Also from the chapter on plots: cases above, stringency below, one shared date axis, panels labelled A and B, then read the date of peak stringency off the figure and check it against the data.

Two ordinary plots, combined with /:

p_cases <- ggplot(covid, aes(x = date, y = daily_cases)) +
  geom_line() +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "2 months", date_labels = "%b") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_comma()) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "New cases per day")

p_stringency <- ggplot(covid, aes(x = date, y = stringency_index)) +
  geom_line(colour = nus_colours[["crimson"]]) +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "2 months", date_labels = "%b") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Stringency index")

(p_cases / p_stringency) +
  plot_annotation(
    title    = "Policy reached its ceiling ten days before cases turned",
    caption  = "Sources: COVID-19 Data Hub; Oxford COVID-19 Government Response Tracker.",
    tag_levels = "A"
  )



Policy stringency and reported cases, Singapore 2020.



Both panels use the same scale_x_date(), which is what makes them readable as one figure. Patchwork does not force a shared axis; it stacks two independent plots, and if one of them had a different date range the tick marks would not line up and the comparison would be silently wrong.
Reading it off the figure, panel B rises in a step in early April and flattens at its ceiling, and panel A is still climbing at that point. Checking against the data:

covid %>%
  filter(stringency_index == max(stringency_index)) %>%
  arrange(date) %>%
  select(date, stringency_index, daily_cases)
#> # A tibble: 3 × 3
#>   date       stringency_index daily_cases
#>   <date>                <dbl>       <dbl>
#> 1 2020-04-10             82.4         198
#> 2 2020-04-25             82.4         618
#> 3 2020-05-01             82.4         932

The maximum of 82.41 is reached on three separate days and the first is 10 April 2020. slice_max() would give you the same three rows, which is why the exercise warns you about it: with n = 1 and default with_ties = TRUE you get all three, and arrange(date) then puts the earliest first. Taking slice_max(..., n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) and calling the result “the date” would be a guess dressed as an answer.
Cases had not peaked on 10 April. The peak was 1,426 on 20 April, ten days later, and on 10 April the count was 198:

covid %>% slice_max(daily_cases, n = 1) %>% select(date, daily_cases)
#> # A tibble: 1 × 2
#>   date       daily_cases
#>   <date>           <dbl>
#> 1 2020-04-20        1426

Ten days between the policy ceiling and the case peak is consistent with an incubation period plus a testing and reporting delay, and it is also consistent with a dormitory testing programme that was expanding through April independently of anything the index measures. This file cannot separate those, so the sentence to write is about the sequence, not the cause.
One thing not to do with panel B: read the small steps after July. There are 23 changes in the index after 1 July and several last a single day, which is indistinguishable from an encoding artifact in the source. A one-day tick is not a policy announcement.

title: Appendix A — Worked solutions
text:
A.15 Generalise the alert

From the chapter on writing functions: let the caller choose which mobility series to check, keeping retail as the default, then count the days below −60 for workplaces and for parks.

Passing a column name into a dplyr verb from inside a function needs { } around the argument, which tells dplyr to look for the name in the data frame rather than in the calling environment:

mobility_alert <- function(df,
                           column    = retail_and_recreation_percent_change_from_baseline,
                           threshold = -30) {
  if (threshold > 0) {
    stop("`threshold` should be negative. Mobility is measured as percentage change ",
         "from baseline, so a drop of 30% is -30, not 30.", call. = FALSE)
  }

  df %>%
    filter({{ column }} < threshold) %>%
    pull(date)
}

The default is a bare column name, not a string, and it works because R does not evaluate a default argument until the function body needs it, by which point filter() has the data frame in scope. Existing calls are unaffected:

length(mobility_alert(covid))
#> [1] 88

Eighty-eight, the same answer as before the rewrite. Adding an argument in the middle of a signature is the usual way to break other people’s code, and putting the new argument after df with a default that reproduces the old behaviour is what keeps that from happening.
The two counts:

length(mobility_alert(covid, workplaces_percent_change_from_baseline, threshold = -60))
#> [1] 41

length(mobility_alert(covid, parks_percent_change_from_baseline, threshold = -60))
#> [1] 37

Forty-one days for workplaces and 37 for parks. Both counts exclude the 24 days with no mobility data, because filter() drops rows where the condition is NA, and that behaviour is now inherited by every call to this function.
The deepest workplace days:

covid %>%
  slice_min(workplaces_percent_change_from_baseline, n = 8) %>%
  select(date, workplaces_percent_change_from_baseline) %>%
  mutate(weekday = wday(date, label = TRUE))
#> # A tibble: 8 × 3
#>   date       workplaces_percent_change_from_baseline weekday
#>   <date>                                       <dbl> <ord>  
#> 1 2020-04-10                                     -83 Fri    
#> 2 2020-05-01                                     -83 Fri    
#> 3 2020-05-07                                     -83 Thu    
#> 4 2020-05-25                                     -82 Mon    
#> 5 2020-08-10                                     -73 Mon    
#> 6 2020-07-10                                     -72 Fri    
#> 7 2020-07-31                                     -72 Fri    
#> 8 2020-12-25                                     -70 Fri

All eight are public holidays: Good Friday on 10 April, Labour Day on 1 May, Vesak Day on 7 May, Hari Raya Puasa observed on 25 May, National Day observed on 10 August, polling day for the general election on 10 July, Hari Raya Haji on 31 July, and Christmas Day.
The interesting one is 10 July. The other seven are religious or seasonal holidays that recur every year and drag other things along with them, so a mobility trough on Good Friday tells you about Good Friday rather than about COVID-19. Polling day has none of that. It is a one-off public holiday, it sat inside Phase 2 with no change in restrictions around it, and workplace mobility fell 72% below baseline anyway. If you want a clean read on how far this series can move for a reason that has nothing to do with the epidemic, that is the day to look at.
What people get wrong. Writing filter(column < threshold) without the braces. R then looks for an object called column in the calling environment, does not find one, and the error is object 'column' not found, which points at the wrong thing entirely. Or, worse, there is something called column in your global environment and the function quietly filters on that.

title: Appendix A — Worked solutions
section: A.16 Add a judgement to the summary
text:
A.16 Add a judgement to the summary

Also from the chapter on writing functions: give month_summary() a verdict column, run it on September and April, and decide whether five High days is a defensible cut-off.

summarise() cannot reliably refer to a column it is creating in the same call, so the verdict goes in a mutate() afterwards. I have also made the cut-off an argument, for reasons below:

month_summary <- function(df, which_month, high_cut = 5) {
  start <- floor_date(as.Date(which_month), "month")

  if (!start %in% df$month) {
    stop("No data for ", format(start, "%B %Y"), ". The data covers ",
         format(min(df$month), "%B %Y"), " to ",
         format(max(df$month), "%B %Y"), ".", call. = FALSE)
  }

  df %>%
    filter(month == start) %>%
    summarise(
      month      = start,
      days       = n(),
      total      = sum(daily_cases),
      mean_daily = round(mean(daily_cases), 1),
      peak       = max(daily_cases),
      peak_date  = date[which.max(daily_cases)],
      high_days  = sum(severity == "High")
    ) %>%
    mutate(verdict = if_else(high_days > high_cut, "Escalate", "All clear"))
}

month_summary(covid, "2020-09-01")
#> # A tibble: 1 × 8
#>   month       days total mean_daily  peak peak_date  high_days verdict  
#>   <date>     <int> <dbl>      <dbl> <dbl> <date>         <int> <chr>    
#> 1 2020-09-01    30   953       31.8    86 2020-09-11         0 All clear

month_summary(covid, "2020-04-01")
#> # A tibble: 1 × 8
#>   month       days total mean_daily  peak peak_date  high_days verdict 
#>   <date>     <int> <dbl>      <dbl> <dbl> <date>         <int> <chr>   
#> 1 2020-04-01    30 15243       508.  1426 2020-04-20        18 Escalate

September: 30 days, 953 cases, a mean of 31.8, a peak of 86, zero High days, “All clear”. April: 15,243 cases, a peak of 1,426 on the 20th, 18 High days, “Escalate”. Both verdicts match what the case counts say, which is the check the exercise asked for and is not a formality. Run this on twelve months and one of them will surprise you, and that is when you find out whether the rule or the data is wrong.
Is five defensible? Not on the evidence in this file. Look at the whole year:

list_rbind(map(unique(covid$month), function(m) month_summary(covid, m))) %>%
  select(month, days, total, mean_daily, high_days, verdict)
#> # A tibble: 12 × 6
#>    month       days total mean_daily high_days verdict  
#>    <date>     <int> <dbl>      <dbl>     <int> <chr>    
#>  1 2020-01-01    10    13        1.3         0 All clear
#>  2 2020-02-01    29    89        3.1         0 All clear
#>  3 2020-03-01    31   824       26.6         0 All clear
#>  4 2020-04-01    30 15243      508.         18 Escalate 
#>  5 2020-05-01    31 18715      604.         31 Escalate 
#>  6 2020-06-01    30  9023      301.         12 Escalate 
#>  7 2020-07-01    31  8298      268.         12 Escalate 
#>  8 2020-08-01    31  4607      149.          4 All clear
#>  9 2020-09-01    30   953       31.8         0 All clear
#> 10 2020-10-01    31   250        8.1         0 All clear
#> 11 2020-11-01    30   203        6.8         0 All clear
#> 12 2020-12-01    31   381       12.3         0 All clear

Across the twelve months, high_days only ever takes the values 0, 4, 12, 18 and 31. Nothing sits between 4 and 12. Five splits the year into four escalating months and eight clear ones, and so does any cut-off from 4 up to 11. Drop to 3 and August joins the escalating group; go up to 12 and June and July leave it. The rule is stable against small changes, which is reassuring, and the data gives you no reason to prefer five over any other number in that range, which is not.
August is where it bites. Four High days, so “All clear”, on a month that recorded 4,607 cases, more than September through December put together. The rule counts days over 300 and August’s burden was distributed differently.
That is why high_cut is an argument rather than a hard-coded 5. Not because the caller will change it often, but because a number that appears in a function signature with a default is a number somebody chose, and a number buried in the body is a number nobody can find. Set it once, at the top, where a reviewer can argue with it:

month_summary(covid, "2020-08-01", high_cut = 3) %>%
  select(month, high_days, mean_daily, verdict)
#> # A tibble: 1 × 4
#>   month      high_days mean_daily verdict 
#>   <date>         <int>      <dbl> <chr>   
#> 1 2020-08-01         4       149. Escalate

title: Appendix A — Worked solutions
text:
A.17 Cumulative deaths, both ways

From the chapter on loops: difference the deaths column with an explicit for loop, then with lag(), check the two with identical(), and account for the gap against 29.

The loop is the same shape as the one the chapter wrote for confirmed:

daily_deaths_loop <- numeric(nrow(covid))

for (i in seq_along(daily_deaths_loop)) {
  if (i == 1) {
    daily_deaths_loop[i] <- covid$deaths[i]
  } else {
    daily_deaths_loop[i] <- covid$deaths[i] - covid$deaths[i - 1]
  }
}

head(daily_deaths_loop, 8)
#> [1] NA NA NA NA NA NA NA NA

Eight NAs, because deaths is missing for the first 59 days. The vectorised version:

daily_deaths_lag <- covid %>%
  mutate(dd = deaths - lag(deaths, default = 0)) %>%
  pull(dd)

identical(daily_deaths_loop, daily_deaths_lag)
#> [1] TRUE

TRUE. The two agree, including on where the NAs fall, which is the part worth checking: identical() treats NA as a value like any other, so a version that produced NA in a different place would come back FALSE even if every real number matched.
The reconciliation:

sum(daily_deaths_loop, na.rm = TRUE)
#> [1] 27

max(covid$deaths, na.rm = TRUE)
#> [1] 29

sum(is.na(daily_deaths_loop))
#> [1] 60

Twenty-seven against a final cumulative figure of 29, with 60 missing values in the differenced series.
Sixty, not 59. That is the detail to account for. deaths is NA for rows 1 to 59, and row 60, which is 21 March 2020, is the first day with a recorded value. Its difference is 2 - NA, which is NA, so the differenced series is missing for one row longer than the raw column is:

covid %>%
  slice(58:62) %>%
  select(date, deaths, daily_deaths)
#> # A tibble: 5 × 3
#>   date       deaths daily_deaths
#>   <date>      <dbl>        <dbl>
#> 1 2020-03-19     NA           NA
#> 2 2020-03-20     NA           NA
#> 3 2020-03-21      2           NA
#> 4 2020-03-22      2            0
#> 5 2020-03-23      2            0

The first recorded value is 2, not 1. Two deaths had already occurred by the time the series starts, and differencing recovers changes rather than levels, so those two are unrecoverable from this column. 29 minus 2 is 27, and the arithmetic closes.
None of that is an error in your code. It is what the file says, and the useful response is to write it down rather than to patch it. Chapter 7 shows the patch, which is a decision about whether the leading NAs mean “zero deaths so far” or “not reported”, and those two readings give different answers.

title: Appendix A — Worked solutions
section: A.18 An SIR model with an intervention
text:
A.18 An SIR model with an intervention

Also from the chapter on loops: add a circuit breaker to the SIR model between days 40 and 95, plot the infectious compartment against the unmodified run, and say what happens when the intervention lifts.

The trick is that beta does not have to be one number. Make it a vector of length days and index it inside the loop:

sir_run <- function(beta, gamma = 0.1, N = 100000, days = 150, I0 = 10) {
  if (length(beta) == 1) beta <- rep(beta, days)

  S <- numeric(days)
  I <- numeric(days)
  R <- numeric(days)

  S[1] <- N - I0
  I[1] <- I0
  R[1] <- 0

  for (t in 2:days) {
    new_infections <- beta[t - 1] * S[t - 1] * I[t - 1] / N
    new_removals   <- gamma * I[t - 1]

    S[t] <- S[t - 1] - new_infections
    I[t] <- I[t - 1] + new_infections - new_removals
    R[t] <- R[t - 1] + new_removals
  }

  tibble(day = 1:days, S = S, I = I, R = R)
}

beta_cb <- rep(0.3, 150)
beta_cb[40:95] <- 0.15

baseline     <- sir_run(0.3)
intervention <- sir_run(beta_cb)

Wrapping the loop in a function is the change that makes this exercise tractable. Two runs means two of everything, and copying the loop and editing one line in the copy is precisely the failure mode Chapter 11 is about. beta[t - 1] rather than beta[t] because the transmission that produces day t’s infections happened on day t - 1, which matches the rest of the loop’s indexing.
Both runs in one tibble, so they can be plotted together:

runs <- bind_rows(
  baseline     %>% mutate(run = "No intervention"),
  intervention %>% mutate(run = "Beta halved, days 40-95")
)

ggplot(runs, aes(x = day, y = I, colour = run)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = 40, xmax = 95, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf,
           fill = nus_colours[["muted"]], alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_comma()) +
  labs(
    x = "Day", y = "Infectious", colour = NULL,
    title = "The intervention flattens the peak and leaves a second one behind",
    caption = "Illustrative parameters. Not a model of Singapore."
  )



A 56-day reduction in transmission from day 40, against the unmodified run. Illustrative parameters, not fitted to any data.



The two questions, answered from the output rather than from what a model is supposed to do:

tibble(
  run       = c("No intervention", "Beta halved, days 40-95"),
  peak_day  = c(baseline$day[which.max(baseline$I)],
                intervention$day[which.max(intervention$I)]),
  peak_I    = round(c(max(baseline$I), max(intervention$I))),
  final_R   = round(c(tail(baseline$R, 1), tail(intervention$R, 1)))
)
#> # A tibble: 2 × 4
#>   run                     peak_day peak_I final_R
#>   <chr>                      <int>  <dbl>   <dbl>
#> 1 No intervention               55  31211   94649
#> 2 Beta halved, days 40-95       55  12072   76470

The peak gets much smaller, from about 31,200 infectious to about 12,100, and with these parameters it does not get later at all. Both peak on day 55. That surprised me the first time and it has a clean explanation: the peak occurs when susceptibles fall to \(\gamma N / \beta\), and halving \(\beta\) doubles that threshold, so the intervention run reaches its (higher) threshold at roughly the same time the baseline reaches its (lower) one. Change the dates or the depth of the intervention and the peaks separate. The generalisation “interventions delay the peak” is not something the arithmetic guarantees.
After day 95 the intervention lifts and there is a second rise:

intervention %>%
  filter(day %in% c(95, 100, 108, 120, 150)) %>%
  mutate(across(c(S, I, R), round))
#> # A tibble: 5 × 4
#>     day     S     I     R
#>   <int> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1    95 38867  4157 56976
#> 2   100 36771  4208 59021
#> 3   108 33127  4396 62477
#> 4   120 28367  4018 67615
#> 5   150 21722  1808 76470

Infections bottom out around day 95 and climb again to a local peak near day 108. The reason is in the S column. At day 95 the intervention run still has 38,867 susceptibles against the baseline’s 5,713. With \(\beta\) back at 0.3 and \(\gamma\) at 0.1, each infectious person infects more than one other while \(S/N\) stays above one third, so the epidemic restarts.
Would I have predicted it? The direction, yes, once you look at where the susceptibles are. The size, no. The final attack rate falls from 95% to 76%, so the intervention prevented about 18,000 infections in a population of 100,000 despite the rebound, which is more than the shape of the curve suggests at a glance. Suppression without immunity postpones; it does not cancel. Whether the postponement is worth it depends on what you do with the time, and that is not a question this model contains.

title: Appendix A — Worked solutions
section: A.19 Write the August 2020 situation report
text:
A.19 Write the August 2020 situation report

From the capstone chapter: the one-page report for August 2020, with a table, two figures, three sentences and a note on what the analysis cannot tell you.

August’s decision is 5 August, and everything below turns on how it gets handled. So the maximum, the median and the date of the maximum come out first, before anything else is computed:

report_month <- as.Date("2020-08-01")

august <- covid %>% filter(month == report_month)

nrow(august)
#> [1] 31

august %>%
  summarise(
    days         = n(),
    cases        = sum(daily_cases),
    mean_daily   = round(mean(daily_cases), 1),
    median_daily = median(daily_cases),
    peak         = max(daily_cases),
    peak_date    = date[which.max(daily_cases)],
    deaths       = sum(daily_deaths)
  )
#> # A tibble: 1 × 7
#>    days cases mean_daily median_daily  peak peak_date  deaths
#>   <int> <dbl>      <dbl>        <dbl> <dbl> <date>      <dbl>
#> 1    31  4607       149.           91   908 2020-08-05      0

A mean of 148.6 and a median of 91. When those two are that far apart, the mean is describing one day rather than the month. Look at the top of the distribution:

august %>%
  slice_max(daily_cases, n = 5) %>%
  select(date, daily_cases)
#> # A tibble: 5 × 2
#>   date       daily_cases
#>   <date>           <dbl>
#> 1 2020-08-05         908
#> 2 2020-08-02         313
#> 3 2020-08-01         307
#> 4 2020-08-06         301
#> 5 2020-08-04         295

908 on 5 August, and the next highest day is 313. One day carries 19.7% of the month’s cases. This is the decision the exercise refers to, and the wrong response is to delete the day. It happened, the cases were real, and MOH attributed the count to clearance testing in the dormitories picking up past infections: 903 of the 908 were dormitory residents and 581 were linked to a single cluster at Acacia Lodge. A case detected on 5 August was not necessarily an infection that occurred on 5 August, and that distinction belongs in the report, not in a filter.
So I report both figures and say why:

august %>%
  filter(date != as.Date("2020-08-05")) %>%
  summarise(
    days         = n(),
    cases        = sum(daily_cases),
    mean_daily   = round(mean(daily_cases), 1),
    median_daily = median(daily_cases),
    peak         = max(daily_cases)
  )
#> # A tibble: 1 × 5
#>    days cases mean_daily median_daily  peak
#>   <int> <dbl>      <dbl>        <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1    30  3699       123.           89   313

Without 5 August the mean falls from 148.6 to 123.3 and the median barely moves, from 91 to 89. The median was already telling you what a typical August day looked like. That is the argument for putting a median in every monthly table.
Deaths are 0 for August. The cumulative column reads 27 on 31 July and 27 on 31 August, so this is a real zero and not a gap, and August is late enough in the year that the leading NA problem in deaths does not touch it.

A.19.1 The table

august_weeks <- august %>%
  mutate(week = floor_date(date, "week", week_start = 1)) %>%
  group_by(week) %>%
  summarise(
    days         = n(),
    cases        = sum(daily_cases),
    median_daily = median(daily_cases),
    peak         = max(daily_cases),
    retail       = round(mean(retail_and_recreation_percent_change_from_baseline)),
    stringency   = round(mean(stringency_index), 1)
  )

august_weeks
#> # A tibble: 6 × 7
#>   week        days cases median_daily  peak retail stringency
#>   <date>     <int> <dbl>        <dbl> <dbl>  <dbl>      <dbl>
#> 1 2020-07-27     2   620          310   313    -20       50.9
#> 2 2020-08-03     7  2279          242   908    -22       51.7
#> 3 2020-08-10     7   643           83   188    -22       50.9
#> 4 2020-08-17     7   606           91   117    -24       51.7
#> 5 2020-08-24     7   418           54    94    -21       51.7
#> 6 2020-08-31     1    41           41    41    -21       50.9

Read days first. August 2020 began on a Saturday, so the first row covers two days and the last covers one, and comparing cases across those rows would be comparing different amounts of time. median_daily is in the table instead of a mean for the reason above, and it does the job: 310 and 242 in the first two weeks, then 83, 91, 54 and 41. The month steps down sharply after 9 August and then drifts, which is not what the cases column shows, because week two’s total is inflated by the 5 August spike.

A.19.2 The first figure

spike <- as.Date("2020-08-05")

p_aug_cases <- ggplot(august, aes(x = date, y = daily_cases)) +
  geom_col(fill = nus_colours[["blue"]]) +
  annotate("text", x = spike + 1, y = 880, hjust = 0, size = 3,
           colour = nus_colours[["crimson"]],
           label = "5 Aug: 908 cases,\n903 of them dormitory residents") +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "1 week", date_labels = "%d %b") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_comma()) +
  labs(
    title    = "One day carries a fifth of August's cases",
    subtitle = "Singapore, new COVID-19 cases reported each day, August 2020",
    x = NULL, y = "New cases reported",
    caption  = "Source: COVID-19 Data Hub. Reported cases, not infections."
  )

p_aug_cases



Daily reported cases in Singapore, August 2020.



Bars rather than a line, because 31 discrete daily counts are exactly the case where individual days matter and there is nothing measured in between. The annotation does the work that a footnote would otherwise have to do, and the title makes a claim rather than naming the axes.

A.19.3 The second figure
The case curve says what was reported. The second figure has to answer a different question, and in August the interesting one is whether anything else changed while cases fell:

august_mobility <- august %>%
  select(
    date,
    `Retail and recreation` = retail_and_recreation_percent_change_from_baseline,
    Workplaces              = workplaces_percent_change_from_baseline
  ) %>%
  pivot_longer(-date, names_to = "series", values_to = "change")

ggplot(august_mobility, aes(x = date, y = change, colour = series)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = nus_colours[["muted"]], linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_line() +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "1 week", date_labels = "%d %b") +
  labs(
    title    = "Cases fell through August; movement did not move",
    subtitle = "Percent change from Google's 3 January to 6 February 2020 baseline",
    x = NULL, y = "Change from baseline (%)", colour = NULL,
    caption  = "The 10 August workplace trough is National Day observed, a public holiday."
  )



Retail and workplace mobility in August 2020, as percent change from Google’s pre-pandemic baseline.



Retail sits between 15% and 27% below baseline all month with no trend in it. Workplaces oscillate with the week, and the one deep trough, 73% below baseline on 10 August, is National Day observed rather than anything epidemiological. Stringency moves almost as little: 50.93 on 28 of the 31 days, with three scattered days at 56.48 that are exactly the one-day ticks Chapter 10 warns against reading as announcements.
The weekly median more than halved while neither of those series went anywhere. That constrains the explanations available and it does not identify a cause, which is a sentence worth writing down rather than talking yourself out of.

A.19.4 The three sentences

August recorded 4,607 cases across 31 complete days and no deaths, with the median daily count falling from 248 in July to 91, and 4 of its days above 300 against July’s 12.


One day, 5 August, accounts for 908 of those cases, nearly a fifth of the month, and MOH attributed that day’s figures to clearance testing in the dormitories detecting past infections, so August’s mean of 148.6 falls to 123.3 when that day is set aside while the median barely moves.


Retail mobility held between 15% and 27% below baseline for the whole month and the stringency index sat at 50.93 on 28 of the 31 days, so August’s decline in reported cases came without any measurable change in movement and with policy essentially unchanged.

Three sentences, three jobs. The first sizes the month and states the denominator. The second addresses the thing a reader would otherwise get wrong. The third brings in the second data source and reports what it rules out.

A.19.5 What this analysis does not tell you
It cannot separate a fall in transmission from a fall in testing. There is no test-count column in this file, so test positivity is not computable. August’s declining curve is consistent with fewer infections and it is also consistent with the dormitory testing programme winding down after clearance was completed. Those are different worlds and this file does not distinguish them.
The 5 August spike is a dating problem as well as an outlier. Cases reported that day include infections that occurred earlier, so the shape of August’s curve is partly an artifact of when swabs were processed. Every weekly comparison in the table above inherits that.
The national total is still averaging two epidemics. Through August the dormitory outbreak and community transmission had different sizes and different testing intensities, and this file carries one number for both. Every mean in this report is a weighted average with weights that are not in the data.
Flat mobility is weak evidence about the population that mattered. This is my reading rather than something the file establishes. Google’s mobility series come from location history on phones where that setting is switched on, and Google does not publish them broken down by nationality or work-permit status. Whether the movement of people in dormitories under quarantine appears in these curves at all is unanswerable from here, so I would not use the flat retail line to say anything about behaviour inside the dormitories, which is where 903 of the 908 cases on the month’s biggest day were recorded.

title: Appendix B — The data
text:
B.1 Where it came from
Three sources, stitched together into one rectangle.
The case and death counts come from the COVID-19 Data Hub (Guidotti and Ardia, 2020), an R package and web service that collects national COVID-19 reporting into a single schema, so that a query for Singapore returns columns with the same names as a query for Italy. The Hub does not generate numbers. It collects what national authorities publish, sometimes by way of an intermediate aggregator, and reshapes it. For Singapore the chain ends at the Ministry of Health’s daily reporting. If you need to say exactly which feed the Hub was reading on a given date, that is documented country by country on the Hub’s own site, and that documentation, rather than this appendix, is what you should cite.
The three index columns are the Oxford COVID-19 Government Response Tracker, usually written OxCGRT (Hale et al., 2021). A team of coders read government announcements and scored each country each day on a fixed list of policy indicators: school closures, workplace closures, restrictions on gatherings, testing policy, contact tracing, income support, and so on. The indices are weighted averages of those indicator scores, rescaled to run from 0 to 100. In this extract they range from 19.44 to 82.41.
The six mobility columns are Google’s COVID-19 Community Mobility Reports, built from location history for users who had that setting switched on. Each value is a percentage change against a baseline, and the definition of the baseline is the single most important thing to know about these columns. It is the median value for that day of the week over the five weeks from 3 January to 6 February 2020. Not a single day, not the whole of January, and not a rolling window. Google stopped updating the reports in October 2022, so these series will never be revised again.
Google’s column names are passed through unchanged, which is why they are 50 characters long and end in percent_change_from_baseline. You will be typing them a lot. Tab completion in RStudio exists for exactly this reason.

title: Appendix B — The data
text:
B.1.1 Citing the sources
If you use this data in coursework or a paper, cite the sources, not the book.

Guidotti, E. and Ardia, D. (2020). COVID-19 Data Hub. Journal of Open Source Software, 5(51), 2376. https://doi.org/10.21105/joss.02376


Hale, T., Angrist, N., Goldszmidt, R., Kira, B., Petherick, A., Phillips, T., Webster, S., Cameron-Blake, E., Hallas, L., Majumdar, S. and Tatlow, H. (2021). A global panel database of pandemic policies (Oxford COVID-19 Government Response Tracker). Nature Human Behaviour, 5, 529–538. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41562-021-01079-w


Google LLC. Google COVID-19 Community Mobility Reports. https://www.google.com/covid19/mobility/


B.1.2 Regenerating it
The file in this repository is a frozen snapshot with 13 of the Hub’s columns kept. A full query returns a good deal more: testing and vaccination counts, hospital and ICU occupancy where a country reported them, population, and a set of identifier codes. Thirteen is what fits on a screen, and a beginner’s first data frame should fit on a screen.

# install.packages("COVID19")
library(COVID19)
sg <- covid19(country = "Singapore", level = 1)

Run that today and you will not get this file back byte for byte. Countries revise historical counts long after the fact, and the Hub’s own upstream source for a given country has changed over the years. That is normal rather than corruption, and it is a large part of why the snapshot lives in the repository instead of being downloaded at render time. A book whose numbers move under it is not a book you can teach from.

title: Appendix B — The data
text:
B.2 What one row is
One row is one calendar day in Singapore. Nothing finer, nothing coarser.

range(covid$date)
#> [1] "2020-01-22" "2020-12-31"
n_distinct(covid$date)
#> [1] 345
all(diff(covid$date) == 1)
#> [1] TRUE

345 rows, 345 distinct dates, and every consecutive difference is exactly one day. No gaps, no duplicates, nothing to reconcile. That is unusual enough in real epidemiological data that it is worth naming: most surveillance extracts you meet later will have missing days, repeated days, or both, and the check above is the one to run first.
The series opens on 22 January 2020, the day before the count moves off zero.

covid %>%
  select(date, confirmed, deaths) %>%
  head(4)
#> # A tibble: 4 × 3
#>   date       confirmed deaths
#>   <date>         <dbl>  <dbl>
#> 1 2020-01-22         0     NA
#> 2 2020-01-23         1     NA
#> 3 2020-01-24         3     NA
#> 4 2020-01-25         3     NA

administrative_area_level_1 is the Hub’s name for the top administrative level, which for a city-state is the whole country. It is constant.

count(covid, administrative_area_level_1)
#> # A tibble: 1 × 2
#>   administrative_area_level_1     n
#>   <chr>                       <int>
#> 1 Singapore                     345

It is kept because dropping it would hide the fact that the Hub’s schema has a geography column at all, and because a student who later pulls three countries and forgets to group by this column will produce a very confident, very wrong national total.

title: Appendix B — The data
text:
B.3 The counts are cumulative
confirmed and deaths are running totals, not daily counts. Every day’s value includes every previous day’s.

covid %>%
  select(date, confirmed) %>%
  tail(3)
#> # A tibble: 3 × 2
#>   date       confirmed
#>   <date>         <dbl>
#> 1 2020-12-29     58542
#> 2 2020-12-30     58569
#> 3 2020-12-31     58599

58,599 is the total number of confirmed cases in Singapore in 2020, not the number on 31 December. The number on 31 December is 30, and you get it by subtracting the previous row. That subtraction is what lag() is for, and it is done in the transform chapter.
Two consequences follow, and both bite people.
The first is that a plot of confirmed against date is a monotone rising line for any epidemic anywhere. It cannot show you a peak, a wave, or a circuit breaker, because it never goes down. It looks informative and tells you almost nothing about tempo.
The second is arithmetic. max(confirmed) is the annual total. sum(confirmed) is a number with no meaning at all, and R will compute it for you without a murmur.

% change vs baseline

That last row is not a typo. Five of the six mobility series count visitors to a category of place. The residential series measures duration instead, because almost everyone is at home for some part of almost every day, so a visitor count would be flat and useless. The consequence is that residential moves on a much smaller scale than the others: everybody sleeping two hours more at home is a large behavioural change and a small percentage change in total hours. Do not put residential on the same axis as workplaces and read the sizes across.
Now the computed part. Missing counts and observed ranges, straight from the file:

column_summary <- tibble(
  column   = names(covid),
  missing  = map_int(covid, ~ sum(is.na(.x))),
  smallest = map_chr(covid, ~ if (is.numeric(.x)) format(min(.x, na.rm = TRUE)) else "-"),
  largest  = map_chr(covid, ~ if (is.numeric(.x)) format(max(.x, na.rm = TRUE)) else "-")
)

print(column_summary, n = 13)
#> # A tibble: 13 × 4
#>    column                                             missing smallest largest
#>    <chr>                                                <int> <chr>    <chr>  
#>  1 administrative_area_level_1                              0 -        -      
#>  2 confirmed                                                0 0        58599  
#>  3 deaths                                                  59 2        29     
#>  4 date                                                     0 -        -      
#>  5 stringency_index                                         0 19.44    82.41  
#>  6 government_response_index                                0 19.27    78.65  
#>  7 containment_health_index                                 0 22.02    79.17  
#>  8 retail_and_recreation_percent_change_from_baseline      24 -70      -4     
#>  9 grocery_and_pharmacy_percent_change_from_baseline       24 -35      23     
#> 10 parks_percent_change_from_baseline                      24 -73      35     
#> 11 transit_stations_percent_change_from_baseline           24 -75      -9     
#> 12 workplaces_percent_change_from_baseline                 24 -83      5      
#> 13 residential_percent_change_from_baseline                24 5        55

Read the deaths row carefully. Its smallest observed value is 2, not 0 and not 1. That is not a typo, and the next section is about why.
The mobility columns are whole numbers. Google rounds to the nearest percent before publishing, so a change of 0.4 percentage points and a change of 0 look identical in this file. The three indices carry two decimal places.

title: Appendix B — The data
text:
B.5 Missing values
There are exactly three missingness patterns in this file, and each has a different cause.
Six columns are complete. administrative_area_level_1, confirmed, date and the three indices have no NA at all. OxCGRT coded Singapore every day of 2020, including the many days when nothing changed, which is why the indices are complete while everything around them has holes.
deaths has 59 missing values, all at the start. The Hub carries no death figure for Singapore until 21 March 2020.

covid %>%
  select(date, confirmed, deaths) %>%
  slice(58:62)
#> # A tibble: 5 × 3
#>   date       confirmed deaths
#>   <date>         <dbl>  <dbl>
#> 1 2020-03-19       345     NA
#> 2 2020-03-20       385     NA
#> 3 2020-03-21       432      2
#> 4 2020-03-22       455      2
#> 5 2020-03-23       509      2

The first recorded value is 2, on a day when nothing in the file says whether that 2 arrived as one death plus one death, or as two deaths at once, or as a backfill of earlier events that were never reported daily. Whatever happened, the file cannot tell you. So if you difference deaths to recover daily deaths, the first two of Singapore’s 29 deaths in 2020 are outside the differencing window and you recover 27.

sum(diff(na.omit(covid$deaths)))
#> [1] 27
max(covid$deaths, na.rm = TRUE)
#> [1] 29

Twenty-seven against twenty-nine. That gap is small and real, and if you report daily deaths from this file you should say so in a footnote rather than hope nobody adds them up.
All six mobility columns have 24 missing values, on the same 24 days.

covid %>%
  summarise(
    any_missing = sum(if_any(ends_with("_baseline"), is.na)),
    all_missing = sum(if_all(ends_with("_baseline"), is.na))
  )
#> # A tibble: 1 × 2
#>   any_missing all_missing
#>         <int>       <int>
#> 1          24          24

any_missing and all_missing are both 24, which tells you the six columns go missing together rather than independently. They are the first 24 rows of the file:

covid %>%
  filter(is.na(parks_percent_change_from_baseline)) %>%
  summarise(n = n(), first = min(date), last = max(date))
#> # A tibble: 1 × 3
#>       n first      last      
#>   <int> <date>     <date>    
#> 1    24 2020-01-22 2020-02-14

22 January to 14 February 2020. The reason is the baseline definition. Google measures each day against the median for that weekday over 3 January to 6 February, and there is no honest way to publish a comparison for a day that falls inside, or before the end of, the period you are comparing against. The mobility series start after the baseline window closes.

covid %>%
  select(date,
         retail = retail_and_recreation_percent_change_from_baseline,
         parks  = parks_percent_change_from_baseline,
         work   = workplaces_percent_change_from_baseline) %>%
  slice(22:27)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 4
#>   date       retail parks  work
#>   <date>      <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1 2020-02-12     NA    NA    NA
#> 2 2020-02-13     NA    NA    NA
#> 3 2020-02-14     NA    NA    NA
#> 4 2020-02-15    -14   -10    -4
#> 5 2020-02-16    -19   -18    -7
#> 6 2020-02-17    -12    -7    -4

That is the seam. Nothing on 14 February, real numbers on 15 February.
One practical trap follows from it. January is entirely inside the missing window, so any January-only summary of a mobility column has nothing to average, and na.rm = TRUE does not save you:

covid %>%
  filter(date < as.Date("2020-02-01")) %>%
  summarise(
    mean_retail = mean(retail_and_recreation_percent_change_from_baseline, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
#> # A tibble: 1 × 1
#>   mean_retail
#>         <dbl>
#> 1         NaN

NaN, not NA and not an error. na.rm = TRUE removed every value, mean() divided zero by zero, and R returned the IEEE answer for that. It will propagate silently through everything downstream. The missing-data chapter goes into this properly.

title: Appendix B — The data
section: B.6 What this file cannot tell you
text:
B.6 What this file cannot tell you
It has no ages, no sexes, no nationalities, no residency or work-permit status, no clusters, no test counts, no split between imported and locally transmitted cases, and no split between dormitory and community cases. Every question of that shape has to go somewhere else.
That absence shapes what you can honestly say. The migrant-worker dormitory outbreak dominates Singapore’s case counts from April to August 2020, and you can see its shape in confirmed clearly enough. What you cannot do is quantify it from this file, because there is no column that separates it out.
The mobility columns need the same caution and it is harder to apply. Google built these series from users who had Location History switched on, which is a self-selected slice of everyone in the country. My own reading is that the population living in purpose-built dormitories, roughly 200,000 people across the 43 large dormitories, is likely to be represented differently from the general population in a measure built that way: device ownership and account settings vary, and the categories Google reports are ordinary consumer destinations. Google does not publish these series broken down by nationality or permit status, so there is no way to check any of that from the data. Read the previous sentence but one as my inference with the mechanism stated, not as an established finding.

title: Appendix B — The data
section: B.7 Quirks worth knowing before you plot anything
text:
B.7 Quirks worth knowing before you plot anything
5 August 2020 shows 908 new cases. August’s median is 91 and the next highest day in August is 313, so this single point rescales any August axis you draw. It came out of dormitory clearance testing. MOH reported that 903 of the 908 were dormitory residents, and that 581 were linked to a single cluster at Acacia Lodge, and its account of the clearance-testing programme was that it was detecting past infections as well as current ones. Treat the day as a reporting event, describe the mechanism the way MOH described it, and stop there.
The indices are step functions. OxCGRT scores change on the day a policy changes and then sit flat, sometimes for weeks. stringency_index takes only 13 distinct values across the whole year. A line plot of it is a staircase, and any smoothing you apply is inventing intermediate values that never existed.
Small index movements are not evidence of much. There are 23 changes in stringency_index after 1 July alone, most of them tiny, and the coding of a single indicator being revised looks exactly the same in the data as a real policy shift. A one-day tick is not a policy announcement. If you want to attribute a movement to a decision, go and find the decision.
The mobility series have a strong weekly cycle. Workplaces drop every weekend and every public holiday, by a lot. Comparing a Tuesday with a Sunday tells you which day of the week it is. Google’s baseline is computed per weekday partly to control for this, but the residual cycle is still the largest signal in several of these columns, and it will drown whatever you were actually looking for unless you handle it.
The deepest workplace drops in the whole year are holidays, not policy. The eight lowest days are Good Friday, Labour Day, Vesak Day, the observed Hari Raya Puasa holiday, the observed National Day holiday, polling day for the 2020 general election, Hari Raya Haji, and Christmas Day. If you find yourself explaining one of those troughs with an epidemiological story, check the calendar first.

title: Appendix C — How this book is built
text:
C.1 The repository
Two of those directories are generated and both are in version control anyway, which is unusual enough that it gets its own section further down.
One file per chapter, and the chapter list in _quarto.yml is the only place the reading order is written down. Renaming a file means editing _quarto.yml, and forgetting to means the chapter silently disappears from the book while still sitting in the repository. It is the most common way to lose a page.

title: Appendix C — How this book is built
text:
C.2 _quarto.yml, section by section
The whole build is one YAML file. It opens with a warning to future me:
# Verified against Quarto 1.4.554. The project: and book: schemas are closed,
# so an unrecognised key there is a hard render failure — check
# /Applications/quarto/share/schema/definitions.yml before adding one.
That is worth reading twice. Under project: and book:, Quarto validates keys against a fixed schema. A typo does not get ignored, and it does not warn. The render stops. The schema files shipped with your Quarto installation are the authority, and they are more reliable than a blog post about a different version.

C.2.1 project:

project:
  type: book
  output-dir: docs
  execute-dir: project
  resources:
    - .nojekyll
type: book is what turns a folder of .qmd files into a numbered book with parts, appendices, previous and next links, and a single search index.
output-dir: docs writes the rendered site into docs/ rather than the default _book/. That one word is the entire publishing strategy, and there is a section on it below.
execute-dir: project sets R’s working directory to the project root for every chunk in every chapter. Without it, each chapter would execute in its own directory, which is fine here because every file sits at the top level, but stops being fine the moment anyone puts a chapter in a subfolder. Setting it means here::here("data", "sg_covid_data.csv") resolves identically from every chapter, including this one.
resources: lists files to copy into docs/ on every project render. .nojekyll is an empty file whose entire job is explained in the publishing section.

C.2.2 book:

Metadata first: title, subtitle, author, date: today with an explicit date-format, and a description that becomes the page’s meta description and the social preview text.
site-url and repo-url together are what make the “Edit this page”, “Report an issue” and “View source” links work. repo-actions: [edit, issue, source] turns all three on. They appear in the right-hand margin of every page, and they are the cheapest error-reporting mechanism a teaching resource can have. A student who spots a wrong number is two clicks from telling me, and one of those clicks lands them in a text editor with the offending line in front of them.
repo-branch: main matters because Quarto builds the edit URL from it. Point it at a branch that does not exist and every edit link 404s, on every page, silently.
Then the reading conveniences: search: true, reader-mode: true (the button that collapses both sidebars), page-navigation: true and back-to-top-navigation: true.
The sidebar is docked rather than floating, collapsed to one level so the parts are visible but the sections are not, and carries two tools: a link to the source on GitHub, and a direct download link for the CSV. The download link points at raw.githubusercontent.com, not at the repository page, so it downloads the file instead of showing a preview of it.

C.2.3 chapters: and appendices:

  chapters:
    - index.qmd
    - part: "Before you write any code"
      chapters:
        - setup.qmd
        - good-practice.qmd
The parts are headings in the sidebar and nothing else; they carry no files of their own. index.qmd sits outside any part because a book’s front page is not a chapter.
appendices: is a separate list, and Quarto numbers it separately: chapters get 1, 2, 3, appendices get A, B, C, D. The crossref: appendix-title: "Appendix" setting at the bottom of the file is what makes a reference to one of them read “Appendix B” rather than just “B”.

C.2.4 page-footer:

The footer carries the three institutional logos as a raw HTML block, plus the licence on the left and the Quarto credit and issue link on the right. The logos are <img> tags pointing at assets/logos/, styled by a .footer-logos rule in scss/nus.scss. They are raster PNGs rather than SVGs because that is the artwork as supplied, and redrawing an institution’s mark is not a thing to do casually.

C.2.5 format:

format:
  html:
    theme: [litera, scss/nus.scss]
Bootswatch litera underneath, the project’s own SCSS on top. litera was chosen for a reason that has nothing to do with taste: it is one of the few bundled themes that does not fetch a web font from fonts.googleapis.com. The book renders the same on a plane as it does on a fast connection. For a course whose first session is often held on university wifi, that is worth more than a nicer typeface.
The rest of the HTML block, in the order it appears:
toc: true with toc-depth: 3 and a custom toc-title. number-sections: true, so sections can be referenced by number. anchor-sections: true gives every heading a link target, which is what lets me point a student at one paragraph rather than a chapter. smooth-scroll: true is cosmetic.
code-copy: true puts a copy button on every code block. code-overflow: wrap wraps long lines instead of adding a horizontal scrollbar, because a line that scrolls off the right edge on a phone is a line nobody reads.
code-link: true is the good one. It turns every function call in every code block into a link to that function’s documentation, so filter() in a chunk is clickable and lands on the dplyr reference page. It needs downlit and xml2 installed. Neither is called by name anywhere in the book, so both are in the lockfile only because _dependencies.R names them, which is a trap the renv section comes back to.
code-annotations: hover is how the numbered callouts in code blocks behave.
df-print: default is a deliberate refusal. Set it to kable and every data frame in the book renders as a tidy HTML table with proper borders. It would look better. It would also look nothing like what the student sees in their own console, and a beginner comparing the book to their screen would conclude they had done something wrong. Console output stays console output.
Figures: fig-width: 7, fig-height: 4.2, fig-align: center, fig-format: svg. SVG because plot text stays sharp at any zoom and the files are usually smaller than PNG for this kind of chart. tbl-cap-location: bottom follows the usual convention of captions below tables and above figures.

C.2.6 execute: and why chapters must not fight it
execute:
  freeze: auto
  echo: true
  warning: true
  message: true
Warnings and messages are on, globally and on purpose. read_csv()’s column specification, geom_histogram()’s note about picking 30 bins, and summarise()’s .groups notice are all messages, and the book teaches students to read all three. A chapter that sets message: false to make its output tidy is deleting the lesson.
Because these are set globally, chapters should not set them again. Repeating #| echo: true on a chunk is harmless but noisy; repeating it inconsistently is how a chapter ends up with three different behaviours for no reason anybody can reconstruct later. The same goes for comment, collapse, and the figure dimensions, all of which are set once in the knitr: block at the bottom:
knitr:
  opts_chunk:
    comment: "#>"
    collapse: true
    dev: "svg"
comment: "#>" prefixes every line of output. It means you can select a whole block, code and output together, paste it into your console, and have it run: the output lines are comments. collapse: true puts code and its output in one block rather than two.
Two per-chunk options are used, and only these two. #| eval: false for anything that must not run during a render, which means install.packages(), renv:: calls, setwd() demonstrations, View(). #| error: true for chunks that are supposed to fail, where the error message is the point.

title: Appendix C — How this book is built
text:
C.3 _common.R

Every chapter opens with the same four lines:
```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
source("_common.R")
```
include: false hides the chunk and its output. The reader never sees it.
The repetition is not laziness. Quarto’s freeze machinery gives each chapter its own R session, which is what makes a single chapter re-renderable without re-running the whole book. A variable created in chapter 4 does not exist in chapter 5. So anything more than one chapter needs has to be defined in a file that every chapter sources, and _common.R is that file. It attaches the packages, sets the ggplot2 theme, defines read_covid() and covid_daily(), and runs the guard described in the next section.
The leading underscore is a Quarto convention: files and directories starting with _ are not treated as book content and are not copied to the output.

title: Appendix C — How this book is built
section: C.4 renv, and the one that will get you
text:
C.4 renv, and the one that will get you
renv records the exact version of every package the book was built with. It does this in renv.lock, a JSON file with one entry per package:
    "here": {
      "Package": "here",
      "Version": "1.0.2",
      "Source": "Repository",
      ...
      "Repository": "CRAN"
    },
(Trimmed. Each real entry also carries the package’s title, licence, dependencies and maintainer.)
The lockfile is a manifest, not a copy of the packages. It is a few hundred kB of text that says which versions to go and get.

lock <- renv::lockfile_read()
lock$R$Version
#> [1] "4.6.1"
length(lock$Packages)
#> [1] 109

109 packages, for a book whose _common.R calls library() four times. Almost all of them are dependencies of dependencies, which is the honest reason to use a lockfile at all: nobody can hold that graph in their head, and “install the tidyverse” resolves to a different set of versions every month.
The three commands you need:
renv::restore() reads the lockfile and installs exactly those versions into renv/library. This is the first thing to run in a fresh clone. It takes a few minutes once.
renv::status() compares what is installed against what is recorded, and tells you which way they disagree.
renv::snapshot() writes the current state back into the lockfile. Run it after adding a package, and commit the resulting diff along with the change that needed it.
The library itself is not in version control. renv writes and maintains renv/.gitignore for you:
library/
local/
cellar/
lock/
python/
sandbox/
staging/
renv.lock, renv/activate.R and renv/settings.json are tracked. Those three plus the ignore rules are what makes a clean checkout reproducible without committing several hundred megabytes of compiled code.
.Rprofile is one line, and renv wrote it:
source("renv/activate.R")
R runs .Rprofile from the working directory at startup. That line activates the project library, and it is the whole mechanism.

C.4.1 _dependencies.R

renv finds dependencies by scanning source files for library() calls. Its scanner automatically adds rmarkdown when it sees .Rmd files, but not for .qmd. This book has no .Rmd files, so without intervention renv::snapshot() leaves knitr and rmarkdown out of the lockfile entirely, and a clean checkout fails to render with an error that points nowhere near the cause.
_dependencies.R is a file that exists only to be scanned. It is never sourced and never rendered. It lists the packages the chapters use plus the ones the toolchain needs but nothing calls by name: knitr, rmarkdown, downlit, xml2, sessioninfo. If you add a package to a chapter, add it there too, or it will work on your machine and nowhere else.

C.4.2 The gotcha
This is the one that cost me an evening.
Quarto decides which renv to activate by reading .Rprofile relative to the directory you invoked it from, not relative to the project you asked it to render. So this is fine:
cd ~/r-intro
quarto render
and this is not:
cd ~/sph5421-course      # another R project, with its own .Rprofile and its own renv
quarto render ../r-intro
The second one starts R in ~/sph5421-course, reads that project’s .Rprofile, activates that project’s library, and then renders this book against whatever versions happen to be sitting there. execute-dir: project moves the working directory afterwards, so here() and every relative path still work, and the render completes.
That is what makes it dangerous. The versions in a neighbouring project are usually close enough that most of the book builds, and you find out three chapters later when a dplyr deprecation warning appears on a page that never had one.
So _common.R checks, before it does anything else:
local({
  proj <- getwd()
  while (!file.exists(file.path(proj, "_quarto.yml")) && dirname(proj) != proj) {
    proj <- dirname(proj)
  }
  expected <- normalizePath(file.path(proj, "renv", "library"), mustWork = FALSE)
  active   <- normalizePath(.libPaths()[1], mustWork = FALSE)

  if (!startsWith(active, expected)) {
    stop(
      "Wrong package library.\n",
      "  active:   ", active, "\n",
      "  expected: ", expected, "/...\n",
      "Run `quarto render` from the project root (", proj, ").",
      call. = FALSE
    )
  }
})
It walks up from the working directory until it finds _quarto.yml, works out where that project’s library ought to be, and compares it against the library R is actually using. When they disagree the render stops on the first chapter with:
Error: Wrong package library.
  active:   /Users/you/sph5421-course/renv/library/macos/R-4.6/aarch64-apple-darwin25.4.0
  expected: /Users/you/r-intro/renv/library/...
Run `quarto render` from the project root (/Users/you/r-intro).
The two paths will be yours. The fix is always the same: cd into the project root and render from there.
Here is the library this page was built against:

.libPaths()[1]
#> [1] "/Users/swapnil/Documents/GitHub/r-intro/renv/library/macos/R-4.6/aarch64-apple-darwin25.4.0"

If that path does not contain r-intro/renv, the guard has a bug, which would also be worth an issue.

title: Appendix C — How this book is built
text:
C.5 Freeze
freeze: auto means a chapter’s R code is executed when the chapter’s .qmd changes, and not otherwise. The output of every chunk is cached under _freeze/, and _freeze/ is committed.
The payoff is that anyone can clone the repository and rebuild the site without R, without renv, and without the several minutes of computation. It also means a one-word fix to chapter 9 does not re-execute chapters 1 through 8, which turns a two-minute render into a five-second one and is the difference between previewing your changes and not bothering.
The cost is a trap. Freeze watches the .qmd file, not the things it depends on. Edit _common.R, change the colour palette in R/nus_theme.R, or replace the CSV, and nothing re-runs. The book will render happily and every page will still show the old output. There is no warning, because from Quarto’s point of view nothing changed.
There is no command-line flag to force it. When you have changed something shared, delete the cache:
rm -rf _freeze/
quarto render
or delete one chapter’s directory under _freeze/ if you know that only one is affected. Doing this after any change to _common.R is a habit worth building, and the reason _freeze/ is listed in .gitattributes as generated is that the resulting diff is enormous and nobody should read it.
crumbs: C  How this book is built

title: Appendix C — How this book is built
text:
C.6 Publishing
The site is rendered locally into docs/, and docs/ is committed. GitHub Pages is configured to deploy from a branch: main, folder /docs. Push, wait a minute, done. There is no CI workflow, no gh-pages branch, and no build step on anybody’s server.
That is not the fashionable choice. The alternative is quarto publish gh-pages, or a GitHub Action that installs R, restores renv, renders, and pushes. Both are better for a project with several contributors. This one is better here for two reasons. The rendered page and the source that produced it land in the same commit, so git log on a chapter shows you exactly what the site looked like at every point. And there is no CI to break: a course resource that stops publishing in the middle of teaching week because an action’s Ubuntu image changed is a worse failure than a slightly larger repository.
.nojekyll is the other half. GitHub Pages runs Jekyll over your site by default, and Jekyll ignores every file and directory whose name begins with an underscore. Quarto’s HTML output is full of them. An empty .nojekyll file at the root turns Jekyll off entirely, and listing it under project: resources: is what copies it into docs/ on every render, including after quarto render cleans the output directory. Miss it and the site deploys with no CSS, which looks exactly like a broken theme and is not.

C.6.1 The leading slash in .gitignore

# The leading slash is load-bearing. An unanchored `*_files/` also matches
# docs/<chapter>_files/, which is where every rendered figure lives — the site
# would look right locally and ship with every image broken.
/*_files/
Knitr writes a chapter’s figures into <chapter>_files/ next to the source, and those working directories are rubbish that should not be in git. The obvious rule is *_files/.
The obvious rule is wrong. A pattern with no slash at the start matches at any depth, so *_files/ also matches docs/visualise_files/, docs/groups_files/, and every other directory in the rendered site that holds the actual published images. Git would ignore all of them. You would render, see a perfect site on localhost, commit, push, and get a live site where every plot is a broken-image icon. Nothing in your local build would ever show the problem.
The leading slash anchors the pattern to the repository root, so it matches ./visualise_files/ and stops there. One character.
.gitattributes finishes the job, marking both generated directories so they stay out of GitHub’s language statistics and out of diffs:
docs/** linguist-generated=true
docs/** -diff
_freeze/** linguist-generated=true
_freeze/** -diff
Without that, GitHub reads the repository as mostly HTML and JavaScript rather than R, and a one-line prose fix arrives as a pull request with thousands of changed lines.

title: Appendix C — How this book is built
text:
C.7 Forking it
The licence says you can, so here is how.
git clone https://github.com/CERM-NUS/r-intro.git my-course
cd my-course
Open r-intro.Rproj in RStudio. The .Rproj file keeps its old name after a clone, so rename it now if the old one will confuse you later. Then, in the R console:
renv::restore()
Answer yes. Go and make coffee. When it finishes, from a terminal in that directory:
quarto preview
That builds the book and opens it in a browser with live reload: save a .qmd and the page updates. It is the right mode for writing. quarto render is the right mode for publishing.
Four things to change before you publish your version:
_quarto.yml needs a new site-url, repo-url and probably repo-branch, or every edit link on your site will point at mine.
The logos in assets/logos/ have to go, or be replaced with your own. They are the trade marks of NUS, the Saw Swee Hock School of Public Health, CERM and the ML & GHN network, and the MIT licence on the text and code does not cover them. Remove the page-footer HTML block along with the files.
LICENSE should keep the original copyright line if you keep any of the original text, and add yours.
If you swap the dataset, _common.R is the only place that reads it, but data.qmd documents the columns of this file and will be wrong the moment you change it. Rewrite that appendix or delete it. An out-of-date data appendix is worse than none.
Then render, commit docs/ and _freeze/ along with your sources, push, and switch on Pages for /docs.
